#6375. Blood Rain Has Terrified People for Thousands of Years. The Culprit Might Be Growing on Lamp Posts.

From Tennessee's 1841 flesh shower to Kerala’s crimson monsoon, the sky has some explaining to do—unless the source isn’t coming from on high.

On an August afternoon in 1841, something ominous fell from the sky near Lebanon, Tennessee. Two enslaved people working in a tobacco field were horrified when they heard a pattering on the leaves around them, followed by what appeared to be blood raining down from the heavens. With that blood came putrid chunks of flesh and fat, turning the field into a scene from the apocalypse.

The farm’s owner reported the event to his neighbors, and samples soon made their way to the scientist and collector Gerard Troost. In his report in The American Journal of Science, Troost wrote that “some particles appeared to have been clear blood uncombined with anything else; others, blood united with muscular fiber and fat.” He had no doubt that the substance was animal matter that “belongs to our globe” and hadn’t fallen from the heavens. He believed it could have come only from the shredded carcass of an animal, though he couldn’t tell which kind. When he soaked some of the matter in water, he could make out reddish-brown muscle fibers that he said looked much like dried beef, along with “a distinct smell of animal matter in a state of putrefaction.”

Not everyone was satisfied with a scientific answer. As Popular Science recently recounted, one Wisconsin newspaper reported that some Northerners saw the shower as a judgment from heaven against the slavery that still plagued much of the antebellum South. Troost, for his part, hypothesized that a powerful wind had swept up part of a decomposing animal and carried it into an electrically charged storm cloud, where it “was kept in a state of partial fluidity or viscosity.” He also cited earlier unexpected showers of particles that had been mistaken for sulfur. Despite the limits of mid-19th-century science, Troost was partly right. Lebanon’s shower wasn’t the first blood rain, or even the first rain of flesh and blood. The phenomenon goes back thousands of years, and science now offers several plausible explanations for it.

Blood showers (with or without flesh) appear in texts as old as The Iliad and the Bible. Some were explained by superstition and folklore, while skeptics looked for a natural cause they couldn’t find. These accounts echo reports of frogs and fish raining from the sky, which once seemed just as inexplicable. Today, meteorologists have a more down-to-earth answer. The 1997 reference work Complete Weather Resource explains that such creatures, and almost anything else once seen as heavenly vengeance, can be caught up in a whirlwind or tornadic waterspout. A waterspout forms when a column of low-pressure air spins violently over a body of water. Powerful updrafts inside its funnel can pull up water, and whatever is in it, then carry it aloft and drop it somewhere else.

Lebanon has several lakes nearby today, but they’re 20th-century reservoirs made long after this “blood rain.” In 1841, the closest large body of water was the Cumberland River, several miles to the north, but that distance shouldn’t rule out a waterspout, because these storms can carry what they pick up for miles. Alternatively, if vultures had left a carcass nearby, an ordinary whirlwind could have done the job. Unfortunately, the event happened more than a century before weather satellites could have captured it. No one can say for certain whether a tornado, a tornadic waterspout, or hurricane-force winds (which can also carry some unexpected things) dropped rotting flesh onto the tobacco field. Any strong enough updraft could have been behind it. Wild weather offers a plausible explanation for globs of flesh falling from the sky, but many blood rains have fallen with no flesh at all. That raises a different question: what turns rain red?

For much of history, the answer was religious. A decade before the Lebanon shower, in 1831, the enslaved preacher and carpenter Nat Turner had visions he took as signs from God, including “drops of blood on the corn, as though it were dew from heaven.” Later he found hieroglyphic marks written in blood on leaves in the woods. Soon afterward, he led a rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia, in which his followers killed about 55 white people. In the backlash, militias and mobs killed an unknown number of enslaved and free Black people. Was the blood rain in Lebanon another such omen?

Modern science suggests a less ominous answer. During the 2001 monsoon season, crimson rain fell on and off across Kerala, India. Physicist Godfrey Louis examined samples under a microscope and found what looked like biological cells. He argued that they were alien microbes released by a comet that broke apart in the atmosphere. However, a government-commissioned investigation found that they were spores of Trentepohlia, a reddish-orange alga that grows abundantly on trees, rocks, and even lamp posts in the region. When researchers grew samples of local lichen in the lab, they produced the same alga found in the rainwater. The spores didn’t come from space or from thousands of miles away. They most likely came from nearby, released in huge numbers and swept into rain clouds by the wind. Other blood rains have been traced to windblown red dust, often from the Sahara, which mixes with raindrops and turns them red.

Anyone who wonders whether Peter Gabriel’s 1986 hit “Red Rain” was inspired by such strange weather may be surprised by its actual origin. Gabriel told Mojo that the song began with a recurring dream in which the sea was parted by two walls. Glass-like figures screwed themselves into the walls, filled with blood, and were lowered across the sand to empty on the other side. It turns out that nightmares, like storm clouds, can carry some unexpected things.

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6374. A Natural “Varnish” May Explain How 37,000-Year-Old Cave Art Survived

A new technique uses UV light to reveal a natural mineral varnish that may have helped preserve Chauvet Cave’s 37,000-year-old charcoal drawings.

About 37,000 years ago, Paleolithic people entered a limestone cave in southeastern France and drew the animals around them, including cave bears, cave lions, bison, and horses. An ancient rockfall later sealed away the artwork, leaving it undiscovered until the 1990s. Today, Chauvet Cave holds some of the oldest artwork in existence, along with clues to how the cave itself helped preserve it.

Getting close to those clues requires care. The site is so historically important and fragile that its location is kept secret and access is secured behind a huge steel door. Inside, prehistoric footprints lie in front of the artwork. Researchers examining the walls must also protect these traces of the people who once walked through the cave.

Researcher Philippe Walter describes the purpose of that painstaking work. “We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time.”

In a study reported in ACS Omega, Walter and his colleagues investigated the charcoal drawings without touching the cave walls. They focused on mineral deposits that had formed over the artwork, looking for evidence of how the drawings were created and how the cave’s geology may have contributed to their preservation.

To work around the fragile footprints, the team placed a portable spectrometer on a protective walkway about 8 feet (2.5 meters) from the wall. This instrument measures light, allowing the researchers to examine materials from a distance.

Their approach used ultraviolet, or UV, fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique researchers have used to reveal fluorescent mineral deposits invisible to the naked eye. Certain materials emit light when exposed to UV illumination. By shining a UV beam onto the wall and analyzing the resulting glow, the team could investigate both the mineral deposits and the pigments in the artwork.

Two different colors offered clues to what had happened on the cave walls:

“Our methodology is much like forensic investigation: We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time,” says Walter.

The team anticipates applications beyond cave art, from forensic science to monitoring biofilms aboard the International Space Station. Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. A project applying the technique to monitoring them aboard the station is already underway.

Reference: “In Situ Ultraviolet Fluorescence Spectroscopy for the Characterization of Translucent Calcite Coatings over Prehistoric Cave Art” by Yohan Boulard, Thiéry Guillou, Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Maguy Jaber and Philippe Walter, 29 September 2026, ACS Omega. DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061

The authors acknowledge funding from the French Ministry of Culture, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), and Sorbonne University.

Disclosure: One of the authors is a founder of Lumentis, a company developing imaging instruments for historical artwork analysis.

#6373. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6370. Scientists finally link human fossils found in China fifty years ago to the Denisovans, early human ancestors that we still know very little about

Two bones from Xujiayao, dug up in China in 1976-79 and dated to 199,000-138,000 years ago, yielded 18 proteins that point to Denisovans.

Between 1976 and 1979, excavators in the Nihewan Basin of northern China recovered 20 human fossils at a site called Xujiayao. From there, it took nearly five decades to tie them to the Denisovan lineage, an extinct human group first identified from DNA in a Siberian cave.

The finds included pieces of skull and jaw and some teeth, buried with animal bones and artifacts that were mostly scrapers and spheroids. Researchers later filed them under five different names.

A team that includes Song Xing and Qiaomei Fu of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) in Beijing has now recovered 18 ancient proteins from two of those bones.

One small change in a collagen protein points both to the Denisovan lineage, although the proteins cannot show which Denisovan population the people belonged to.

Uranium-series and electron-spin-resonance dating place the Xujiayao layer at around 199,000 to 138,000 years ago. The first studies noted a thick skull vault and teeth that resembled those of Neanderthals.

Those early descriptions led scientists to call the people Homo sapiens neanderthalensis, early Homo sapiens or archaic Homo sapiens. When the arguments over sapiens stalled, some papers fell back on the neutral term archaic Homo.

A later study of the partial skull called Xujiayao 6 measured a braincase of about 1.8 quarts (1,700 milliliters). That unusually large figure made the skull the type specimen of a proposed species, Homo juluensis, one of several new names listed in a 2024 article in Nature Communications.

The name placed Xujiayao in a group apart from the Homo longi skull from Harbin and from fossils at Dali and Jinniushan. The new paper argues against that divide.

Animal bones from the same layer came first, and they gave a positive result for ancient protein. Next came the human fossils, a right parietal bone from Xujiayao 6 and a piece of the Xujiayao 14 mandible, labeled PA1490 and PA1497 in the lab. Each went through a 3D scan before anyone touched it with a drill.

Researchers in protective gear drilled one small hole in each bone in a clean room at the institute’s Molecular Paleontology Laboratory. They wrapped the surrounding surface in aluminum foil and kept the holes as small as they could.

The powder went into hydrochloric acid and then a 149-degree Fahrenheit (65-degree Celsius) bath for three hours, which split each sample into three fractions.

Empty blanks ran alongside to catch contamination, and the bone of a modern Bactrian camel went through the same steps.

Two labs read the fragments on mass spectrometers, one at Capital Medical University and one at Fudan University in Shanghai.

One software search returned 15,194 unique peptides, the short chains of amino acids that make up proteins, across the two samples.

Old proteins carry a chemical wear called deamidation, and the team used it to separate ancient material from modern traces. Keratins and the trypsin used in the lab showed far less of it.

After further filtering and a check in a second software program, 18 proteins remained, 13 in the skull bone and 15 in the jaw.

The decisive signal sits in COL1A2, one of the chains of type I collagen, the main protein in bone. At position 996, Neanderthals and modern humans carry the amino acid arginine.

Every Denisovan tested so far carries lysine there instead, according to the paper. That reference group consists of two individuals from Xiahe, Penghu 1, the Harbin skull and Denisova 3 from Siberia.

Both Xujiayao bones showed lysine. The skull bone gave 57 peptides with the variant and the jaw gave 61, while each sample gave only one low-quality peptide with arginine.

The researchers then built a family tree from 2,074 amino acid positions in eight proteins, adding Neanderthals, 50 present-day people and a chimpanzee for comparison. Xujiayao grouped with Denisova 3 and other Denisovan-related individuals with a probability above 99 percent.

Xujiayao ranks “among the earliest molecularly confirmed Denisovans,” the authors wrote in Nature. Similar protein work identified a jaw from a Tibetan Plateau cave at Baishiya Karst in Gansu, dated to at least 160,000 years ago.

With the fossils assigned, the team compared their anatomy against other human relatives, using CT scans at a resolution of 37.56 microns.

They took 26 linear measurements, three angles and two indices from the Xujiayao 6 skull. C.-H. Chang shared a 3D model of the Penghu mandible, and X. Wu allowed the scanning of casts from Xuchang and Hualongdong.

Parts of the skull look like Homo erectus. The vault measures 0.30 inches (7.7 millimeters) thick at the top of the head and 0.47 inches (12 millimeters) at the parietal bulge, and the braincase is low and wide.

Other parts look more recent. A strongly arched temporal bone also appears in later species, including modern humans, while the inner-ear layout and, in the Xuchang fossils, a small pit at the back of the skull recall late Neanderthals.

The mix also has its own signature. The authors list a low skull with nearly parallel side walls, a massive brow ridge, a flat cheek region and a lower face that barely juts forward.

The paper reaches beyond Xujiayao. Its authors compared the anatomy with the Harbin skull known as Dragon Man and a jawbone from Penghu, off Taiwan, and they assigned most of East Asia’s late Middle Pleistocene fossils to the Denisovan lineage, including Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong.

The team also rejected the brain-size argument for Homo juluensis. Braincases in that group hold 1.8 to 1.9 quarts (1,700 to 1,800 milliliters) and the other East Asian fossils 1.2 to 1.5 quarts (1,120 to 1,420 milliliters), but modern humans alone span 1.15 to 2 quarts (1,090 to 1,880 milliliters).

If shape and molecules count together, the authors argued, Denisovans lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago. The authors linked their disappearance from the region to a major migration of modern humans around 40,000 years ago.

The authors wrote that adding other skulls gives “a nearly complete picture of the cranial morphology of Denisovans.” That portrait is a composite.

Its account of a sloping forehead, square eye sockets and a broad nasal opening relies on facial bones from Harbin, Jinniushan, Hualongdong and Dali, and it also matches features predicted from Denisovan DNA.

Only Harbin among those four has molecular confirmation in the paper. Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong join the lineage on shape alone, and the authors note that the full set of traits does not appear together in any single specimen.

The protein evidence also has limits. It rests on one reliable variant, known from five reference individuals, and it comes from two of the 20 Xujiayao fossils. Within the Denisovan branch, individuals formed an unstable arrangement with probabilities below 50 percent.

A test for a variant specific to Penghu produced no reliable result, so the team placed Xujiayao only in a late Middle Pleistocene East Asian Denisovan population. The 1970s excavators left the bones with a site name, and a drill hole in each of two pieces has now added a lineage.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6369. An Egyptian villager working near his house discovered the buried remains of two colossal pharaoh statues

A villager's discovery in Egypt led archaeologists to two colossal royal statues, including a confirmed Ramesses II figure once about 28 feet tall.

A resident of Behbeit El-Hagar, a village in Egypt’s Gharbia Governorate, was working a plot he owns in front of his house. There he found a strange inscription on a stone block, and he reported it right away.

From there, a rescue excavation by Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) uncovered the remains of two colossal royal statues. Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the finds on October 13, 2026.

One statue is confirmed as Ramesses II. Its head alone stands about 5.2 feet (1.6 meters) high.

Behbeit El-Hagar lies in the central Nile Delta. The village holds the ruins of a major temple to the goddess Isis, according to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The resident alerted the local antiquities inspectorate. Inspectors examined the stone and confirmed that it was an ancient artifact, and the SCA sent a specialist team to excavate the spot.

Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy praised the resident for reporting the stone immediately. He said public involvement is key to protecting Egypt’s heritage for future generations.

Fathy called the discovery an important addition to Egypt’s recent finds. In his view, it sheds further light on the history and archaeological significance of Behbeit El-Hagar.

The block that started the search is pink granite, about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) long. Its hieroglyphs preserve two royal titles of Ramesses II.

One is Nesu-bity, or “King of Upper and Lower Egypt.” The other is Sa-Ra, or “Son of Ra.”

Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the SCA, described the first statue. The king wears the Double Crown, which symbolized the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

The upper part of the statue’s back pillar also survives. It is inscribed with the king’s Horus name, Hor-ka-nakht-mery-maat, often rendered as “Strong bull, beloved of Maat.”

Based on the size of the head, El-Leithy estimated that the complete statue stood about 28 feet (8.5 meters) tall, including its base. The estimate rests on proportions, since only parts of that statue have been recovered.

Ramesses II, whose monuments include a Luxor obelisk now in Paris, reigned for 66 years. His rule, from about 1279 to 1213 B.C., fell within the 19th Dynasty of Egypt’s New Kingdom.

The second find is the main body of a royal statue, about 7.9 feet (2.4 meters) long. Its legs and base are missing.

This figure wears the nemes, the striped royal headcloth, and part of its top is lost. The face remains clear and well preserved.

Those features resemble the first statue’s, and archaeologists believe the second figure may also depict Ramesses II. That identification has not been confirmed.

The granite block lay roughly 3.3 feet (1 meter) north of this second statue.

Excavation and study will continue at the site, El-Leithy said. The goal is a clearer picture of the statues, the area’s history and its architectural development.

The Isis temple at Behbeit El-Hagar is much younger than Ramesses II. Nectanebo II, who ruled from 360 to 343 B.C., built most of it in dark granite, in a severe style typical of his dynasty’s Delta temples.

That work came roughly 850 years after Ramesses II’s reign ended. Nectanebo II decorated only one important chapel before the second Persian invasion of Egypt.

The temple probably replaced an earlier one begun in the 26th Dynasty. Ptolemy II later completed the sanctuary and chapels, and Ptolemy III added a hypostyle hall and the western facade.

The temple collapsed sometime after Ptolemy III and before the early third century A.D. Weak foundations may have played a part, and an earthquake, possibly in 24 B.C., may have brought it down.

Blocks from the temple have reached museums abroad. One granodiorite relief at the Met shows Nectanebo II offering incense and a collar to the god Osiris.

The ministry’s announcement does not connect the two statues to the Isis temple.

Ramesses II had statues of himself made across his empire. Among them are seated figures about 69 feet (21 meters) tall at Abu Simbel.

His mortuary temple, the Ramesseum, stood on the West Bank at Thebes, modern Luxor. One colossal seated figure there was carved from a single block of granite quarried near Aswan, according to the British Museum.

The surviving head and torso, now in London, measure just over 8.2 feet (2.5 meters). The complete seated figure would have reached roughly 23 feet (7 meters).

A red granite sphinx found at Memphis carries Ramesses II’s titles, but his sculptors reworked it from an earlier king’s monument. Flinders Petrie excavated it near the temple of Ptah in 1913.

The sphinx’s original owner was erased so thoroughly that he is unlikely ever to be identified. Ramesses II’s son and successor, Merenptah, later added his own cartouches to its shoulders.

The information was obtained from Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

#6367. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

R. Motani et al. A fully marine stem amphibian from the Late Triassic of China. Nature Ecology & Evolution. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41559-026-03209-9

B.P. Kear et al. Revision of the trematosaurid Erythrobatrachus noonkanbahensis confirms a cryptic marine temnospondyl community from the Lower Triassic of Western Australia. Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. 2026. doi: 10.1080/02724634.2025.2601224

#6366. Voyager 1 went silent in deep space right before reaching a historic milestone of one ‘light day’ away from Earth

NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1 in October 2026. The signal returned just weeks before the spacecraft reaches a historic milestone.

On Oct. 18, 2026, the antennas of NASA’s Deep Space Network tried to pick up Voyager 1 during a scheduled contact and found nothing. A second attempt 24 hours later also failed.

The signal came back on Oct. 20, and the team at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California has kept in touch with the probe since then.

NASA schedules Nov. 18 as the day Voyager 1, already the farthest human-made object, reaches one light-day from Earth, according to JPL. They had not previously said what caused the October problems.

The Deep Space Network has large antennas at Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The largest dish at each site measures about 230 feet (70 meters) across.

Those antennas handled the two contact attempts in October. Mission controllers logged no detectable signal on Oct. 18 or Oct. 19.

Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager at JPL, said the episode was new to his team. “This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this,” he said in the JPL statement.

He also said the mission has reached a stage where the team has “to expect the unexpected.” The probe has surprised its operators before, including the time it began talking through a radio system not used since 1981.

After contact returned, the team worked out that one group of thrusters on the spacecraft had gone offline and that a backup group had turned on.

The onboard computers carry instructions to make that swap by themselves when they detect a problem with the active thrusters.

JPL calls this kind of automatic reaction fault protection. It puts the probe in a safe, stable state and pauses normal operations so that engineers on the ground can study the problem.

In March 2025, engineers revived a set of roll thrusters that had stopped working in 2004.

Early in September, about six weeks before the probe dropped out of contact, JPL engineers sent the commands that turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and turned on three lower-power substitutes.

Inside the team, the job goes by the name Big Bang. The devices double as a source of warmth for the spacecraft, so JPL could not do them one at a time and all three changed at once.

Voyager 2 got the treatment first, and NASA reported on Aug. 4, 2026 that the swap there should keep three instruments powered for at least one more year. An instrument on Voyager 2 would otherwise have gone dark before the end of 2026.

Nothing in the Oct. 29 note ties the September commands to the thrusters.

Both probes run on radioisotope generators, which turn the heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. The output on each probe falls by about 4 watts a year and, with margins now thin, JPL has been shutting off whatever is not essential.

Ten science instruments went up on Voyager 1 in 1977. A NASA status page updated in April lists only two still running on it, the magnetometer and the plasma wave subsystem.

Controllers switched off the cosmic ray subsystem on Feb. 25, 2025, in one of a series of shutdowns meant to stretch the remaining power. The low-energy charged particle instrument was next, on April 17, 2026.

Without the Big Bang swap, another Voyager 1 instrument would likely have been turned off as early as summer 2027, JPL said.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after its twin, passed Jupiter and Saturn, and entered interstellar space in August 2012. It is moving at about 38,000 miles per hour (61,155 kilometers per hour).

NASA’s light-day page sets the crossing on Nov. 18, when the probe will sit about 16.09 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from Earth.

Light covers the distance to the Moon in 1.3 seconds. Artemis II astronauts needed about three days for the same trip.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory explains how far away Voyager 1 is when it reaches one light-day from Earth. Credit: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Voyager 2 took a different route so it could visit Uranus and Neptune, and NASA expects it to reach the same distance in November 2035. The nearest star system, Proxima Centauri, lies about 4.24 light-years away.

Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd described what the distance does to a conversation. “If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response,” she said in the JPL statement.

JPL’s Oct. 29 note does not say what knocked the thrusters offline, and engineers are still investigating. It also does not confirm that the thruster switch was what interrupted the signal.

The note does not name the three devices replaced in September or give the amount of power saved. It also says nothing about when the mission might end, although the team expects more surprises before summer 2027.

The light-day crossing itself will change nothing on board or around the spacecraft, JPL said. Its value lies in showing the length of the mission and the size of the distances involved.

At one light-day, a command sent from Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra needs a full day to reach Voyager 1. The answer needs another.

The information was obtained from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

In the run-up to the COP31 U.N. climate change conference, scientists have revealed that global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to drop by 0.4% this year, driven by growth in installed wind and solar power capacity, as well as oil price hikes caused by the Iran conflict. But climate goals are still unlikely to be met.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The world's carbon emissions from oil, gas and coal are projected to decrease by 0.4% this year, driven partly by the expansion of solar and wind power capacity and the price increases caused by the Iran conflict, according to a new report.

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget report was published in the journal Earth System Science Data Nov. 10 and is due to be presented at the U.N. Climate Change Conference's COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, this week.

Global carbon emissions have increased steadily since record-keeping began. This year is projected to have a slight decrease in fossil-fuel emissions, but that is partly due to price increases caused by the Iran conflict.

It is the first time annual carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels have fallen since the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. But the overall emissions picture suggests the world is still likely to miss key climate goals.

"It is an encouraging sign that the growth of emissions is slowing and decarbonisation efforts are starting to make a difference," said Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London who wasn't involved in the research. "However, at 0.4%, the projected decline is very small," Rogelj told Live Science in an email.

The report projects 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons) of emissions of the climate-warming greenhouse gas CO2 from fossil fuel sources this year. Greenhouse gases trap heat by absorbing the sun's radiation, and as their concentrations in the atmosphere increase, so do global average temperatures, leading to altered weather patterns and higher sea levels, as well as other major impacts.

The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand

Part of the 0.4% reduction in CO2 emissions is attributable to 40 countries that have cut emissions over the past decade while growing their economies. These include the U.S., Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Japan and about 30 countries in the European Union, the researchers reported.

When it comes to some of the biggest emitters, annual CO2 emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9% in China, 1.3% in the U.S., 1.5% in the European Union and 1% in Japan, but India's annual CO2 emissions are projected to grow by 4.4%.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Carbon emissions are projected to decrease slightly in the U.S., China and the E.U. but to increase in India.

Fossil-fuel-linked CO2 emissions from the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%, driven mainly by a 1.9% drop in oil emissions. Some of the report authors suggested in an accompanying paper in Nature Climate Change that this is a short-term response to the global supply constraints and increased prices triggered by the Iran conflict.

"The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand," Rogelj said.

While fossil fuel emissions and demand for oil are declining globally, overall demand for energy is actually increasing.

"Based only on the demand for energy, which has grown, we would have expected an increase in fossil CO2 emissions by about 0.8 gigatonnes," said study co-author Judith Hauck, a biogeoscientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research in Germany.

About two-thirds of that increase in demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, showing that clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions, Hauck said. However, the hike in energy prices that resulted from the Iran conflict also decreased demand by 0.4%, she said.

"So only together with the energy crisis did we bring the change in emissions down to negative," Hauck told Live Science, adding that she expects CO2 emissions to rebound if the conflict ends, as they did after the temporary emissions drop caused by the lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The exceptional circumstances that energy markets experienced this year make it clear that the small projected emissions decline is no reason to declare that emissions are now reducing, but there are hopeful signs, Rogelj said.

"Despite my muted enthusiasm about whether these lower emissions for 2026 represent the start of a long-term decline, the analysis shows encouraging signs of deeper long-term structural changes," he said. "But this shift must accelerate to ensure it is not outpaced by energy demand growth."

The report found that clean energy growth isn't yet fast enough to drive a steady decline in global CO2 emissions attributable to fossil fuels. The study authors expect that to happen in the next few years, Hauck said, as long as there is a continued push to deploy solar and wind power, batteries and electric vehicles.

CO2 emissions from fossil fuels are just part of the picture, though. Because of increases in human-caused peat fires, deforestation and forest fires linked to dry El Niño conditions, total global CO2 emissions from all sources this year are projected to increase slightly from 42.8 billion metric tons (47.2 billion U.S. tons) last year to reach a record 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons) this year, according to the report.

This means that the total budget of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming reaches 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels is now just 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) ‪—‬ equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

Hauck, like many climate scientists, thinks we have already missed our chance to hit the 1.5 C target and could only get back to that level through extensive removal of CO2 from the atmosphere.

"I'm still hopeful for something between 1.5 and 2 C [3.6 F]," Hauck said. "But for 1.5 degrees, we would need to see such a drastic strong drop in emissions. Based on what we've seen in the past years, even with this strong increase in avoided emissions, I don't think we can make that."

To halt global warming from increasing ever further, the world needs to be more ambitious in its planned emissions cuts, said Rogeli. We need to bring annual emissions down to zero to protect future generations from a double whammy of “having to try to transform economies so that they produce less climate pollution, while dealing with the impacts and damages of an increasingly adverse climate system," he said.

Editor's Note: This article was updated on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 8:45 a.m. E.D.T. to note that the conclusions about the effect of the Iran conflict on fossil fuel emissions came from a Nature Climate Change paper written by some of the report authors.

Chris Simms is a freelance journalist who previously worked at New Scientist for more than 10 years, in roles including chief subeditor and assistant news editor. He was also a senior subeditor at Nature and has a degree in zoology from Queen Mary University of London. In recent years, he has written numerous articles for New Scientist and in 2018 was shortlisted for Best Newcomer at the Association of British Science Writers awards.

From mysteries of the universe to how a lawn mower works, we want to hear what you can’t stop thinking about.

When NASA asked U.S. grade-school students in 2019 to submit potential names for its new Mars rover, a 12-year-old girl suggested the name “Curiosity,” writing that it is “the passion that drives us through our everyday lives,” and that “we have become explorers and scientists with our need to ask questions and to wonder.” Since 1902, it’s been our mission at Popular Mechanics to satiate curious readers with the skills and wisdom to command—and appreciate—the world around them, empowering you to ask the right questions, get your hands dirty, and find creative solutions.

Now, we want to hear directly from you about what makes you most curious. Our editors will select the most head-scratching and fascinating questions, then reach out to experts to track down answers.

#6363. Scientists got a much better look at endangered red pandas by putting cameras in trees

The red panda has a false thumb, and there's a good reason for that. To photograph a shy wild animal, researchers usually set up a motion-sensing camera near…

To photograph a shy wild animal, researchers usually set up a motion-sensing camera near the ground and wait for the animal to walk by. For red pandas, a camera placed near the ground misses a lot, because these endangered animals live mostly up in the trees.

At 19 sites in eastern Nepal, cameras about 16 feet (5 meters) up in trees took eight times as many pictures of red pandas as cameras near the ground. With cameras in the trees, researchers can watch an animal that is very hard to spot in the wild.

Sonam Tashi Lama of the Red Panda Network, a conservation group, led the work with Kathryn Bugler, James Ross, and Adrian Paterson at Lincoln University in New Zealand.

“Red pandas are very elusive,” Lama said. In eastern Nepal, oak trees are often covered in a reddish moss, and a red panda’s reddish fur blends into it. Researchers sometimes mistake pieces of moss for red pandas from a distance.

Lama said the camouflage helps protect red pandas from predators. Those predators likely include clouded leopards and common leopards, and sometimes yellow-throated martens, tree-climbing animals that usually hunt in pairs.

The same camouflage makes red pandas hard to study. Their behavior in the wild hasn’t been studied much, because the animals are so difficult to find and follow.

Researchers in earlier studies watched red pandas in person, fitted them with GPS tracking collars, or looked for their droppings. Lama’s team tested whether cameras could help, and whether they work better near the ground or in the trees.

From late 2017 to mid-2018, the team set up 19 pairs of motion-sensing cameras, known as camera traps, in the forests of eastern Nepal. Each pair stayed in place for at least a month.

The team picked trees that red pandas were already using. Fresh droppings and feeding marks showed which trees those were. Local people called Forest Guardians, who monitor red pandas for the Red Panda Network, helped choose the sites.

One camera in each pair was mounted on a tree trunk, about 16 inches (40 centimeters) above the ground. The other was placed up in the branches, about 16 feet above the ground.

There’s a reason for that height. Red pandas leave their droppings at regular spots in trees, and those spots are about 16 feet up on average.

Together, the cameras took almost 60,000 pictures. More than three-quarters of them showed no animal at all. Moving leaves and the heat of sunlight can set off a camera’s sensor, and that happened far more often in the trees.

Red pandas appeared in only 903 pictures, at 11 of the 19 sites. The tree cameras took 807 of those pictures, and the ground cameras took 96.

The team also counted how many separate times a red panda showed up. Tree cameras recorded 38 appearances. Ground cameras recorded 21. But a single appearance in a tree could produce a long series of pictures.

In one case, the team wrote, a tree camera recorded a single red panda over a period of 2 hours and 18 minutes. In that time, the animal slept in different positions, groomed itself, and explored its surroundings and the camera.

Red pandas sometimes investigated the tree cameras, but they didn’t touch them. One camera, aimed down a tree trunk, recorded a red panda climbing down headfirst.

The pictures also showed red pandas active at all hours of the day and night. The animals were busiest between 4 and 6 in the morning. They eat constantly, Lama said, taking only short naps between meals of bamboo.

Putting a camera in a tree is harder than setting one up near the ground. Reaching a tree camera takes a ladder or climbing gear. The team wrote that each one also took about 30 minutes longer to set up and to check.

The Forest Guardians are skilled tree climbers, Lama said. Tree cameras also took many more pictures with no animal in them, which gave the team more pictures to sort through.

Even so, the team wrote that the extra effort is worth it, because wild red pandas have been so difficult to observe. They recommended that researchers who want to monitor red pandas mount cameras in trees, about 16 feet up.

At that height, a camera can show whether red pandas are present, when they are active, how they behave, and possibly which predators are nearby. At one site in this study, a marten was photographed in a tree that a red panda often visited.

Ground cameras still have a use, the team wrote. They can record red pandas, but they are better suited to recording the other mammals that live on the forest floor.

Pictures from the tree cameras were clear enough to show the markings on each red panda’s face. Those markings differ from one animal to the next, so researchers can use them to tell red pandas apart.

Local populations of red pandas in Nepal are very small, typically 20 to 50 animals. Lama’s team didn’t use the pictures to estimate how many red pandas live in the study area. In future studies, the team wrote, the face markings could make that kind of estimate possible.

Biologists often estimate how many animals live in an area by learning to recognize individual animals, then recording how often they see the same ones again. The method is called mark-recapture.

The next question is whether that method works for red pandas. To make the animals easier to identify, the team suggested aiming cameras so they capture a red panda’s whole body.

The full study was published in the journal Wildlife Society Bulletin.

#6362. Bed bugs aren’t just a poverty problem, new study reveals

Genetic research across three states challenges the idea that persistent bed bug populations are confined to disadvantaged neighborhoods.

There’s a stubborn myth that bed bugs are a poverty problem.

In this view, infestations are confined to neglected housing, overcrowded apartments, and neighborhoods where residents can’t afford an exterminator.

New genetic research suggests the reality is more democratic – and more unsettling.

Bed bug reservoir populations, the persistent colonies that seed new infestations across a city, turn up in neighborhoods with both high and low social vulnerability.

The study was led by Cari Lewis from the Los Alamos National Laboratory and Warren Booth from Virginia Tech.

It is the first to combine population genomics with census-derived measures of social vulnerability to map how bed bug populations are structured across American cities.

Bed bugs have been living alongside humans for a very long time. The human-adapted lineage of Cimex lectularius split from its bat-associated ancestor roughly 245,000 years ago.

Bed bugs can’t fly or jump. Human-associated populations shelter indoors and spread by hitchhiking on our belongings.

“Bed bugs are expert hitchhikers,” Booth said. “They readily move into luggage, backpacks, purses, clothing, and other personal belongings.”

Adults are about the size of an apple seed. Immature stages are much smaller.

“Their ability to hide in tiny crevices makes accidental transport remarkably common,” Booth added.

The researchers collected specimens from 195 infestations between 2018 and 2022 across three states: Oklahoma, Illinois, and Ohio.

They extracted DNA and sequenced it using a technique called ddRADseq. This method surveys thousands of single nucleotide polymorphisms scattered across the genome.

Then they used network analysis and principal components analysis to identify genetically distinct populations within each state.

The genetic signatures were striking: Oklahoma’s bed bugs fell into seven distinct clusters, Ohio into ten and Illinois five.

Within each state, genetic differentiation between clusters was significant despite some clusters spanning huge geographic distances. Oklahoma’s most distant infestations were nearly 200 miles apart.

Geographic proximity alone did not explain the genetic relationships between infestations.

“Rather than spreading simply between nearby locations, these populations are connected through networks of human movement and the transport of personal belongings, similar to the models used to examine disease transmission within populations,” Booth explained.

The researchers layered their genetic data onto the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index.

This standardized measure scores census tracts across four themes: socioeconomic status, household characteristics, racial and ethnic minority status, and housing type and transportation.

In Oklahoma and Illinois, certain genetic clusters were associated with higher or lower social vulnerability.

But the reservoir populations – the genetically cohesive groups that persist over time and keep seeding new infestations – showed up across the entire spectrum.

They were found in rich neighborhoods and poor ones, in multi-unit housing and single-family homes.

In Ohio, no significant association between genetic clusters and any vulnerability measure was detected at all.

“A key finding of the research was the identification of reservoir populations: bed bug populations that persist over time and contribute to the spread of infestations beyond communities in which they are established,” Booth said.

“Importantly, these reservoirs of bed bugs occur across the socioeconomic spectrum, challenging the misconception that bed bugs are primarily a problem of disadvantaged communities.”

The genetic data revealed something else about bed bug biology. These populations are extremely inbred.

Average inbreeding coefficients were high across all three states – up to 0.353 in Illinois.

Estimated effective population sizes averaged just 3.5 to 5.5 across the three states. This genetic measure is not a count of the breeding bugs present.

Each infestation essentially starts from a handful of founders, reproduces in near-isolation, and builds its own genetically distinct colony.

The bugs don’t need large populations or high genetic diversity to establish and spread.

A few hitchhikers in a suitcase are plenty enough.

The insects are also increasingly resistant to the chemicals designed to kill them.

“Many bed bug populations are resistant to products that were once highly effective, especially pyrethroid-based insecticides,” Booth said.

“When infestations survive treatment, they continue to reproduce, spread, and increase the likelihood of additional introductions elsewhere.”

Detection is another problem. “Not all people who get bitten by bed bugs react to them,” Booth said.

Some people only discover they have an infestation when black spots start appearing on white bed sheets.

“That’s because they feed and then defecate and a little blood comes out,” he said. By that point, the colony may already be well established and spreading through wall voids to neighboring units.

If reservoir populations span the socioeconomic spectrum, then targeting pest management at disadvantaged neighborhoods alone won’t work.

The reservoirs that keep reintroducing bed bugs into treated areas are scattered across the entire urban landscape.

Booth advocates coordinated communitywide control, using early detection and infestation mapping to tackle bed bugs as a shared problem.

Management would focus on “simultaneous inspections and treatments of connected units and buildings, reducing re-infestation from neighboring sources.”

Regional policy differences already hint at what this might look like. Chicago has implemented landlord reporting requirements, education programs, and mandatory treatment protocols.

The study didn’t directly test whether Chicago’s regulations affect infestation patterns.

Yet, the finer-scale genetic structure detected in Illinois suggests that denser management and policy infrastructure may shape how bed bug populations organize and spread.

The research is published in the journal Parasites & Vectors.

#6361. Archaeologists Found 2,500-Year-Old Battle Lines From a Conflict No One Knew Ever Happened

The Iron Age palisade likely blocked an invading army. But who built it—and who were they afraid of?

Archaeologists sifting through portions of Denmark’s western peninsula ahead of a highway expansion keep uncovering remnants of the area’s past, often in small snapshots: a grave here, an axe there, or maybe sometimes even the foundation of an ancient home. They certainly weren’t expecting to find the remains of battle lines in West Jutland, indicating a conflict they didn’t know ever transpired.

“The find came as a complete surprise to us,” Michael Alrø Jensen, curator at Museum Vest, said in a translated statement. “It points to previously unknown conflicts in West Jutland dating back to the earliest part of the Iron Age.”

The find showed up via a 2,500-year-old line of pits, which experts believe fighters created during the Iron Age to block hostile incursions along an ancient West Jutland thoroughfare. The discovery came as archaeologists from the museum examined fields along Route 11, between Varde and Korskro, before the Danish Road Directorate began a highway expansion.

Experts dubbed the battle lines, which were found beneath a field near Schaefergården, a “post-hole alignment,” likely from around 500 B.C.E. The lines feature a long series of closely spaced holes in which one end of pointed wooden posts were buried to form a defensive palisade.

“Our best theory is that there was a fear of an invading army arriving from the north via the ‘Drivvej’ route, and that attempts were therefore made to control and block the passage,” Jensen said.

More evidence may still lie buried at the site. Experts note that the current Route 11 alignment between Varde and Korskro matches the ancient “Drivvej,” or Drove Road, that was the main transportation line through West Jutland for centuries. The modern road project adds an additional lane to the two-lane highway and shows how closely the ancient road—whose origin date remains unknown—matches the modern setup.

Still, the find raises questions. Archaeologists and historians don’t know who developed the defensive structure—or why. The team hopes that additional work in the area may offer fresh clues about the ancient mystery.

Attempts to pinpoint answers to a 2,500-year-old question got a bit muddy as the excavations revealed artifacts from a range of eras in spots that hadn’t been searched previously. Archaeologists now have evidence of human activity along the road from the first Stone Age farmers, who buried their dead in small mounds through the Bronze Age, Iron Age, and into the Viking Age (including the discovery of a 4,500-year-old battle axe buried alongside a Stone Age warrior).

“What we are most excited about is that we have found traces from so many different periods within a relatively small area,” Jensen said. “We have suddenly gained a wealth of new pieces that provide much greater insight into how people lived and moved about in this region over several thousand years.”

Every new discovery provides nuance to the historical record, whether the remains of a house, farm, or grave. Museum Vest hopes to learn more by excavating additional burial mounds. The various discoveries in the region together form a narrative of humans’ transformation of the land, first into farming plots and then into villages. “Once our work is complete, we hope to be able to offer the local community a more cohesive narrative about the area they live in,” Jensen said.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6360. Rose-colored rock found in the Sahara holds a rare piece of ancient Mars

A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara is a piece of ancient Martian crust that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago.

Although most of the surface of Mars is ancient rock, most Martian meteorites that land on Earth are young.

Found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, a rose-colored stone is an exception. It’s a piece of the planet’s early crust that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago.

Scientists rarely get to study a sample of the crust Mars had when it was young. The stone is called Teghaza 001, after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered.

Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California led the new study.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” she said. “One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.”

The rock weighs nearly 2 pounds (800 grams). It’s one of roughly 435 known meteorites from Mars, and the new study is a first description of it rather than a full accounting.

Like every Martian meteorite, Teghaza 001 was blasted off the planet’s surface by an impact and later landed on Earth.

Collectors often find meteorites in deserts and snowy plains, where they stand out against the bare landscape.

Researchers at the University of New Mexico first identified the rock as Martian by checking its oxygen.

Oxygen atoms come in slightly different forms, called isotopes, and the mix of those forms differs from one planet to the next. Teghaza 001’s mix matched the mix in other Martian meteorites.

Scientists also confirm a Martian origin by comparing a meteorite’s minerals and chemistry with data from NASA missions, including the Viking landers and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.

At first, Teghaza 001 looked like a shergottite, the most common kind of meteorite from Mars.

Liu studies planetary samples and has seen plenty of those, so she almost passed on the chance to examine it. She looked anyway and found odd textures and unusual minerals she hadn’t seen before.

Liu and her colleagues found zircon crystals in the meteorite. Zircon records clues about how a rock formed, and geologists use it to date a sample precisely.

François Tissot, a coauthor at Caltech, helped the team use a dating method his group developed. Some dating methods require dissolving the sample being analyzed.

Tissot’s method instead measures single mineral grains on the surface of a piece smaller than a fingernail, so most of a rare rock stays intact for future studies.

“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said.

“Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons, and asteroids.”

Liu was shocked by the results. Water on Mars had changed the rock sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, which suggests the rock itself formed even earlier.

Only two other Martian meteorites found on Earth are counted among the most ancient. One of them, ALH84001, is about the same age but is made almost entirely of one mineral.

The third, nicknamed Black Beauty, is made of small fragments of volcanic rock.

Teghaza 001’s mix of minerals formed as molten rock cooled slowly into crust. Later, water moving underground changed some of them.

That mix matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed in the heavily cratered southern highlands of Mars.

The rock’s exact birthplace on Mars remains unknown, but the team identified several locations that match its minerals and chemistry.

Lee Saper, the study’s second author, did the research as a postdoctoral scholar at JPL and is now a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before. It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water,” Saper said.

The water that reacted with Teghaza 001 was enriched in oxygen-18, an isotope with two more neutrons than the most common form.

Clues in the oxygen isotopes, the texture, and the chemistry of the rock’s minerals point to an active water cycle on early Mars.

A second study, published in June in Science Advances and led by Saper, measured water in the meteorite’s minerals.

It found that water on Mars about 4.1 billion years ago held at least roughly twice the share of heavy hydrogen that Earth’s seawater does.

The authors wrote that this result supports models in which young Mars lost hydrogen to space quickly.

So far, Liu, Saper and their colleagues have described the rock in broad terms. Later studies of it could help show how water and rock interacted on ancient Mars.

“We’ve only scratched the surface,” Liu said.

Liu and her coauthors now want to see what other research teams can learn from Teghaza 001.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

A 2019 astronaut photo shows the near-perfect cone of a highly active volcano poking its heavily scarred and partially snow-covered head above a thick bank of low-lying clouds over the Kuril Islands.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Atlasov Island, off the coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula [50.84755357, 155.56126752]

What's in the photo? The summit of Alaid volcano peeking above a thick layer of low-lying clouds

Who took the photo? An unnamed astronaut on board the International Space Station

This eye-catching astronaut photo shows a towering, highly active Russian volcano poking its head above a thick bank of swirling clouds over the Kuril Islands.

The lofty peak is located on Atlasov Island, the northernmost of the Kuril Islands — a chain of roughly 50 largely uninhabited volcanic landmasses stretching along a fault line that runs between Russia and Japan in the Sea of Okhotsk. Altasov lies 40 miles (65 kilometers) off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, which is also renowned for its volcanic activity.

The island consists mainly of a single, massive volcano, called Alaid, which is known for its near-perfect cone shape. Alaid reaches up to 7,497 feet (2,285 meters) above sea level, making it the tallest peak in the Kuril Islands.

Alaid has erupted at least nine times in the past 50 years, including a major outburst in April 1981 that ejected a 1,250-mile-long (2,000 km) plume of thick smoke and ash into the atmosphere, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

Its most recent eruption occurred between September and November 2022, when a river of lava flowed down its flank (see below). During this outburst, the volcano also spit out smoke and ash that was spotted from space alongside another eruption plume coming from the nearby island Paramushir.

Alaid last erupted in November 2022 and unleashed a scorching lava flow down its snow-covered slopes. This photo also shows what Atlasov Island looks like when it is not obscured by clouds.

In the astronaut's photo, roughly half of Atlasov Island rises above a deep, low-lying bank of swirling clouds. The summit of Alaid, crowned by a roughly mile-wide (1.6 km) caldera, is also obscured by clouds. (The volcano was not erupting when the photo was taken.)

Farther down the volcano's flanks are a series of snow-filled gullies carved out by lava flows from previous eruptions. Eagle-eyed viewers may also be able to spot some parasitic cones — small openings where lava burst through in the past — around the edge of the cloud layer, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The area surrounding a cluster of parasitic cones on the volcano's northwest flank (top right in the photo) is devoid of vegetation ‪—‬ a result of another major eruption in 1972, which scoured the surrounding landscape with hot ash. A 2009 study revealed fresh signs of recovery in the affected area, but noted that it could take hundreds of years for vegetation to return to pre-eruption levels.

The clouds are not the only thing the island rises above. Alaid is essentially the summit of a much larger underwater volcano that lies beneath the Sea of Okhotsk. The rest of the island has grown around the exposed cone as lava flows have reached sea level and solidified. Millions of years ago, this larger volcano was likely connected to the Kamchatka Peninsula via a land bridge that has since been submerged.

In 1981, a major eruption caused Alaid to unleash a massive plume of smoke and ash that reached up to 1,250 miles long.

Astronauts and satellites have snapped several other stunning shots of intriguing landmasses nearby, including a quartet of end-to-end volcanoes on Simushir Island and a set of volcanic "nesting dolls" on Onekotan Island.

And in 2022, the Landsat 8 satellite also spotted the iconic summit of Mount Vesuvius peeking through a gap in the clouds over Italy, just like Alaid.

A 2024 astronaut photo shows the icy surface of Pangong Lake breaking apart in the lofty Tibetan Plateau. The point where the ice meets the water almost perfectly matches a disputed border between China and India.

A 2020 astronaut photo shows the unique structure of Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active stratovolcano in Tanzania that was recently adorned with a bright white "ash cone." The explosive peak produces a rare type of lava that is unusually cool but travels remarkably quickly.

A 2010 satellite photo shows the point where a small lake bisects the snowy rim of an ancient glacier on Canada's Baffin Island. The rippling, snow-rimmed structure is the last remaining fragment of a colossal ice sheet that once covered large parts of North America.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.
