#6358. Deadly eel virus can spread in a surprising way

Scientists found that infected European eels can spread a dangerous virus through bites, raising new concerns for conservation.

A herpesvirus that kills European eels can jump from one fish to the next when they bite each other.

A Belgian study provides the first evidence that biting can transmit this virus.

Fish live in water, so the assumption has been that their viruses travel through it too. For plenty of aquatic diseases, that holds up. But anguillid herpesvirus 1 does not last well outside its host.

At 77°F (25°C) about 90% of its infectivity had gone within 12 hours in lab tests. The mucus coating an eel’s skin works against it as well.

The virus spreads between eels all the same. A team led by Natacha Delrez at the University of Liège says biting may help explain how.

When infected and healthy eels were made to bite one another, every healthy animal involved became infected. That held whether the contact was at the mouth or the tail, and whichever animal did the biting.

The fish were anesthetized and kept in laboratory tanks. So the work shows a bite can pass on the infection.

Whether that happens regularly in the wild is left open.

Infected tissue in fish is normally located by examining organs after the animal has been euthanized.

The method gives detailed information. But it does not allow one infection to be followed in the same living animal.

Delrez and her colleagues inserted two genes into the virus.

One of them was a firefly gene for light production. In eels infected with the altered virus, tissues where it was multiplying emitted a faint glow.

The light is invisible to a person looking at the animal, but specialized imaging equipment picks it up.

The images recorded which parts of the body were infected first and where infection appeared later.

The modified virus was compared with the original. Growth rates in cell cultures were the same.

Disease symptoms and mortality in infected eels were comparable. On that basis the team used the altered virus for the rest of the work.

Four strains were used at first, collected in the Netherlands, Denmark, and the United Kingdom. Genome analysis was done with the MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research.

One strain was used in the later experiments, which reduced the number of animals needed.

Age turned out to matter. European eels arrive on the continent’s coasts as glass eels, tiny and close to transparent. They darken once they push into rivers and other inland habitats.

Then they settle into a yellow eel stage, which may go on for years of feeding and growing before the final migration back to sea.

Glass eels held in contaminated water showed no detectable infection.

Among slightly older juveniles, infection was detected in one of six animals on both day three and day six, and in two of six on day nine.

Yellow eels did worst, with all six animals infected within six days.

Imaging put the earliest signals in the gills and in tissues inside the mouth, areas around the teeth and lips among them.

That detail became important later. In three separate waterborne exposure experiments, all yellow eels showed symptoms between days eight and 12. About 20% died.

The virus appeared to enter at the mouth and gills. But in eels kept together, imaging showed glowing patches elsewhere.

The patches were farther down the body, particularly around the tail. They did not match the pattern seen earlier.

Yellow eels housed in groups of 20 were then compared with infected yellow eels housed individually.

At nine days, group-housed eels had several glowing patches around their heads and tails. Eels housed alone had visible signals around the mouth and gills and none along the rest of the body.

Solitary eels were still seriously infected. Tests found virus in internal organs, including the brain and heart. They lacked only the separate patches on the outer body.

The team turned to behavior. Yellow eels generally live alone, can defend territory aggressively, and sometimes bite one another when sharing limited space.

Eel farmers documented the behavior decades earlier. They described bites around the mouth and nips at the tail, particularly in crowded conditions.

The patches were in those same locations. Some, the researchers proposed, had developed where another infected eel had bitten.

They were not part of the ordinary progression of the disease. The team tested that directly.

For the biting experiments the eels were anesthetized. Three kinds of contact were then arranged between infected and healthy animals.

In one, an infected eel bit a healthy eel around the mouth. The other two involved the tail. The healthy eel delivered the bite in one case, the infected eel in the other.

The healthy animals were afterward placed in separate tanks, which ruled out further biting between them.

Every one became infected, and some showed glowing tissue three days after the bite. The team took that as strong evidence that the physical contact itself could transfer the virus.

Handling might still have moved contaminated mucus or water from one fish to another by accident.

To separate that from the bite, they washed the heads or tails of infected eels in small quantities of water. Healthy animals were then exposed to the wash water.

Much less infection followed. None of the healthy eels tested positive three days after exposure to the head-washing water, and two showed weak signals at six days.

In the biting experiments, every exposed animal was infected. A bite, the team concluded, does more for the virus. It is not simply moving a little contaminated water from one animal to the next.

None of this rules water out. The team drew water from a tank of 15 infected eels and transferred it to tanks of healthy fish.

All six exposed animals became infected. So did all six when the water had been standing for 24 hours.

The picture changed once the scientists started diluting.

Water diluted a hundredfold infected five of six eels while fresh. Twelve hours later the same dilution reached only three animals, and a day later it reached none at all.

Water diluted ten-thousandfold and left to stand for 12 hours caused no detectable infection in the tested eels.

Infectivity also dropped fast in ordinary water, and eel skin mucus cut it further.

Viral concentration helps determine whether water spreads the disease.

A crowded eel farm keeps it high. A river does the opposite: the water moves, the virus thins out, and fish may be far apart. A bite skips all of that.

Numbers matter too. Young eels reaching European coastlines are now at roughly 1% of early-1980s levels, a fall linked to dams, overfishing, pollution, and climate change.

In a tank, under anesthesia, with the bites arranged by hand, anguillid herpesvirus 1 passed from eel to eel every time.

What eels get up to in a river is harder to know. Their interactions are difficult to observe. Little is known about how often they bite one another at today’s reduced population densities.

What the researchers will say is that nothing like it has been reported before.

They call this the first case of a virus spreading between members of the same fish species through biting in water.

No one has yet documented a naturally occurring bite that transmitted this virus between two wild eels.

The findings raise concerns for eel farms, where animals are housed together and aggressive encounters may be more likely.

Restocking programs worry the authors for a related reason. Young eels are sometimes raised or held together, then released into rivers that may already contain infected animals.

European eels are critically endangered, and dams and other barriers divide their remaining river habitats.

Protecting them means understanding diseases, not just releasing more fish.

Researchers suggest exploring vaccines for farmed eels and conservation programs that move young glass eels into rivers.

The findings show that the virus may spread through more than water. A bite between eels can also pass it on.

The full study was published in the Journal of Virology.

#6357. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6355. Alzheimer’s discovery reveals a breakdown in the brain’s defenses

A mouse study reveals how the Alzheimer’s-linked gene CASS4 helps brain immune cells surround plaques and limit nearby nerve damage.

An immune cell can’t do much for damaged brain tissue if it can’t get there. That problem seems to lie at the heart of a new study on CASS4, a gene linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

Mice without CASS4 had less contact between their brain immune cells and the protein clumps associated with Alzheimer’s.

Bigger clumps, looser packing and more damage followed, although the brain still had about as many immune cells to work with.

Microglia, as these cells are called, crawl about in brain tissue checking for damage and collecting waste. Those clumps are called plaques.

For over a decade, genetics studies have pointed to CASS4 without explaining much about its work in a living brain.

It belongs among the Alzheimer’s risk genes that do their work outside nerve cells, despite nerve cells bearing the damage most of us know about.

Adeline Walsh, a physiology graduate student at the University of Virginia, led the research with neuroscientist John Lukens. He heads a lab at the university’s Center for Brain Immunology and Glia.

“Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper,” Walsh said.

The work points to CASS4 as a possible drug target. Alzheimer’s affects more than six million Americans and ranks sixth among the country’s causes of death.

For the plaque experiments, the team needed mice that would grow amyloid deposits while still young.

They used mice carrying five mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s disease, then removed CASS4 from some of them.

A separate characterization of the strain found plaques arriving sooner and more consistently in females, hence the choice to use females throughout.

In mice without CASS4, the cortex and the memory-related hippocampus both had extra buildup by five months old.

The largest size group, over 1,000 cubic micrometers, accounted for more deposits in those brains.

More swollen nerve endings surrounded each plaque, and a second marker of nerve fiber damage was elevated in both brain areas.

At four months old, 10 mice from each group had a swimming test. Somewhere in the cloudy water was a platform to stand on, hidden just under the surface.

For four days, both groups found it at about the same pace, and both did equally well on a memory test the next day.

Then the platform moved to the far side of the pool, and the mice missing the gene began to struggle.

The mice went back to where the platform used to be, and swam farther from the new location than the other mice did.

The team took the platform out for a final test, and these mice still spent more time at the old position than the new one.

They covered as much water, just as fast, as the other mice, and two tests of activity and anxiety came out much the same.

Mice without Alzheimer’s mutations showed no such difficulty after losing CASS4, suggesting that the effect depended on the disease model.

An old habit can be hard to shake for people with Alzheimer’s, and researchers have much left to learn about it.

Of course, a swim in a pool doesn’t capture what it’s like for a person.

Differences in microglial numbers did not explain the findings. Mice without CASS4 had about as many microglia as their littermates with the gene intact.

A check of cell division, and of the signs of cells going on alert near a plaque, found much the same in each group.

The cells also swallowed labeled amyloid at much the same rate.

Within 10 to 20 micrometers of a plaque, though, the mice without CASS4 had much less microglial material. That distance is a fraction of the width of a human hair.

Reduced microglial contact was accompanied by less rounded, less densely packed plaques, with amyloid spread loosely around the core.

A 2015 study described that packing job. Microglia put a barrier around a plaque and squeeze the protein into a tighter clump, so less of it can reach the neighboring nerve cells.

There was still something to sort out. Every cell in the first mice had lost CASS4, which left open where the trouble really started.

In another group, two weeks of medicated food after weaning switched CASS4 off in cells bearing a particular surface marker.

After a few weeks, blood cells with working CASS4 had replaced the affected blood cells, but microglia live for years and stayed without the gene.

The second group again had more plaques in the hippocampus, more of the largest deposits and more damage to nerve fibers nearby.

Those plaques were less round and less densely packed, despite the brains having no shortage of microglial material compared with the controls.

“Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer’s. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system,” Lukens said.

Pulling a cell across a surface is a job for tiny gripping points, and the protein made from CASS4 helps organize them.

The protein acts as a scaffold for structures called focal adhesions, which help cells grip their surroundings.

The team found 98 genes working at different levels in microglia without CASS4, with less activity in systems that build and tighten the fibers used to move.

A separate test with 1,318 antibodies picked out 93 differences in phosphate tags, little chemical additions that control proteins, with 17% involving proteins central to focal adhesion signaling.

Grown in a dish, these microglia spread less of a key gripping protein beneath them. A scratched layer of related immune cells also took longer to close the gap.

Through a window in the skull, the team watched how microglia responded to a tiny brain injury created with a laser.

Normal microglia sent branches toward it over the next 40 minutes, and the ones missing CASS4 hardly stirred.

People aren’t mice with CASS4 deleted. We inherit small differences in its DNA, and the team still needs to find out what those differences mean for the protein.

Mice with human versions of the gene would help, including versions that turn its activity up. They’d still be mice, of course, with all the limits of studying human disease in another animal.

“We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it,” Lukens said.

There’s no drug to boost CASS4 yet, or evidence that doing so slows Alzheimer’s in people.

Getting a treatment into microglia and following what happens to plaques over time would be necessary steps along that road.

The study is published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine.

#6354. Seabirds that nest together spend winter thousands of miles apart – and DNA may predict where

Seabirds that share nesting sites can winter thousands of miles apart, with their genes helping guide their migration.

Two seabirds can nest side by side and leave for winter at about the same time. You might expect them to fly together. In the western Mediterranean, they often do not.

Cory’s shearwaters and Scopoli’s shearwaters nest in the same colonies in parts of the western Mediterranean and leave on migration at about the same time each fall.

A new study found that birds from those shared colonies generally wintered in areas typical of their own species.

Some ended up thousands of miles from their neighbors, while hybrids tended to travel intermediate distances.

The results suggest that genes shape these birds’ routes more than their colony neighbors do.

Beñat Garcia-Urdangarin, a doctoral student at the University of Barcelona, is the study’s first author.

Raül Ramos and Jacob González-Solís, who heads the university’s Seabird Ecology Lab, are among the lead authors.

The team tracked the migrations of 50 breeding shearwaters and sequenced the genomes, or complete sets of DNA, of those birds and eight others.

Only seven of the 58 birds were hybrids. For that reason, the team wrote, the hybrid result should be interpreted cautiously.

Across most of their ranges, the two species breed apart. Cory’s shearwaters nest mainly on Atlantic islands such as the Azores, Madeira and the Canaries.

Scopoli’s shearwaters nest on small islands across the Mediterranean, as far east as the Aegean Sea.

The two species separated about 350,000 years ago. Today their ranges overlap around the Alboran Sea, the part of the western Mediterranean closest to the Strait of Gibraltar.

Garcia-Urdangarin’s team worked in that overlap zone, at four colonies where both species nest. For comparison, the researchers also sampled a Cory’s colony in the Canary Islands and a Scopoli’s colony on Zembra Island in Tunisia.

Why would neighbors matter? Some migrating birds do learn routes from each other. Pink-footed geese set up a new migration route and breeding area within a decade. Birds from the original population switched to the new route.

Shearwaters that copy their neighbors should winter where the rest of their colony winters, whatever their ancestry. With an inherited route, each bird should follow its ancestry instead.

Each bird wore a small light sensor on one leg for a year or two. The sensor recorded light levels. The team used the timing of each dawn and dusk to estimate the bird’s position twice a day.

The estimates are rough. Each one can be off by a couple hundred miles (a few hundred kilometers).

When the researchers recovered a sensor, they took a blood sample from the bird. The blood was used to sequence its genome. That genome showed how much of the bird’s ancestry came from each species.

From 2008 to 2020, the team recorded 127 migrations, including eight by the same shearwater.

The tracks are available through the Seabird Tracking Database.

The two single-species colonies showed what each species normally does.

About 70% of the trips tracked from the Canary Islands ended off southern Africa, along the Agulhas Current and the area where it meets the Benguela Current.

Most trips tracked from Tunisia ended in the tropics instead, around the Gulf of Guinea and the equatorial Atlantic.

In the mixed colonies, most birds went where their own species goes. Palomas Island, a colony of fewer than 100 pairs, had only one tagged Cory’s shearwater.

That bird flew to the Agulhas Current four years in a row, while every Scopoli’s shearwater tracked from the same island wintered along the tropical African coast.

The team’s statistical model estimated that Cory’s shearwaters from the mixed colonies traveled about 7,200 miles (11,660 km) to their wintering areas.

For Scopoli’s shearwaters there, the estimate was about 2,100 miles (3,340 km). Both figures are for males. Females of both species traveled almost 1,900 miles (3,000 km) farther.

A few Cory’s shearwaters from the mixed colonies did winter off West Africa, in food-rich waters heavily used by the other species. But Cory’s shearwaters from colonies outside the overlap zone are known to winter there too.

The team also found seven recent hybrids in the mixed colonies, 17.5% of the birds sampled there. Two were first-generation hybrids, with one parent from each species. The rest had mostly Scopoli’s ancestry.

Six of the seven hybrids were tracked. Four of them wintered off Namibia and the other two off West Africa.

For hybrid males, the model’s estimate was about 3,800 miles (6,060 km). That distance falls between the estimates for the two species.

“This provides solid evidence that the long-distance migrations of these species have a genetic basis,” Ramos said.

In-between routes have been reported before, in songbirds. A past study found hybrid songbirds taking routes between those of their parent populations.

Birds tracked across multiple years tended to travel similar distances each year.

In the team’s model, differences among individual birds accounted for 82% of the variation in travel distance.

The authors suggested that this habit builds up over time. A young bird starts with an inherited tendency, then refines the route as it gains experience.

Young shearwaters have years to gain that experience. They typically begin breeding at about nine years old.

Earlier tracking studies found that young Cory’s shearwaters shortened and straightened their routes as they aged.

The two species may also meet in their wintering areas. Both seabirds use the food-rich waters off West Africa, Angola and Namibia.

Birds that mix there may later settle in a colony of the other species, the team proposed.

González-Solís said conservation strategies need to consider the zones where the two species breed together, including the transfer of genes between species there.

For now, the hybrid result rests on nine migrations by six birds.

That is too few to test how the trait is inherited, or to compare first-generation hybrids with birds whose ancestry is mostly Scopoli’s.

Hybrid wintering areas also looked more like those of Scopoli’s shearwaters than those of Cory’s shearwaters, the authors wrote.

Every tracked bird was also a breeding adult, so the study didn’t follow young birds on their first migrations.

The next question is which parts of the genome are involved.

The team wrote that finding them will take many more tracked and sequenced birds, sampled across the full breeding ranges of both species.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Ecology.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

#6351. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7

#6350. Tiny spider named for Stephen Colbert has more DNA than you do

Scientists sequenced the genome of Stephen Colbert’s trapdoor spider, revealing repeated DNA and clues to spider evolution.

Stephen Colbert once used his TV show to demand that a spider be named after him. The trapdoor spider that got his name is about the size of a quarter, yet it carries more DNA than a person does.

The genome of Aptostichus stephencolberti, its full set of DNA, contains billions of base pairs.

Most of that length isn’t genes. It’s the same stretches of DNA, copied again and again.

A team led by researchers at UC Davis sequenced the genome. Jason Bond, a professor in the Department of Entomology and Nematology, is the study’s senior author.

Genome length is counted in base pairs, the paired chemical letters that spell out DNA.

“At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it’s not the largest genome among the spiders, but it’s significant,” Bond said.

He said the spider is the first member of its family to have its genome sequenced. The team’s report was published in September 2026.

The team estimated that the spider’s DNA is split among 52 chromosomes, the bundles that hold a cell’s genetic material. A single set of human chromosomes has 23.

Repetition fills most of that space. About 77% of the genome is made of sequences that appear many times over, scattered across the chromosomes.

Genes take up far less room. An automated computer search, drawing on genetic material from whole adult spiders, identified 14,067 of them.

Future studies of this spider and its close relatives can use the genome as a reference for comparison.

In many animals, each chromosome ends in a short string of DNA letters repeated over and over. That repeated tip, called a telomere repeat, helps protect the end of the chromosome.

The team searched this spider’s genome for a five-letter version of that repeat and found none.

When the researchers widened the search to other spiders, the repeat was missing from every one they checked.

The findings suggest that this repeat disappeared in an early ancestor of today’s spiders.

“[The genome] lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life,” Bond said.

Female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground. Each one lives in a burrow lined with silk and sealed by a camouflaged, hinged door.

A female waits for the vibrations of prey moving nearby, then comes out quickly to grab whatever wanders too close.

People walking through the spider’s coastal dune habitat often pass close to the burrows without knowing it.

The spider’s venom isn’t dangerous to people, though. Of the more than 50,000 known spider species, only 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to humans, Bond said.

Colbert’s connection goes back to 2008. Bond had named another trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young, and Colbert, playing his pompous pundit character on The Colbert Report, wanted one too.

He used a segment called “Who’s Not Honoring Me Now?” to demand a spider of his own, and Bond obliged.

As in the comedian’s own name, the t in stephencolberti is silent. Another spider species carries the name of Bob Marley.

The spider lives only in coastal sand dunes between the San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey. Those dunes are broken into separate patches, and trapdoor spiders rarely travel far.

Staying put has a cost. Spiders that stay on one patch can end up genetically distinct from the next patch over, and the team wrote that the same habits make trapdoor spiders prone to extinction.

The genome is part of the California Conservation Genomics Project, a state-funded effort to build genetic data for conservation.

Researchers can use data like these to spot distinct populations that may need protection.

“We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us,” Bond said.

“We’re hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.”

Rising sea levels threaten this narrow strip of habitat. “They’re going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they’re also very sensitive to invasive species,” he said.

Genomes like this one could also help researchers find useful compounds in venom.

Some compounds that come from venom could work as painkillers, and others might help control pests, Bond said.

Scientists already study animals such as cone snails for the same reason.

“We don’t really know what’s out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms,” he said.

The researchers haven’t yet worked out which patches of dune hold genetically distinct groups of these spiders, or which of those groups are most at risk.

The team’s genome, which is publicly available in an online data archive, gives researchers the reference they need to compare spiders from one dune to the next.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Heredity.

#6348. Volcanic eruptions leave a lingering chill in the ocean

Major volcanic eruptions may briefly strengthen ocean cold spells, but their cooling effects vary widely across different regions.

Pinatubo’s eruption was over long before the cooling was. The 1991 eruption cooled the lower atmosphere worldwide by as much as 0.9°F (0.5°C), with effects lasting about two years.

At sea, that chill had an uneven reach. A spell of unusually cold water could grow stronger in one region without doing so in another.

A new study follows those cold spells through six big eruptions. Each eruption preceded an increase in their strength overall, a short-lived reversal of the weakening seen across 175 years.

Marine cold spells are runs of days when the sea surface is unusually cold. An icy sea isn’t necessarily having one; it may just be as cold as it usually is.

The study used the coldest 10% of temperatures for a given place and time of year as its cutoff. The water had to stay that cold for five days or longer, rather than just dip for a day or two.

Jan Kempert, at South Westphalia University of Applied Sciences, worked with Raven Quilestino-Olario, at the University of Cologne’s Institute of Geology and Mineralogy, on the research. Both institutions are in Germany.

“We noticed that while the cooling effects of major volcanic eruptions have been widely studied, relatively little attention has been given to how these volcanic winters affect extreme cold events in the ocean,” Quilestino-Olario said.

Their source was COBE-SST3, a record from the Japan Meteorological Agency. It gives daily estimates of ocean surface temperatures from 1850 to 2024, based mostly on readings taken at sea.

For each cold spell they found, the pair added up how far below normal the water was, day by day. That total became the spell’s score.

The score thus counted the length of the spell as well as the cold. A longer stretch or a deeper chill would push it up.

In 79% of the ocean map squares, however, the scores went down over those 175 years.

Cold spells grew less frequent in about the same share of squares, extending a decline that satellites had already recorded for 1982 to 2020.

The eruption list began with Krakatau in 1883 and Santa Maria in 1902. It continued with Novarupta in 1912, Agung in 1963, El Chichón in 1982, and finally Pinatubo in 1991.

The stratosphere, high above the ground, is where sulfur-rich particles from large eruptions can linger. They cut down the sunlight reaching the surface, sometimes leaving months or years of cooling.

The comparison put cold spells from the 30 years before an eruption on one side and a short period after it on the other.

The later run always started the next year and lasted five years for Krakatau, two for Pinatubo, and one for each of the other four.

There was more than a volcano to reckon with in some of those years. El Chichón, in particular, had some inconvenient company.

The eruption came in 1982. Across 1982 and 1983, the Pacific also experienced one of only six “super” El Niño events since 1850.

Both events could leave a mark on the temperature record, so the researchers had to allow for the overlap.

Kempert and Quilestino-Olario removed the influence of El Niño and La Niña, along with the long-term weakening of cold spells.

After those adjustments, marine cold spells were stronger than expected following all six eruptions.

“Our study shows that although cold extremes in the ocean have generally become less frequent and less intense over the past 175 years, major volcanic eruptions may temporarily interrupt this long-term pattern,” Kempert said.

They also tried choosing the years without looking at eruption dates at all. In 10,000 random draws, each containing six years, they checked for an increase in cold-spell strength.

Just about 2.4% of the draws produced an increase as large as the one after the eruptions. In other words, most random choices of years didn’t produce anything of that size.

The world average was one thing, though. The maps were another.

From 1884 to 1888, about 80% of the ocean squares had stronger cold spells than expected. That was the period following Krakatau; for Pinatubo, the share came to 70%.

For Santa Maria and Agung it was roughly half. El Chichón and Novarupta came in below half, a reminder that an increase in the world average needn’t appear in most places.

Five eruptions had their biggest response in the middle latitudes, the bands between 30 and 60 degrees north or south of the equator. Novarupta broke that pattern.

The only high-latitude eruption in the six, Novarupta also had the weakest effect on the global average. The authors were cautious about that result.

None of these eruptions occurred in an otherwise unchanging ocean. Ocean circulation was still shifting water around, the seasons were changing, and natural swings in climate were still going on.

According to the authors, volcanic cooling and those ongoing changes together could account for the patchy map. Changes in circulation can even bring warmer winters to parts of the far north after an eruption.

Some parts of the ocean have very few nineteenth-century observations. The record is less reliable in places with few historical readings, and in places where sea ice was present.

For Pinatubo, the team ran the analysis again with a satellite-era record from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The two records agreed in 79% of the map squares about whether cold spells were stronger or weaker than expected.

Another choice affected the answer: the years used to stand for normal temperatures. Comparing each eruption with its previous 30 years gave stronger cold spells after all six.

When the researchers used the same modern reference period for every eruption, fewer eruptions showed an increase.

The count was five with 1961 to 1990 as the comparison, and four with 1981 to 2010.

How much extra cold can be pinned on the volcanoes themselves remains uncertain. The records describe the aftermath, but can’t separate out every cause.

Additional tests removed a North Atlantic climate pattern as well as El Niño.

Several other natural cycles remained, partly because their consistent monthly records don’t reach as far back as 1850.

There’s a further difficulty with El Niño: an eruption may affect it. Remove El Niño from the calculation and some of the volcanic effect may go with it.

The authors call for further checks using other temperature records, measurements beneath the surface, and climate models.

Their own next project will look at marine heatwaves, periods of unusually warm ocean water.

“We hope to use the same long-term ocean temperature dataset to explore how marine heatwaves have changed over the past 175 years, this time placing greater emphasis on the uncertainties associated with historical observations,” Quilestino-Olario said.

The heatwave work could help establish whether eruptions change unusually hot conditions at sea as well as cold ones.

The full study was published in the journal Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research.

#6347. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6346. Britain’s coastal floods have a surprising connection to distant skies

Air pressure patterns over the Atlantic and Arctic help explain where extreme storm surges strike Britain’s coast and northwestern Europe.

Storm surges look like local disasters, but which stretch of Britain’s coast floods can often be traced to air pressure patterns over the Atlantic and the Arctic.

Those far-off patterns help decide whether northern or southern coasts take the high water.

A surge is hard to forecast, because wind, low air pressure, and the shape of the coast all play a part at once.

Understanding why surges hit certain places, such as East Anglia in eastern England, could give coastal towns earlier flood warnings.

Lisanne Blok of the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Cambridge led the work, with colleagues at the National Oceanography Centre and the British Antarctic Survey.

Her team studied more than 70 years of sea levels around northwestern Europe.

A computer model rebuilt those levels day by day from 1950 onward, using past weather data rather than tide gauge readings.

The team first removed the tides and the normal seasonal rise and fall of the sea. Then they used machine learning to sort the coastline into regions that tend to get extreme surges on the same days.

They ended up with six regions across the seas of northwestern Europe, plus eight smaller ones inside the North Sea.

“If we can identify conditions emerging in, for example, the Atlantic that might result in a storm surge in East Anglia, then we can pinpoint parts of the coast that should prepare for flooding,” said Blok.

Big, repeating pressure patterns over the ocean are what scientists call climate modes.

“Computer models used to forecast risk of coastal flooding don’t always account for large-scale climate modes, instead focusing on localized weather variables,” she said. “But what our findings tell us is that climate modes are really key.”

A storm surge builds when strong winds and low air pressure push a bulge of seawater toward land.

Sometimes it rises high enough to spill over flood defenses. If that happens at high tide, with big waves on top, the sea can reach extreme heights and flood the coast.

Over January 31 and February 1, 1953, a deep low-pressure system moved down the North Sea and pushed a huge mass of water along Britain’s east coast.

It arrived with a spring tide, the extra-high tide that comes around a new or full moon, and sea levels rose about 10 feet (3 meters) above predicted levels.

Floods swept through parts of Britain, the Netherlands, and Belgium.

Another surge struck Britain’s east coast on December 5 and 6, 2013, with water levels in some places higher than during the 1953 flood, but modern defenses prevented a disaster on that scale.

The North Sea’s narrow funnel shape, tightest between East Anglia and the Netherlands, pushes water toward land. Its shallow floor, roughly 30 to 490 feet (10 to 150 meters) deep, makes the surge taller.

On the worst 1% of days in the rebuilt records, surges added at least 22 inches (57 centimeters) to the North Sea’s water level, more than in any other region.

“The storm surges are very dynamic and complex in this region,” said Blok. “There is also heightened risk, because lots of people live along the low-lying coastal regions bordering the North Sea.”

Next, the team compared each region’s surges with those big pressure patterns.

“We can link regional storm surge extremes to very distinct climate patterns,” Blok said. “I didn’t expect such clear relationships, especially across the large distances involved.”

The strongest links were to pressure patterns across the Northern Hemisphere, including the North Atlantic Oscillation, a seesaw in air pressure between the regions around Iceland and the Azores.

When Iceland’s pressure is low compared with the Azores, the jet stream, a fast wind high up, moves north, and surges become more likely on northern and central coasts.

“As the storms shift to the north, they also deliver high seas to more northerly coasts,” said Blok.

When pressure over Iceland is unusually high instead, the pressure difference with the Azores shrinks.

The jet stream slows and bends south. Storms then take southern routes, bringing high seas to southern coasts.

Storms behind extreme surges off southwest England and west of Ireland tended to start near Newfoundland, off eastern Canada, thousands of miles away.

Storms behind surges farther north, in the seas toward Norway, more often began off Greenland or in the central North Atlantic.

Those southwestern surges were also more common in autumn, while the other regions saw most of theirs in winter.

Ali Mashayek, an associate professor in Cambridge’s Department of Earth Sciences, was the study’s senior author.

“Conditions in the Arctic have a big impact on UK weather,” he said. “That’s something we’ve known for a while, although we haven’t been able to link it to storm surge distribution before.”

Mashayek said Arctic warming will weaken the pressure difference that powers the jet stream, and “that means it is likely we will see a shift in UK storm patterns, including where storm surges occur, in future.”

But he added that “this is something we are still trying to understand.”

It’s time to view local weather extremes in a global context, Mashayek said. “We now have more evidence that the extreme weather in our backyard may be driven by what happens in very distant parts of the world.”

“This speaks to the broader issue that climate change and the extremes it induces are a truly global problem that need global solutions.”

The surge records left out waves and long-term sea level rise. The team also didn’t check whether the links change from season to season.

Next, the researchers want to run the same analysis on future climate projections, to see whether the surge regions shift as the planet warms.

The full study was published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans.

#6345. Our Universe Is Held Together by Invisible Galactic Glue—And We Wouldn’t Exist Without It

Its transformative emergence might have occurred within the very first seconds of time, physicists say.

Dark matter isn’t like other matter. It doesn’t interact with visible light or any other electromagnetic force. And yet, it seems to push around regular matter through its gravitational influence. Dark matter rules the universe, maybe holding galaxies together, but we still don’t know what it is.

A battery of cosmological probes has revealed clues to the presence—and influence—of dark matter in the universe: Stars orbit galactic centers far too quickly. Galaxies zip around clusters with excessive velocities. Massive objects bend the light passing by them with more gravitational force than we can account for with visible observations. And the history of the universe has revealed the incredibly speedy growth of gigantic structures.

The conclusion is that there’s something more to the universe than our traditional electromagnetic measurements can detect. Yet this thing simply doesn’t emit or absorb light. What could it be?

What we know is that it’s cold, heavy, and slow. Yet, new research suggests that it may have once been the complete opposite: hot, light, fast … and insignificant.

How do you turn dark matter from zero to hero? The answer lies in the strange and wonderful physics of superconductivity, which lets electricity flow with zero resistance. In a new paper, theoretical physicists Guanming Liang and Robert Caldwell from Dartmouth College outline a hypothetical scenario for flooding the universe with dark matter when it was mere seconds old.

For decades, cosmologists have been following one particular compelling idea to explain dark matter, known as WIMPs, for weakly interacting massive particles. These are hypothetical particles that only interact with the rest of the universe through gravity and the weak nuclear force (which rules subatomic particles’ behavior). But searches for WIMPs have so far come up empty.

To fill the gaps, theorists have been busy, generating dozens of new theories every year to unravel the mystery of dark matter. The vast majority of these ideas come from the land of high-energy physics, invoking this-or-that exotic process or super-theoretical particle that we might see someday in a collider. These massive machines smash high-energy subatomic particles together in the search for new particles.

But Liang and Caldwell took a different tack, turning instead toward condensed matter physics. This branch of physics makes major breakthroughs all the time, but without as much public fanfare as the high-energy work.

At a fundamental level, condensed matter physics is the study of stuff. It gives us an understanding of how everyday things work on subatomic levels—from why glass is transparent to how heat flows through new materials. And it’s also the study of everyday materials under extreme conditions, which leads to completely counterintuitive behaviors.

For example, take electrical resistance. Electrons flowing down a wire bump into each other, which saps energy out. This is why we can’t, for instance, have solar arrays in the desert that can pipe their electricity all around the country.

But if you cool some materials down to nearly absolute zero, the electrons bind up together in a new state of matter. And when they do that, all the resistance disappears, and electricity can flow uninterrupted. This is known as superconductivity, and it’s through superconductors that we’re able to harness tremendously large currents to drive technologies like MRI machines and maglev (magnetic levitation) trains.

In Liang and Caldwell’s model, dark matter starts out as a hot soup of fast-moving, massless particles in the extremely early universe. But as the universe expands and cools off, the dark matter particles pair together, the way electrons do in a superconductor. When they do that, the dark matter particles undergo a radical transformation, emerging on the other side with a brand-new set of properties. The pairs become slow-moving, heavy—and dark.

However, the model revealed an unusual quirk: that if the dark matter particles start out with even a tiny bit of mass, then not all of them bind up together as pairs. Most of them stay in the background, where they soak up all of spacetime. This behavior might provide an explanation for another mysterious ingredient in the cosmos, dark energy, which is responsible for causing the accelerated expansion of the universe.

So far Liang and Caldwell’s idea is just that: a guess as to how the universe might actually work. But it’s a testable one. The properties of these paired-up dark matter particles may leave behind a subtle signature in the appearance of the cosmic microwave background. That’s the light left over from when the universe cooled from a plasma to a neutral state, when it was around 380,000 years old.

To be fair, the idea is probably wrong. But that’s okay. We have no idea what dark matter is, and we need to flex every analytical and creative muscle we have to solve a puzzle that spans the entire universe. And we need to draw from as many sources of inspiration as possible, whether it’s high-energy physics, condensed matter physics—or even something else.

We never know when we’re going to be right. It’s only by searching in the dark that we’ll find out.

Paul M. Sutter is a science educator and a cosmologist at Johns Hopkins University and the author of How to Die in Space: A Journey Through Dangerous Astrophysical Phenomena and Your Place in the Universe: Understanding Our Big, Messy Existence.
