#6344. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#6343. Blood tests for a deadly infection have a lingering blind spot

Blood tests for melioidosis, a dangerous infection caused by soil bacteria, can remain positive for nearly three years.

An antibody blood test for melioidosis, a potentially deadly bacterial infection, can remain positive long after someone becomes ill. A positive result does not necessarily mean the infection is still active.

Scientists followed 142 people in Thailand who had been in hospital with melioidosis. A bacterium called Burkholderia pseudomallei causes the disease.

The team found antibodies in the blood of the patients long after they first got sick. In the team’s model of a typical patient, the test stayed positive for about 20 months to nearly three years.

So here’s the catch. These tests can provide evidence of past exposure, but a positive result alone cannot establish whether someone currently has an active infection.

For a doctor picking a treatment, or a health agency trying to count cases, that’s a real gap.

B. pseudomallei lives in soil and water. It gets into people through a cut that touches contaminated dirt, through dust they breathe in, or through water they drink.

Patients do not all have the same symptoms. Some get pneumonia and some get an infection in the blood. In others the signs look like a more common illness.

Ninety of the 142 patients in the study had a fever when they came to the hospital.

The recorded diagnoses included sepsis in 60 patients and pneumonia in 45.

Hospitals confirm melioidosis by growing the bacterium from a patient’s blood or from another sample. A culture like this takes at least two days.

It misses some infections, and the lab has to take special safety steps to do it. In places where staff have not seen the disease before, they may record the organism as a less harmful bacterium from the environment.

A late diagnosis can be serious. B. pseudomallei resists several of the antibiotics that hospitals often give to patients with severe infections. Doctors have to identify it fast to give a drug that works.

Antibody tests are faster and cheaper than cultures. They can be used outside hospitals as well. Scientists can test people in a community to see who has been exposed.

This can show where melioidosis is present but has not been noticed.

Northern Australia and northeast Thailand are the places most often linked with melioidosis, but cases have been reported across Asia, Africa and the Americas.

How far the disease really extends is not known, in part because few places test for it or track it.

In Mississippi, investigators found three patients from the same county. The three got sick over a period of three years.

The investigators tested soil and water on the property of one patient. They found the same strain of the bacterium there.

This was evidence that the organism now lives in the environment of the continental United States.

Kristen Aiemjoy, an assistant professor in the UC Davis Department of Public Health Sciences, is a co-senior author of the study.

“One of the things that makes this organism concerning is its ability to persist in the environment for very long periods of time,” said Aiemjoy.

“Once Burkholderia pseudomallei becomes established in soil and water, it can continue to survive and replicate, creating an ongoing risk of exposure.”

For this reason, scientists want to know who has been exposed. That includes people who did not get sick.

The patients were treated in hospitals in Mukdahan, Roi-Et and Surin, three provinces in northeast Thailand.

A lab had confirmed melioidosis in all 142 of them. The team compared them with 76 healthy people who had given blood.

The patients had a median age of 54. Ninety-nine of them were men and 98 had diabetes. Diabetes is a major risk factor for severe melioidosis. Nine patients died.

The team used samples that had been stored from earlier studies. They tested 656 blood samples in total.

The samples were taken at different times. The first were taken in the hospital and the last were taken up to one year later.

They measured antibodies against two targets on the bacterium, a protein called Hcp1 that it produces during infection and a sugar structure on its surface called OPS.

For each target they measured two classes of antibody, IgA and IgG, so there were four markers in all.

The team saw antibody levels rise fast in the first days after symptoms began. The four markers reached a peak between about day four and day 17. The team then saw the levels fall, but very slowly.

In the researchers’ model, the two IgA markers stayed above the cutoff for a positive test for 597 and 710 days. The two IgG markers lasted longer, at 902 and 1,080 days.

Fifty-two patients were tested again a full year on. Depending on which marker you look at, 30 to 34 of them were still positive.

The tests worked well when patients were acutely ill. At the first visit, the best single marker found about 80% of infections. It gave a correct negative result for 96% of healthy donors.

It’s later on that things get murky, when a positive might just be the immune system remembering an old infection, not flagging a new one.

Pairing up the measurements helped. Combining measurements of the two antibody classes against OPS identified 88.7% of patients and correctly classified 94.0% of healthy donors.

And with a higher combined threshold, the estimated stretch of lingering positivity dropped to under a year.

Diabetes changed the results too. For one marker, peak antibody levels were about twice as high in patients with diabetes.

Three of the markers also went down more slowly in these patients.

“In places where melioidosis is rare or newly emerging, such as parts of the United States, these antibody tests may be especially useful because few people have been previously exposed,” Aiemjoy said.

“But in areas where the disease has been circulating for decades, previous infections can make results more difficult to interpret.”

The study has some limits. All 142 patients were adults in hospital. No children or people with mild infections took part.

The 76 healthy donors were younger than the patients. The team set the cutoffs for the tests with the same group of people, and nobody has validated the cutoffs independently.

The team measured antibodies in the samples. They did not test if live bacteria were still in the patients’ bodies. For that reason the team cannot rule out that some patients with a long antibody response still had an infection.

The findings could still help scientists read the results of future surveys. Some of those surveys may be done along the US Gulf Coast.

Scientists could test people who have never been diagnosed with melioidosis. That could show how far the bacterium has spread.

The pattern of antibodies might also help them estimate when a person was exposed.

“Better tools for tracking exposure will help us understand where this pathogen is today and where it may emerge in the future. As environmental conditions change, surveillance becomes increasingly important,” Aiemjoy said.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Microbe.

#6341. Hubble captures a dying star’s tangled farewell – and an intriguing mystery

Hubble’s view of NGC 5189 reveals a twisting ribbon of glowing gas, enormous knots, and clues to the complex final stages of a star’s life.

Today’s Image of the Day from the European Space Agency features a dying star that has shed its outer layers, creating a twisting cloud of glowing gas.

Some of the small knots visible within it are roughly the size of our entire solar system.

The cloud is NGC 5189, a planetary nebula in the southern constellation Musca, the Fly.

Captured by the Hubble Space Telescope, this elaborate formation reveals dense knots and fine filaments within the glowing gas.

The image was released in December 2012, but its intricate details still offer a remarkable view of stellar change.

Despite their name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets.

Early astronomers gave them that label because some appeared as small, rounded disks through their telescopes, resembling distant worlds.

Better observations eventually revealed something entirely different: expanding clouds of gas released by stars approaching the ends of their lives.

Stars with low to intermediate masses can produce these nebulae as they lose their outer layers, exposing their hot cores.

Ultraviolet radiation from the remaining core strips electrons from atoms in the surrounding gas. As electrons recombine with ions and atoms release energy, the material shines.

The result can take many forms, from relatively simple rings to hourglass shapes and sprawling structures with several lobes.

NGC 5189 belongs among the more complicated examples.

The most striking feature is a bright, golden band that bends across the nebula, contributing to its backward S-shaped appearance.

Look more closely, and that band breaks into numerous strands and dense clumps. Some resemble tiny comets, with bright heads and trailing material.

These “cometary knots” are features within the gas, rather than actual comets traveling through the nebula. Radiation and winds from the central star help shape them.

Around the golden structure, bluish lobes extend outward, giving the scene a layered appearance.

NASA describes two nested structures tilted relative to one another and expanding in different directions.

Their arrangement suggests that the star’s loss of material was uneven, changing over time and sending gas along different paths.

Hubble’s sharp view makes it tempting to treat the nebula’s finer details as small decorations.

Their true dimensions tell another story.

According to ESA, individual knots in NGC 5189 can rival the size of our solar system.

Gas flowing outward encounters these denser pockets, creating curved, bow-wave-like features.

The image therefore captures structure on very different scales: a broad, twisting nebula assembled from countless smaller formations, each enormous by everyday standards.

At its center, the stellar remnant appears only as a point of light.

Much of the spectacle comes from material that once belonged to the star and now stretches far beyond it.

When the image was released in 2012, astronomers suspected that a second star might help explain the nebula’s unusual shape.

A companion’s gravity could influence how material escapes, helping produce patterns more complex than a simple expanding shell.

Later research strengthened that possibility.

In a study published in 2015, researchers reported periodic changes in the central star’s measured motion, revealing a close binary system with an orbital period of about four days.

The researchers considered another white dwarf the most plausible companion.

That finding added an important piece to the picture, although identifying a binary system does not explain every filament and curve.

The nebula preserves the combined effects of escaping gas, radiation, stellar winds, and the system’s history.

Hubble observed NGC 5189 on July 6, 2012, using its Wide Field Camera 3.

The observations included filters selected to isolate light emitted by oxygen, hydrogen, and sulfur.

Other filters captured a broader range of visible and near-infrared light, helping record the surrounding stars.

Combining these observations produced the detailed color image.

The different filters allow astronomers to examine particular components of the nebula, separating signals that would otherwise blend together.

The resulting portrait reveals both its overall shape and the fine texture within its glowing clouds.

A planetary nebula marks a comparatively short phase of stellar evolution. Its gas continues expanding, while the exposed core eventually cools as a white dwarf.

Our Sun is expected to undergo a broadly similar transformation, although its surroundings may take a very different shape.

For now, NGC 5189 offers a vivid glimpse of that distant stage of a star’s life: material once held inside a star, spread across space in luminous folds.

Image credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

#6340. What is fueling the brightest gamma-ray star pair ever found?

A warm gas trail near LMC P3 offers new clues to the extraordinary gamma rays coming from this mysterious binary system.

One pair of stars in a small galaxy next to the Milky Way gives off more gamma rays than any other pair of its kind.

Gamma rays carry more energy than any other form of light, and astronomers have struggled to explain where this pair’s gamma rays come from.

In the cold gas near the stars, they have now found a long, straight streak of warmer gas that lines up with the pair.

The warm streak is strong evidence that the pair, called LMC P3, is shooting out a jet of fast-moving matter. A jet like that could account for the gamma rays.

The work was led by Yasuo Fukui, a professor emeritus at Nagoya University, with colleagues at Gifu University.

“We discovered a gigantic molecular jet,” said Fukui. The team didn’t see the jet itself, though. What they measured is gas they think the jet has heated.

LMC P3 lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy that orbits our own. When astronomers look toward the middle of the Milky Way, dust blocks much of the view.

The Large Magellanic Cloud has far less of that problem.

One member of the pair is a big, very hot star. The other is a compact object, the crushed core left behind when a giant star exploded.

That core is either a black hole or a neutron star, and nobody has yet confirmed which.

The two circle each other about every 10 days. They orbit inside the debris from the explosion that made the compact object, a leftover cloud called DEM L241.

LMC P3 is the most luminous known gamma-ray binary and the first discovered outside the Milky Way. Astronomers first reported it in 2016.

Starting in 2022, the team pointed the ALMA observatory in Chile at the region.

The array of radio dishes picked up the faint signal of carbon monoxide in the cold gas near the stars.

That signal told the researchers how the gas was spread out, how it moved, and how warm it was.

One streak of gas stood out. It runs about 26 light-years long and three light-years wide, and it lines up with LMC P3.

That length is roughly six times the distance from the Sun to the nearest star.

The streak is still extremely cold: minus 400°F to minus 352°F (33 to 60 K). The gas around it measured about minus 433°F (15 K), which is normal for quiet gas clouds in that galaxy.

Measured from absolute zero, the streak is two to four times warmer than its surroundings.

The team found no nearby hot stars that could have warmed the gas by shining on it.

Fukui said the warm temperatures, spread across a large part of the gas cloud, make “a very strong case” that the gas is being struck by a high-energy jet from the compact object.

That same kind of jet can power gamma rays.

For years, there were two main explanations for LMC P3. In the first, the compact object is a fast-spinning neutron star that blows out a wind of charged particles.

The wind slams into the wind coming off the big star, and the collision speeds particles up enough to make gamma rays.

In the second, the compact object pulls gas off its partner. The gas swirls into a flat, spinning disk around it, which astronomers call an accretion disk.

A disk like that can launch narrow jets of matter moving close to the speed of light.

The second setup is a small version of a quasar.

Quasars, among the brightest objects in the universe, are powered by giant black holes feeding on gas at galactic centers. Some also launch powerful jets.

A star-sized version is called a microquasar. The new streak supports the microquasar idea.

Because black holes generally drive stronger jets than neutron stars do, Fukui sees LMC P3’s huge gamma-ray glow as a clue to what kind of object powers it.

The high gamma-ray output “provides a very strong support for the possibility that its central object is a black hole” rather than a neutron star, Fukui said.

In the paper, the team argues for a jet but doesn’t name the compact object.

Roughly 20 microquasars are known in the Milky Way. Most were found with optical telescopes, radio dishes, or X-ray instruments, aimed at parts of the sky that are mostly clear of dust.

Few microquasars have turned up in the crowded, dusty middle of our galaxy.

The researchers suggest that searching for straight streaks of warm carbon monoxide could turn up microquasars there.

LMC P3 is the second object where this kind of carbon monoxide streak has been found. The first was a gamma-ray source in the Milky Way called HESS J1023-575.

A jet can only build a streak where there’s enough gas in its path. LMC P3 is close to a gas-rich region where new stars are forming.

Around the well-known microquasar SS 433, the gas is thinner, which the team thinks is why only scattered clumps formed there instead of one long streak.

No telescope has detected the jet directly, in radio waves, X-rays, or gamma rays. The researchers wrote that this fits with how sensitive current instruments are.

The streak also shows up only on the north side of the pair, possibly because that’s where the gas cloud is.

The ALMA map didn’t cover the south side, so a matching streak there hasn’t been searched for at this level of detail.

A second, fainter streak runs at an angle of about 16 degrees to the first.

If the jet slowly changes direction over time, it could have made both, but that idea hasn’t been tested.

The team plans sharper ALMA observations that can pick out details smaller than about three light-years.

Those would give better temperature readings and could show whether the jet has been shifting direction.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

#6338. A metal detectorist found Finland’s largest known silver coin hoard, dating back to the Viking Age

A metal detectorist in Finland uncovered the country's largest known Late Iron Age coin hoard.

On September 3, 2026, metal detectorist Kalle Lappinen found two birch-bark containers buried between stones near the village center of Sysmä, in southern Finland. Together they held about 9.9 pounds (4.5 kilograms) of silver.

The hoard is the largest known coin hoard from Finland’s Late Iron Age, according to Lahti Museums, the regional museum that recovered it. It contains thousands of silver coins.

The previous record holder, found in Nousiainen in 1895, contained about 1,700 coins and other objects. It weighed about 4.9 pounds (2.2 kilograms).

The find spot was inspected the next day. Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist at the regional museum responsible for the area, directed the recovery.

The two containers lay about 18 inches (45 centimeters) deep, between stones and roughly 39 feet (12 meters) apart.

Besides the coins, they held a piece of hacksilver, plus a bracelet, a mount and a bead, all made of silver.

The coins have not yet been cleaned, sorted or counted. Their exact weight, number, origin and dating will be set by further study.

The site lies on Ohrasaari, in Sysmä. A new sand-surfaced path now leads to the find spot, and a sign about the discovery is on the way, the municipality reports.

Even before cleaning, Tikkala could date some of the coins to between the 1000s and the 1050s.

The coins come from several regions, including Sweden and the areas of present-day Britain and Germany. The museum has not yet said how many coins come from each region.

The most distant coins in the Sysmä hoard are dirhams, Islamic coins from the area of present-day Turkey and Iran.

The coins should help show how wide the era’s trade networks were. Many similar finds have already been made near Sysmä, but this hoard stands out for its size.

Viking Age coins circulated freely, and their value came mainly from their silver content rather than from where they were minted.

The Finnish Heritage Agency made that point about a smaller hoard found by detectorists in Mynämäki, in southwestern Finland, in 2022. Agency archaeologists excavated that site and recovered the remaining pieces.

That hoard included about 100 silver coins and about 30 pieces of hacksilver, the chopped silver used as currency.

Its coins were minted in places as far apart as England, Denmark, Germany, Iraq and Central Asia. Twelve were struck for the Danish king Harald Bluetooth, who died in 986.

The Mynämäki coins span roughly 250 years. The oldest is an Umayyad dirham from 743 or 744, while most date to the final decades of the 900s.

The makeup of that hoard closely matches hoards from Poland, and the agency concluded that it very likely came from Pomerania. It was apparently buried soon after it reached Mynämäki.

The label “Viking Age” refers to the period, Lahti Museums points out. It does not mean the hoard belonged to Vikings or that Finland was Viking territory.

The discovery has also prompted discussion of why such a large fortune was hidden in two places.

That work is expected to show more about the role of Sysmä and the surrounding Päijät-Häme region in Late Iron Age trade and cultural networks.

“Museums do important work in researching, recording and preserving cultural heritage for future generations,” said Tuulia Tuomi, museum director of Lahti Museums.

She added that the wide attention the discovery received in Finland and abroad shows how broadly archaeological heritage interests people.

In Finland, objects more than 100 years old that are found in the ground belong to the state. Finders must report them to the Finnish Heritage Agency through its online notification service.

Finders should not clean the objects or dig further, and they should record the exact find location. Finds from a known ancient monument belong to the state without compensation.

The agency may redeem a find or pass that right to another museum. For finds containing precious metal, the minimum price is the value of the metal plus 25 percent.

Redemption currently takes about three years, and selling such objects is illegal, the agency’s guidance for finders states.

Tuomi also credited responsible conduct by hobbyists with helping to preserve valuable information about such finds.

The information was obtained from Lahti Museums.

#6337. A Remote Island Holds a Major Warning Sign for the Future of Humanity

A 180-year accidental experiment on a barren volcanic rock could show us how to reverse deserts—or how to break nature.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The word “terraforming” is typically reserved for discussions of other worlds. Sci-fi writers dream up vast galactic empires where humans have bent entire planetary ecosystems to their will while, in the real world, the world’s richest man contemplates a similar future. But on the remote island of Ascension in the South Atlantic, an accidental 180-year-long experiment shows what happens when you terraform our own planet. Some see the story as a small slice of hope for areas around the world facing desertification in the face of climate change, while others see the history of Ascension Island as a warning about humanity’s impact on the natural world.

Around one million years ago, volcanic eruptions along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge pushed the island up out of the Atlantic. It went unseen by humans until 1501, when Portuguese admiral João da Nova came across it. Two years later, Portuguese navigator Afonso de Albuquerque found it again on the Christian holiday of Ascension Day, which is how the island got its name. However, neither of these expeditions set up shop on the island, and it wasn’t until 1815 when Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to St. Helena, an island located some 800 miles away, that the United Kingdom finally established a military outpost Ascension to keep tabs on him (a good idea since he’d escaped exile once before).

Some of the most colorful descriptions of Ascension come from naturalists arriving at the island in the decades following British settlement. Among these voices was a young Charles Darwin, who arrived on the island in the summer of 1836 and described it as possessing a “naked hideousness.”

“Those who have beheld a volcanic island, situated within an arid climate, will be able at once to picture to themselves the aspect of Ascension,” Darwin wrote. “To complete this desolate scene, the black rocks on the coast are lashed by a wild and turbulent sea.”

However, a little less than two centuries after this bleak description, the island is now a lush tropical cloud forest filled with eucalyptus, bamboo, banana plants, araucaria, and Cape bramble—all plants from three separate continents. So how did this happen? Well, the short answer is humans, but the slightly longer answer is the work of the British botanist Joseph Hooker. In 1847, Hooker persuaded the Royal Navy to bring plant specimens from the Kew Gardens in London to catch rain, reduce evaporation, and improve soil health, according to El Pais.

The introduction of these plants, along with more humans (who brought with them insects, rats, and cats, in a cyclical parade of invasive species), essentially terraformed the island, turning a once desolate landscape into something more suitable for human habitation.

Some scientists see this history as a possible blueprint for fighting desertification, which is spreading as climate change threatens vulnerable ecosystems. Among them is Victor Maull, who recently finished a Ph.D. at Pompeu Fabra University focused on the island.

“In the laboratory we are working to make minimal models that can explain changes to ecosystems,” Maull said in a press statement. “Normally, we model ecosystems that degrade, but with Ascension we have the opportunity to understand the reverse process and see if we can invert the collapse.”

However, other experts who spoke to El Pais have a different interpretation of Ascension island’s ecological history—one that stresses caution rather than celebration. Although Darwin had little positive to say about the island on his visit, endemic species did live on the roughly 34-square-mile island back then. Today, those native species are being crowded out by invasive plants that now cover almost the entire island. One of those natives, the Ascension Island parsley fern, was thought to be extinct until 2009, when researchers found four plants clinging to a cliff.

“What remains today is an unusual combination of species—bamboo, eucalyptus, ficus and others—that would never have grown or evolved together naturally in an ecosystem,” Tiffany Simpson, director of Conservation and Fisheries for the Ascension Island Government, told El Pais. Because of this mismatch, even some of the invasive plants are struggling to establish roots in the shallow, volcanic soil, causing many trees to topple over during fierce storms.

Whatever one makes of its history, Ascension offers two lessons. It shows that deliberate intervention may help hold back advancing deserts, and it warns of what can be lost when humans reshape a one-of-a-kind ecosystem to suit their own needs, whether on this planet or another.

#6336. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6335. Coffee drinkers show surprising differences deep inside the gut

A study of 61 adults links frequent coffee drinking with differences in intestinal acidity, contractions, and gut bacteria.

Some people finish their morning coffee and soon need the bathroom. There’s also a less visible side to the coffee habit, according to new research.

The researchers worked with 61 healthy adults in Denmark.

The small intestine was more acidic in people who often drank coffee than in those who rarely did. Their stool contained a wider range of bacteria as well.

Francesca Bucci, a PhD student at the University of Copenhagen (UCPH), is the first author.

Previous studies have also linked coffee consumption to differences in gut bacteria.

“But perhaps more importantly, frequent coffee consumption appears to affect the physiology of the gut itself, in other words how the gut functions,” Bucci said.

Whether coffee caused these differences remains unclear. The study cannot say.

Nobody was asked to drink more coffee or to give it up, so the volunteers kept to their usual habits.

The records come from PRIMA, a project that UCPH’s Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports ran over nine days in 2021.

For eight days, the volunteers weighed all their food and drink and put it in writing. They noted their bowel habits as they went.

Frequent coffee drinkers made up most of the group. Forty-eight volunteers had coffee on at least four of the eight days. Only 13 had coffee on two days or fewer.

Among the frequent coffee drinkers, the average coffee intake was about 11.6 fluid ounces (343.5 ml) a day, a little less than one soda can holds.

The team had daily urine samples as a check on those records.

The researchers tested for caffeine and four substances produced as the body breaks caffeine down.

Fifty volunteers also swallowed a wireless capsule roughly 1 inch (26.8 mm) long.

As the capsule moved through the stomach and intestines, it measured acidity, temperature, and pressure. It radioed each reading to a receiver on the volunteer’s belly.

The acidity scale is called pH. Its numbers run lower as acidity rises. Those readings put frequent drinkers’ small intestines at a lower pH than those of rare drinkers.

The pattern extended beyond that two-group comparison.

Across the volunteers, a lower small intestine pH tended to go with greater coffee intake in the records or higher caffeine levels in urine.

Earlier studies have linked coffee to acid release in the stomach, but here stomach pH showed no link to the drink.

Is a more acidic small intestine good or bad for health? The team cannot say yet. The authors raised a possible indirect route between coffee and microbes.

Acidity helps determine which microbes can live in the gut. Coffee might affect them by changing that acidity, they suggested.

A contraction is a squeezing movement of the gut wall.

The team measured contractions with the capsule’s pressure readings, and in the colon, or large intestine, there were more of them in volunteers whose urine had more caffeine breakdown products.

Bucci said those movements can aid digestion and help prevent constipation. The extra squeezing did not speed the capsule up.

Neither the coffee records nor the urine tests showed a link to the capsule’s time in the colon. The authors think the extra movements may stir the contents rather than push them along.

More stirring could allow the colon to absorb more water. That might help explain another observation: heavier coffee intake went with drier stool.

The link with contractions came from the urine results alone. A direct comparison of frequent and rare drinkers found no reliable difference in colon contractions.

In stool from frequent coffee drinkers, there were more distinct kinds of bacteria than in stool from rare coffee drinkers.

A second measure of bacterial variety found no reliable difference between the two groups. Coffee intake had no link to the bacterial community’s overall mix either.

Among the frequent coffee drinkers, three types of bacteria were more abundant. Lawsonibacter is one of them.

Lawsonibacter had already appeared in coffee studies across several groups of people.

A separate study this year found related bacteria at higher levels in people who drank coffee.

Testing so many bacteria makes chance findings a concern. That’s why the researchers applied a statistical correction.

After that correction, none of the three differences met the cutoff for statistical significance.

Lawsonibacter did have support in a separate analysis using the daily records. People who drank more coffee had more of the bacterium.

Coffee wasn’t PRIMA’s original focus. The project examined how diet, gut microbes, and the conditions inside the gut interact. In 2024, an earlier analysis of the volunteers was published.

Nobody asked the volunteers to write down the type of coffee. The records cannot separate regular from decaf.

Caffeine also comes from tea and energy drinks. Seven people whose records listed no coffee still had caffeine in their urine.

The group that rarely drank coffee had only 13 people.

Many comparisons were also run on the capsule readings without the usual statistical correction for doing so. The authors described the study as exploratory.

Henrik Munch Roager, the study’s senior author and an associate professor at UCPH, pointed to findings from outside the study.

“For example, we already know from other studies that coffee can influence a range of processes in the digestive system, including acid secretion in the stomach,” Roager said.

“So there are good reasons to believe that what we are seeing is not merely coincidence. Anecdotally, many people also report that coffee affects their digestion.”

In the paper, Roager disclosed a consulting or advisory relationship with Nestlé.

Roager said that if researchers can work out how coffee affects contractions, the knowledge might be used to stimulate the gut naturally in people with constipation.

As a next step, Roager proposed a trial in which researchers control how much coffee people drink.

Periods of heavy coffee drinking would be compared with periods of none to see whether a person’s gut changes when they start or stop drinking coffee.

Testing both regular and decaf, the authors wrote, could separate caffeine from the other compounds in coffee.

The study is published in the journal Gut Microbiology.

#6334. After LINK mission failure, Swift reenters atmosphere

Editor’s note: This story was originally published Aug. 24, 2026. Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere Nov. 4, 2026, ending its nearly 22-year mission. See the most recent updates at the end of this story.

NASA announced Aug. 19 that the Katalyst Space LINK spacecraft built to boost the aging Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will still rendezvous with the telescope but won’t raise its orbit, after an attitude-control failure sidelined LINK during on-orbit commissioning.

The Swift Boost Mission was a quick-turnaround rescue attempt designed to save the Swift observatory from an early demise. Thanks to increased atmospheric drag from the effects of solar maximum, NASA predicts the space telescope will reenter Earth’s atmosphere later this year, cutting short the extended run of a spacecraft that has delivered a number of breakthroughs in understanding gamma-ray bursts — the highest-energy explosions in the universe.

NASA contracted Katalyst Space Technologies, a startup based in Flagstaff, Arizona, in September 2025 to attempt the rescue, giving the company less than a year to go from concept to execution. Katalyst designed and built the LINK spacecraft for the express purpose of rendezvousing with Swift in orbit, docking with the telescope, and boosting it to a higher altitude for a few more years of science.

LINK launched July 3 on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket but quickly ran into trouble, losing control of two of its three reaction wheels over the last weekend of July. Reaction wheels are spinning flywheels that use angular momentum to let a spacecraft point itself precisely without burning propellant. Three of them, angled correctly, can hold a spacecraft steady on every axis; NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, set to launch Aug. 30, carries six for redundancy. LINK carries only the minimum three, and losing two sent it tumbling at nearly nine degrees per second, compromising communications with ground controllers. Katalyst spent the following weeks firing LINK’s electric propulsion thrusters to slow the spin, eventually taming it to about 1.47 degrees per second by early August — but for a while, it was an open question whether the mission could continue at all.

RELATED: Is NASA’s Swift Boost Mission spinning away?Katalyst uploaded a flight-software fix Aug. 11 that reestablished LINK’s attitude control. But at that point, the timeline was even tighter. Swift had decayed to an orbital height of 216 miles (347 kilometers), just 31 miles (50 km) shy of the point where an orbit-raising mission would become much more difficult. Then came the Aug. 19 announcement from NASA that the spacecraft would still attempt rendezvous and proximity operations — closing in on and flying near Swift to test the maneuvers any future servicing mission would need — but would make no attempt to boost the telescope’s orbit. Without that boost, Swift is still expected to meet a fiery end before the end of the year.

Neither NASA nor Katalyst has said how LINK’s mission will end — whether the spacecraft will dock with Swift and remain there through the telescope’s final days or drift off on its own.

The Swift Boost Mission was framed from the start as a long shot, and NASA’s messaging hasn’t shifted now that it’s fallen short. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in the Aug. 19 announcement.

“We knew this was a high-risk, high-reward mission — a first-of-its kind attempt, developed on an unprecedented timeline driven by the Sun’s activity,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s Astrophysics Division. “We were all hoping for more science from Swift. But we knew the takeaways from this mission would be worthwhile either way, and we have gained so much through the series of accomplishments up to this point.”

The agency plans to lean on its other missions to help cover the gap in gamma-ray burst monitoring once the 21-year-old Swift telescope is lost, as well as file away whatever lessons LINK’s rendezvous can teach us about robotic servicing for missions that follow.

Update Sept. 15, 2026: On Sept. 4, NASA announced that LINK had made its closest approach to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, closing to within roughly 8 miles (13 kilometers) of the space telescope. That’s as close as the two spacecraft will come, NASA says, now that the agency is no longer planning to boost Swift’s orbit, thanks to lingering attitude-control problems aboard LINK.

In the days following the rendezvous, Katalyst put the robotic servicer through the paces: raising its orbit, aligning it with Swift’s path, unfurling all three robotic arms, and firing all three xenon thrusters at once on Aug. 30. With no further approach planned, Katalyst expects LINK to deorbit later this month.

With the boost off the table, Swift’s team switched its ultraviolet/optical and X-ray telescopes back on Aug. 26, months after powering them down to reduce draft and slow Swift’s decay. A third instrument, the Burst Alert Telescope, should follow in the coming weeks. NASA anticipates the gamma ray observatory will reenter and burn up before the end of the year.

Update Sept. 29, 2026: On Sept. 25, LINK deorbited and reentered Earth’s atmosphere, concluding the mission. LINK was not successful in its attempt to capture and boost Swift’s orbit, but the team collected useful data across 85 days of LINK’s operation that will help inform future missions.

Update Nov. 9, 2026: The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere Nov. 4 at 7:39 a.m. EST, according to NASA, coming down over Indonesia’s North Sumatra region. While some components may have survived the journey and made it to the surface, NASA expected most of the spacecraft to disintegrate completely.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer for Astronomy and is based in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

#6333. El Niño’s global death toll hides a troubling imbalance

Very strong El Niño years are linked to more heat deaths worldwide, with poorer countries bearing a disproportionate share of the burden.

Very strong El Niño years are associated with an estimated 107,000 additional heat-related deaths and 113,000 fewer cold-related deaths annually, compared with neutral conditions.

Globally, those numbers nearly cancel out, but they shouldn’t reassure anyone.

The people dying from heat and the people spared from cold are not the same people.

That’s the core finding of a new study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal).

The research team, coordinated by Joan Ballester Claramunt, analyzed climate and mortality data from 1,667 regions in 125 countries spanning 1980 to 2023.

This period includes three particularly brutal El Niño episodes (1982–1983, 1997–1998, and 2015–2016).

They then extrapolated those relationships to 3,331 regions in 189 countries, covering more than eight billion people.

This is the first study to put global and regional numbers on the link between El Niño intensity and temperature-related deaths.

El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a natural cycle. During El Niño, unusually warm surface waters release heat into the atmosphere, reshuffling weather patterns across the planet.

Temperatures rise in some regions, fall in others. The global average ticks up. But the health consequences don’t distribute evenly.

During very strong El Niño years, the largest jumps in heat-related mortality hit South America (76% increase), Small Island Developing States (66%), sub-Saharan Africa (54%), and South and Southeast Asia (43%).

Many of these areas include tropical populations where additional warming can increase the risk of dangerous heat exposure.

Meanwhile, the cold-related mortality reductions tend to benefit higher-latitude, wealthier countries with better infrastructure and healthcare systems.

The inequality gets sharper when you sort by development. Countries with low or medium scores on the Human Development Index make up 42% of the world’s population.

They account for nearly 68% of the estimated increase in heat-related deaths during a very strong El Niño.

The medium-HDI group alone accounted for an estimated 61,863 additional heat-related deaths annually – 58% of the global increase.

These are countries with growing cities, limited air conditioning, and fragile health systems.

“The fact that these two changes largely offset each other globally does not mean that El Niño is beneficial to health,” said lead author Natalia Shartova from ISGlobal.

“Combined heat- and cold-related mortality increases in countries with fewer resources and, in an increasingly warm climate, future episodes could exacerbate these inequalities.”

“Furthermore, El Niño’s effects extend beyond temperature anomalies to include extreme weather events, such as floods and periods of drought.”

Here’s the frustrating part. El Niño is one of the most predictable climate patterns on the planet.

Meteorologists can forecast El Niño several months ahead, giving governments time to prepare for potential health impacts.

That makes it fundamentally different from a surprise earthquake or an unexpected flood.

The mortality toll it brings is, in principle, something governments could prepare for.

“Our findings identify the regions and seasons most affected by El Niño and, therefore, where health preparedness could be most valuable,” Ballester explained.

“This could support coordinated action plans involving health authorities, region-specific warnings and targeted interventions for populations at greatest risk.”

NOAA forecasts indicate that the ongoing El Niño is likely to remain strong to very strong through early 2027.

The authors note that their estimates come from retrospective data and can’t be used to directly predict mortality for the ongoing event.

But the map of vulnerability they’ve drawn is clear enough: South America, sub-Saharan Africa, small island nations, South and Southeast Asia.

The places that get hit hardest are the places least equipped to absorb the blow.

Mortality records weren’t available for one-third of the countries in the analysis – mostly under-resourced nations.

Estimates for most low-HDI countries and much of sub-Saharan Africa were built from models trained on data from other regions, adjusted for local climate and socioeconomic conditions.

That’s the best available approach, but it means the numbers for the most vulnerable places carry the most uncertainty.

The true toll in those regions could be higher or lower. Either way, the gap in data mirrors the gap in protection.

El Niño has always been part of Earth’s climate system. It isn’t new. But it’s playing out against a background that is.

Global temperatures are rising and baseline heat exposure is climbing.

A strong El Niño episode layered on top of an already warming planet compounds risk in places with little adaptive capacity.

The near-cancellation of additional heat deaths and fewer cold deaths in the global totals masks an uneven burden. In the regions facing the largest increases, there is little comfort in that apparent balance.

The study is published in the journal Nature Medicine.

#6332. Scientists Have Hunted Dark Energy for Decades. They May Be Chasing a Cosmic Ghost.

A new study finds a mathematical solution for the universe’s expansion within the original work of Albert Einstein.

In 1916, Albert Einstein published his foundational paper on the General Theory of Relativity in the German-language science journal Annalen der Physik. Now, 110 years later, scientists are still debating just how right Einstein’s conception of the universe really was, especially as it relates to the accelerated expansion of the universe. Of course, at the time of his revolutionary publication, the world still didn’t know that the universe was expanding, so a year later, Einstein introduced a “lambda” cosmological constant to his equations to form a stable, non-collapsing universe.

Thanks to the pioneering work of Edwin Hubble in 1929, the world learned that the universe was actually expanding, and in response Einstein discarded lambda, calling it his “greatest blunder.” What Einstein couldn’t have known was that, decades after his death, lambda would make a comeback. When astronomers discovered in the late 1990s that the universe’s expansion was speeding up, the constant became central to the modern model of the cosmos, known as “Lambda-Cold Dark Matter,” or ΛCDM. Rising along with the renaissance of the cosmological constant was a concept known as dark energy, the force that made this accelerated expansion possible.

This ΛCDM is a pretty tidy description of the universe with one glaring plot hole—we’ve never directly seen or measured dark energy. Because of this lack of evidence, some scientists have searched for other possible explanations, even disregarding Einstein entirely, but a new study by researchers at the University of California, Davis takes the opposite approach. According to their research, published earlier this year in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A, Einstein was actually more right than he ever knew.

To build their case for a universe without dark energy, UC Davis mathematics professor emeritus Blake Temple and his colleagues turned to Friedmann spacetimes. These are a family of solutions to Einstein’s field equations originally developed by Alexander Friedmann, the Soviet mathematician who first proposed that the universe is expanding.

“The Friedmann family of spacetimes describe a uniform three-dimensional Universe of galaxies expanding in time from an initial Big Bang singularity at a rate determined by Einstein’s field equations,” the authors write in the study.

The researchers rewrote Einstein's equations in a “self-similar” form, meaning the equations keep the same structure at any scale, much like a fractal. This version of the equations let them test a key question: if the smooth, even spread of matter in a Friedmann universe gets slightly disturbed, does it settle back to normal or move further away from it? They found that the small disturbances don’t fade away. Instead, they grow, at both large and small scales. In other words, a perfectly uniform Friedmann universe can’t stay that way.

“Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical. You’ll never observe them in nature,” Temple said in a press statement. “The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy.”

That instability is the heart of the argument. Einstein’s own static universe had a similar flaw: it was so delicately balanced that the slightest nudge would tip it over. “We prove that, like Einstein’s static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales,” Temple added. As the universe drifts away from a perfect Friedmann state, the team argues, its expansion naturally speeds up. That would mean Einstein’s original equations, without lambda, may explain the acceleration we see today, without dark energy.

The work is purely mathematical, though, and it comes with a catch. The team’s model has a center, so we’d need to live near a special spot in the universe for it to match what astronomers see. That goes against a basic assumption of modern cosmology. Temple argues that ΛCDM has the same problem, however.

For now, scientists around the world continue to probe for the elusive dark matter and dark energy that presumably dominates the universe (with some detectors reporting encouraging results). But the study raises an intriguing possibility: we might be chasing a cosmological ghost.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6331. Our increasingly cluttered skies

In the 2013 movie Gravity, Russia destroys its own spy satellite with a missile, creating a cloud of shrapnel and subsequent orbital collisions that rip apart spaceships and astronauts alike. Earth orbit is a place where life imitates art: Eight years later, Moscow launched an actual missile strike on a defunct Soviet satellite, blasting thousands of pieces of metal through space and threatening the International Space Station (ISS) at the nearby altitude of 250 miles (400 kilometers). As the lethal grapeshot sped through space 10 times faster than a rifle bullet, astronauts and cosmonauts huddled in escape pods. Luckily, the debris overshot them, avoiding a real-life Gravity sequel.

This close call was not a lone event. In 2009, history’s first collision between two intact satellites — an American Iridium 33 and a defunct Russian Cosmos-2251 — generated at least 2,000 pieces of debris, some of which passed on uncertain trajectories about 7 miles (11.3 km) from the ISS in March 2012 as crew sheltered in two docked Soyuz craft. And just last year, Chinese crew aboard the Tiangong space station delayed their return to Earth and left their replacements temporarily without an evacuation vehicle when a piece of space junk smaller than 0.04 inch (1 millimeter) hit their docked return capsule. Fallout from these incidents remains in orbit today, along with myriad debris from other adventures. These fragments are collectively known as space junk.

Scientists warn that space junk may be fast approaching a critical threshold that sparks cascading satellite collisions, creating an impassable belt of debris and rendering that region of Earth orbit too dangerous to use. This is called Kessler syndrome, a concept outlined in a 1978 paper by NASA researcher Donald Kessler. Surpassing that threshold is not inevitable, but avoiding it will require considerable engineering and stringent international cooperation.

The most crowded area of space is occupied by the lowest stable Earth orbits, where the equivalent mass of 150 space shuttles currently spins around our planet. Called low Earth orbit (LEO), it is loosely defined as altitudes between 120 miles and 1,200 miles (200 to 2,000 km). LEO is so frequently used because it is the Goldilocks zone where a complete orbit takes two hours or less — high enough to minimize atmospheric drag and stay aloft, yet low enough in the magnetosphere to help shield humans and electronics from radiation damage.

Large constellations of satellites are now being put into LEO. The most numerous of these is SpaceX’s Starlink, whose 10,000+ satellites comprise 66% of LEO traffic. Each rocket carries several dozen satellites weighing as much as a ton each and spanning up to 23 feet (7 meters), providing internet support for remote locations. When they fail, most will reenter the atmosphere and burn up, either within a few weeks of launch if they fail in the initial low orbit, or if they successfully push to their intended higher orbit, within a few years.

But the rate at which LEO is filling up — Starlink had 122 launches in 2025 alone — has some experts worried that we are on the cusp of eventual calamity. “We might not see a substantial change during our own generation, but we will see a steady increase in risks and collisions,” says Hugh Lewis, a University of Birmingham astronautics professor.

Ever since SpaceX launched its first batch of Starlink satellites in 2019, the company has touted its satellites’ avoidance capabilities: Ion-propelled thrusters and autonomous AI guidance systems trigger a Starlink satellite to maneuver away from an object ahead of a close pass if the risk of a collision exceeds a certain threshold. While the industry standard is to maneuver if there is a 1-in-10,000 chance of a collision, SpaceX has tightened its trigger over the years. Today, Starlink satellites take avoiding action if the likelihood of colliding is just 1 in 3.3 million. Based on the current rate of avoidance maneuvers as reported by the company in July 2026, the constellation’s satellites overall are performing more than 400,000 avoidance maneuvers per year.

With other companies and countries joining the LEO space boom — and a lack of coordination between them — SpaceX has taken further action to safeguard its fleet. The company announced in January that it was shifting the bulk of its satellites 13% lower than their original 340-mile (550 km) altitude in large part to reduce aggregate risk, as there are fewer objects that low to collide with. Additionally, lower initial orbits mean failed satellites will naturally deorbit more quickly, preventing them from becoming part of the problem.

OneWeb, a European broadband internet service, sends its satellites to a higher altitude of 750 miles (1,200 km). Because atmospheric drag decreases exponentially with altitude, higher satellites shed drag and gain longevity. But this can generate longer-lasting space junk in the event of failure: At the altitude OneWeb operates, an object could stay in orbit for centuries.

Both OneWeb and Starlink use their own propulsion to deorbit for post-mission disposal, with satellites lasting roughly five years. But if those systems fail, the satellites become space junk, with their orbital altitude determining their longevity.

While operators work to keep space debris in check, external factors can complicate their efforts, either causing orbiting objects to come down prematurely or else increasing the time they’re likely to stay in orbit, crowding the field.

Climate change can cause the latter. When solar photons hit carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, the molecules release energy as infrared heat. The troposphere, the atmospheric layer closest to the ground, is sufficiently dense to trap that heat, causing global warming. But higher up, the atmosphere is so thin that radiation escapes, cooling and thinning the mesosphere, our atmosphere’s middle layer. Excessive greenhouse gases can accelerate this process, causing successive atmospheric layers to pancake downward, reducing drag at any given altitude.

According to a study by Lewis’ team, this means satellites that were expected to come down in a couple of years could stay up much longer, quintupling the lifetime of some space debris by the end of this century.

Solar activity has the opposite effect. “In the critical range of 300 to 500 kilometers [190 to 310 miles], the density of the atmosphere is very dependent on whether we’re at solar maximum or solar minimum,” says Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist formerly at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and now based in the U.K. His decades-long dedication to developing software that catalogs and tracks all rocket launches and reentries has gained him a reputation as the unofficial guru of space traffic and space junk. Each 11-year solar maximum brings an increase in X-ray flux, which ionizes the atmosphere and causes heating, so the atmosphere expands. This, in turn, pushes denser gases higher, increasing drag at the height of LEO. Both effects cause orbiting objects to reenter sooner.

For higher LEO satellites, McDowell says, the question isn’t how many years they are designed to stay in orbit, but how many solar maxima they can survive. For example, the Hubble Space Telescope suffers a pronounced loss of altitude each solar maximum, each bigger than the last as the observatory drops lower and the atmospheric density is greater. Without intervention, it could come down in the next solar maximum.

In a paper accepted for publication in Acta Astronautica, a team led by Samantha Lawler, an astronomer at the University of Regina in Saskatchewan, created a “CRASH clock” characterizing the time it would take for a collision to occur in the absence of all avoidance maneuvers — say, during a “widespread disruptive event” such as a solar storm or massive software failure. (CRASH is an acronym for Collision Realization And Significant Harm.) Once an initial collision takes place, it could cause further, ongoing damage as its debris goes on to spark yet more strikes. Initial calculations based on 2018 satellite traffic allowed 164 days before collisions under the worst circumstances, but as Starlink and other megaconstellations have proliferated, recent calculations bring the countdown to a shocking three days.

While most of the public’s attention is on lower LEO orbits occupied by Starlink, higher LEO altitudes may soon become more crowded as well. SpaceX recently submitted an application to the Federal Communications Commission for space-based data centers with 1 million satellites orbiting much higher than its Starlink fleet. The heavier electrical load of a data center will require vast solar panels and cooling fins, considerably larger than on Starlink satellites. These would also be much more reflective than Starlink, which is already posing serious headaches for astronomers by interfering with observations. But data centers at these altitudes could also create space-junk minefields.

To sustain its million-satellite data center, SpaceX would have to launch about 200,000 satellites each year. If 1% of those fail — the same rate that SpaceX reports for Starlink satellites — “you’re replacing 2,000 satellites a year,” says Lewis. “Those failed satellites alone would meet the critical Kessler threshold, without even looking at the million satellites” making up the functional constellation itself.

Even higher orbits are not immune. Above LEO lies medium Earth orbit (MEO), from 1,240 to 22,000 miles (2,000 to 35,400 km), home to many GPS and navigation satellites. Beyond that sits high Earth orbit (HEO), including geostationary orbit (GEO) directly above Earth’s equator, where satellites sit with 24-hour periods that match Earth’s own rotation. In January, a Russian spy satellite unexpectedly fragmented in an HEO graveyard orbit. The event could have been caused by an impact, suggesting that space junk is infecting even the highest altitudes as well.

The route to addressing orbital crowding requires determining where solutions are most needed. And LEO remains the area most urgently in need of emergency triage. Astronautical engineer Darren McKnight, senior technical officer for LeoLabs, a company that helps coordinate a global network of about a dozen ground-based radars tracking space objects, worries most about LEO orbits above where Starlink — with its state-of-the-art crash-avoidance technology — operates. “I would say that right now we have a contraction of the arteries at about 975 kilometers [600 miles], and if we have a heart attack, it’s going to happen there,” he says.

In the 1970s and ’80s, countries launching spacecraft left rocket bodies and payloads in higher LEO. These large objects have no crash-avoidance capabilities. But this concentration of threats also creates opportunities for reducing risk. “If you take out the 10 worst offenders at 840 and 975 kilometers [520 and 600 miles], you can reduce debris-generating potential by 30%,” McKnight says. These altitudes were two distinct orbital highways historically favored for different missions. Of those top offenders, three are defunct satellites (one European and two Russian) and the rest are rocket stages (one Japanese, two Chinese, one Russian, and three Soviet). That space junk lingers for more than a quarter-century and has the potential to generate even more debris when it is hit, compounding the problem over time. That’s why, McKnight says, removing those worst offenders also offers “much better return on investment” when it comes to resources spent on space junk mitigation — that is, reducing or even retrieving space junk.

Such efforts are gaining traction, but still have a long way to go. Some are managed by national space agencies solely for the purposes of cleaning up their trash, while others are undertaken by private companies purely for profit.

Yet the only true mitigation of space junk to date was in 2022, when the Chinese Shijian-21 satellite retrieved and towed a defunct Beidou-2 G2 navigation satellite from crowded geostationary orbit and parked it in a graveyard orbit 1,865 miles (3,000 km) higher to reduce the risk of collisions. More recently, in 2025, the Shijian-25 satellite launched and docked with fuel-depleted Shijian-21, likely to test refueling capability to prolong its operational lifetime and prevent it from becoming space junk itself. U.S. Space Force officials labeled the maneuver a “priority watch” event due to its potential military use.

Japan-based Astroscale has flown two test missions in LEO that have rendezvoused with targets; its next mission aims to retrieve a OneWeb communications satellite slated for retirement. Other players include Switzerland-based ClearSpace, which is partnering with the European Space Agency, and TransAstra, an aspiring asteroid-mining company based in California. TransAstra has conducted preliminary tests aboard the ISS with a novel capture bag and hopes to launch in 2028 to snag a 100-ton asteroid. That same technology could be adapted for space junk retrieval, especially smaller debris.

For McDowell, the astronomer and spaceflight historian, the satellite boom brings mixed feelings. He wonders if satellite-cluttered skies mean all serious astronomical observing will one day only be done from space telescopes, rather than ground-based observatories. “I am a fan of space exploration,” he says, “but I want us to do it sustainably, in a way that doesn’t trash the environment.”

There is a long way to go. But with the space industry soaring to a value of more than $600 billion, some see the clutter in its wake as an opportunity to profit from clearing space debris out of harm’s way.

Though the sky may be falling, the same genius that placed it there has the capacity to fix it.

Randall Hyman is a science writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including Nature, Science, and Smithsonian.
