#6330. Canada’s endangered wildlife is stuck in a legal loophole

Canada's Species at Risk Act has a stage with no deadline, and since 2017 just 6% of species found to be at risk cleared it on time.

When scientists assess a species as endangered, it is easy to assume legal protections will follow. In Canada, that process often stalls.

Since 2017, the country’s experts have recommended 288 wildlife species for listing under the Species at Risk Act.

Only 17 of them, about 6%, reached cabinet within the government’s own recommended timelines.

Peter Thompson, a postdoctoral fellow at Simon Fraser University, led the study with colleagues from the University of British Columbia and ten other institutions.

They rebuilt the paper trail for 963 species from the federal registry, about 5,700 documents in all.

“Canada boasts a wonderful array of wildlife and Canadians care about protecting our biodiversity,” Thompson said.

“When endangered species are left in endless political limbo, the chance of them going extinct increases, which is really against the best interests of those who care.”

Listing a species in Canada takes two stages. First, an independent panel called COSEWIC assesses how much trouble the species is in and recommends a status.

Then the federal government consults provinces, Indigenous rights holders, industry and the public, weighs the economic fallout, and the cabinet makes the final call.

The law sets deadlines at the start and the end.

The environment minister must respond to the panel within 90 days, and once the file reaches cabinet, a decision is due within nine months.

Both of those deadlines were met for every species in the study.

The middle step, where the minister’s office consults and decides whether to forward the file at all, has no legal deadline.

In 2017, the government published recommended timelines for it: 12 months for most species and 24 months for those needing longer consultation.

The authors call this stage the loophole, and it is where every delay in their data occurred.

Comparing eight years of assessments before 2017 with the eight years after, the team found that fewer species reached cabinet within the recommended timelines.

Before the policy, 16% of assessed species reached cabinet within the recommended timelines. After it, 6% did.

Species that did get forwarded took about 29 months on average.

As of January 2025, 181 species assessed since 2017 were still waiting. Most of those, 153, had already passed their deadline.

The degree of danger made no difference. Species assessed as endangered waited about as long as those assessed as special concern, the lowest tier.

The sharpest pattern was in the water. Of the 49 marine fish and 15 marine mammals assessed since 2017, none had been sent to cabinet by January 2025.

Among freshwater fish, 79% were still waiting, and among land mammals, 90%. Fish and mammals, far more than birds or plants, were the groups left waiting.

The waiting list includes 31 populations of Pacific salmon, every one assessed as endangered or threatened.

In the government’s 2023 report to Parliament, all 31 carried the same sentence: the collection of information needed for a decision is extensive and underway.

Aquatic species answer to a second department, Fisheries and Oceans Canada, which is charged with both the fishing economy and conservation.

The authors wrote that much of the marine delay appears tied to worries about how a listing would affect fisheries, though they could not measure that influence directly.

The 2017 policy requires the government to publish a reason whenever it misses a timeline.

The team checked the 2023 report against the 173 species then in limbo and found entries for only 110 of them. Of the 63 missing, 57 were fish.

Among the entries that did exist, nearly half cited a need for more information and a fifth gave no specific reason.

Four in ten said consultations were already finished, without explaining why the file had then stalled.

“Many of the explanations given are pretty unsatisfactory, often amounting to nothing more than ‘the analysis of information is underway,'” Thompson said.

The Saskatchewan-Nelson River population of lake sturgeon was assessed as endangered in 2017 after a 90% decline since the 1960s.

As of January 2025, it had received no decision, and the panel named dams as a key threat. In the years since, a new hydroelectric station began operating on the Nelson River.

Limber pine, a tree assessed as endangered in 2014, completed consultations in 2021 but was still awaiting a decision in January 2025.

Several caribou herds completed consultations years ago and remained unlisted, leaving them without the Act’s requirement to identify critical habitat.

The study can’t say how many of these species declined because of the wait, only that none of them had the law’s protections while they waited.

The authors propose binding deadlines for every stage, better-resourced consultations, and a specific public reason each time a file stalls, so the listing process can be checked from outside.

The proposed changes would make the process more transparent and give species awaiting decisions a clearer path toward protection.

The full study was published in the journal FACETS.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6328. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

J.R. McConnell et al. Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early 20th C copper production. Nature Sustainability. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9

#6327. Octopus suckers hold a surprising clue to how evolution builds new body parts

Cuttlefish and octopus arms use the leg-building genes of insects, but their suckers run on a gene from the embryo's first days.

Insects and mice lay out their legs with the same small set of genes.

The genetic instructions used to grow an octopus arm are different from the ones used to grow the little suction cups on that arm.

None of the limb-patterning genes the team examined were active in forming suckers.

Instead, the researchers identified an active gene also involved in shaping the early embryo.

A team at the University of Tokyo mapped where two dozen genes are active in the developing arms of cuttlefish and octopuses, and in the foot of a pond snail.

Ryosuke Kimbara led the work at the Misaki Marine Biological Station, part of the university’s School of Science, with Hisanori Kohtsuka, Kohei Oguchi, Daisuke Kurokawa and Toru Miura.

He is now at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology.

Kimbara noted that the search didn’t go where the team expected it to.

“At first, we hypothesized that appendage patterning genes would be involved both in arm and sucker patterning. But we ran into a challenge in identifying the genes expressed in suckers,” Kimbara said.

“Therefore, we changed the method into a more comprehensive one and continued screening until we found a gene with a distinctive expression pattern in developing suckers, and it wasn’t where we expected to find it.”

The main animal was the golden cuttlefish. Adults were netted off the Okusu fishing port in Yokosuka, on Sagami Bay, each spring from 2020 to 2023.

Their fertilized eggs went into seawater tanks held at 66°F to 70°F (19°C to 21°C). Hatchlings were fed small shrimp and crabs caught on the shore outside the station.

A cephalopod‘s arms are thought to come from the flat, muscular foot that its snail-like ancestors crawled on.

So the team also raised embryos of the gold-spot octopus, from adults collected in the Seto Inland Sea and Tokyo Bay.

To compare the arms with a molluscan foot, they also raised great pond snails from a laboratory strain.

To see where a gene is working, the researchers stained embryos with a probe that colors only the cells where that gene is switched on.

They focused on the second pair of arms, at the stages when new suckers were budding along them.

The first genes they checked have names that give away their history.

Distal-less, Dachshund, Homothorax and Extradenticle were discovered in fruit flies, where they help mark off a leg from base to tip. Their counterparts do similar work in a mouse limb.

In the cuttlefish arm, each one colored its own zone. Distal-less lit up the middle and tip of the arm. Homothorax and Extradenticle stayed near the base, where no suckers grow.

A fifth gene marked the back of the arm, opposite the sucker side. The same zones showed up in the octopus arm.

In the snail’s foot, the same genes were on, but spread across the whole foot with no zones at all.

The patterned version, the team argues, is what turned an undivided foot into an arm with a base, a tip and a sucker side.

The team found no activity from those limb-patterning genes in the sucker buds.

A second family of signals, known as BMP, draws the line between the sucker side of the arm and the back.

A gene called Bmp2/4 was active on the back, while Chordin, which blocks Bmp2/4, was strongest on the sucker side and in the newest buds at the arm tip.

In the snail’s foot, those signals were absent, though they were active elsewhere in the larva.

So the front-to-back layout of a cephalopod arm looks like something cephalopods invented.

Chordin has a second known job, in starting nerve tissue, and the staining fit that.

Nerves branching off the arm’s central cord had already grown into a sucker bud before the bud began to dimple inward into a cup.

With none of the leg genes in the suckers, the team changed tactics. They cut the second arms of young cuttlefish into tip, middle and base, and separately into sucker side and back.

Then they sequenced every gene active in each piece, with three animals per piece.

Thousands of genes differed between the pieces.

Only nine were high in both the tip and the sucker side. Just one of those nine, Ets1, was known to encode a protein that regulates other genes.

Ets1 normally works during gastrulation, the stage in which a hollow ball of embryonic cells folds inward to form the body’s layers.

In mollusks and other animals, it is tied to a process in which cells in a sheet loosen their grip on each other and migrate.

In the cuttlefish arm, Ets1 was on across the ridge at the arm tip where new suckers form and in the youngest buds.

As a bud dimpled inward, the gene’s activity narrowed to the dimple. In finished suckers near the base, it was almost gone. The octopus showed the same pattern.

A dye that outlines cell membranes showed the cells doing something that matched the gene. In a young bud, a neat single layer of surface cells covered a loose inner mass.

In a bud forming its cup, the surface cells had stretched into columns. At the deepest point of the dimple, the border between the surface layer and the inner mass had blurred.

Kimbara’s team reads that as cells changing shape and moving, the way they do when an embryo first folds. In the snail, Ets1 was scattered across the foot rather than concentrated anywhere.

Cephalopods have only one copy of Ets1, so the gene was not duplicated and freed up for a new role.

Its sucker job more likely came from changes in when and where it is switched on, or from mutations in the gene itself.

“Our findings suggest that cephalopod arm development involves conserved patterning genes also used in appendage development in other animals like insects and mammals,” Kimbara said.

“But suckers on their arms have a unique developmental mechanism in which genes used in early embryogenesis, Ets1, are reused.”

Everything here is a map of where genes are active, and it isn’t a test of what they do.

Nobody has switched Ets1 off in a cuttlefish embryo to see whether the suckers fail to form, and the team names that as the experiment the finding needs.

Whether sucker cells really repeat the embryo’s folding process isn’t settled either.

A second gene from that process, FoxO, was on in cuttlefish sucker buds but not in the octopus’s, and tracking single cells as a bud folds has not been done. The snail was examined at only one larval stage.

Cuttlefish and octopus suckers also end up built differently and grip differently, Kimbara said.

So the molecular machinery may have evolved separately in each lineage, even though the early steps look alike.

Next, the researchers want to study the nautilus, a member of an ancient cephalopod lineage that grips with sticky, tongue-shaped pads on its tentacles instead of suckers.

Whether Ets1 is active in those pads is the first thing the team wants to check.

The full study was published in the journal iScience.

#6326. An Excavation at a Soviet Gulag Camp Just Discovered What Russia Didn’t Want the World To Know

Bottles, bullet casings, and an eyewitness suggest prisoners stayed locked up long after the camp “closed.”

Between the 1930s and the 1950s, the Soviet Union imprisoned millions of people in the Gulag, a vast network of forced-labor camps where political prisoners and other perceived enemies of the state were worked, starved, and often killed. The Soviet officials who ran it kept careful records, but those records tell only the version of events the captors wanted told. According to those files, Steplag, a Gulag camp complex in central Kazakhstan, operated from 1948 to 1956. But a new archaeological excavation at one of Steplag’s former camps, combined with a local eyewitness’ memories, suggests that at least one camp’s story didn’t end when the paperwork said it did.

Archaeologists from the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen, Czech Republic, worked with Gulag.cz, a nonprofit that has studied Gulag history since 2009. Together they gained official access to a former Steplag camp mainly used for political prisoners in the village of Terekty, near Zhezkazgan in Kazakhstan. What they found tells a brutal story.

“We have found the remains of a women’s camp, a men’s camp with archaeological artifacts as well as standing structures, an entire settlement for guards, and a command headquarters, which was later occupied by people from a nearby village that has since disappeared,” said Pavel Vareka, the university’s lead archaeologist, in a translated statement. “The remains of an economic zone have also survived, where imprisoned men and women were forced to perform slave labor, as well as a forgotten cemetery for the victims.”

The teams documented the remains of the camp, which likely held more than 20,000 prisoners from Ukraine, the Baltic states, and other countries, including more than 20 Czechs.

Stepan Cernousek, chairman of Gulag.cz, said that the official records show camp operations ending in 1956, but that date doesn’t match the archaeological evidence or the eyewitness account. “It appears that although Steplag itself was abolished, with its camp administration being eliminated in Moscow with the stroke of a pen, that did not mean that the camp actually ended,” he told Radio Prague International. “This camp, where the women were held, continued to operate. There were guards and prisoners, but it apparently came under a different structure.”

In other words, Moscow officially dissolved Steplag in 1956, but some camps may not have released all their prisoners. According to Cernousek, the Moscow archives leave this out because the captors were the ones writing the reports.

Physical evidence supports his view. The excavation uncovered glass bottles dating from 1959 to 1961. That matches the account of Terekty’s oldest resident, 78-year-old Mizambai Bralin, who moved to the village in 1959 and remembers the women’s camp still full of prisoners. The excavators also found spent cartridges at the base of the guard towers. “They kept those women there like animals,” Bralin said in a statement. “I cannot imagine how any man could ever shoot a woman.”

Cernousek said Bralin’s testimony was essential. “Many things fell into place,” he said of their conversation. “Without him, we probably would not have answers to 90 percent of the questions—we would only have guesses.”

Cernousek founded Gulag.cz to understand the history of the Soviet Gulag system and its impact on former Soviet satellite states. The group once did research in Siberia but can no longer travel to Russia. Kazakhstan, which had at least 20 camp complexes, has since opened its doors to researchers. The group’s work with the university archaeologists is the first archaeological research of its kind at a Gulag camp in Kazakhstan.

Because archaeology can rewrite Gulag history in ways that archives can’t, Cernousek stressed the importance of exploring the former camps where the Gulag system imprisoned millions of people and forced them into labor. “The lives and horrors took place right there, on the site, in the steppe,” he said. “People spent months and years there in captivity, so that memory has somehow remained embedded in the ground and among the local inhabitants. It is important to go to these places, rather than relying only on archives in Moscow or Kyiv.”

To rebuild the camp’s layout while preserving what remains, the team used drone surveys, surface documentation, metal detection, and limited excavation. The research also addresses a broader question. “Because it is said that the Czechoslovak communist camps were essentially copies of the Soviet Gulag, archaeologists are asking to what extent this is actually true,” Cernousek said. He added that the camps appear to have varied a lot in their appearance, building materials, and layout. Still, much was the same, including three layers of barbed-wire fencing, guard towers, solitary confinement cells, and some of the same everyday equipment.

“Of course, the regime imposed on the prisoners was also the same,” he said.

This first exploration in central Kazakhstan is helping write a new record of the Soviet Gulag camps, and it comes at a critical time. “Putin’s regime is trying to erase the history of the Gulag and Soviet repression from public memory and public space, while at the same time defending many Soviet crimes,” Cernousek said. “Kazakhstan is becoming increasingly open to this kind of research, and we are encountering a great deal of support and understanding here.”

#6325. SpaceX goes for a Starship double catch

On Monday, Nov. 9, SpaceX is targeting 10:03 p.m. EST to launch USSF-627 on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The mission is a classified payload for the U.S. Space Force. The booster will aim for the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

On Wednesday, Nov. 11, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 6:40 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed.

On Thursday, Nov. 12, ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), is targeting 2:50 p.m. EST for a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan, according to Next Spaceflight. Kuaizhou 11 is a solid-fueled rocket designed for fast-turnaround launches of small satellites. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Later Thursday, Nov. 12, SpaceX returns to Vandenberg at 11:23 p.m. EST for USSF-317, another classified Space Force mission on a Falcon 9. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Nov. 13, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is targeting 12:54 p.m. EST for Vulcan Leo 1 from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The launch ends a nine-month grounding that followed a nozzle failure during February’s USSF-87 mission; ULA says the boosters now carry a redesigned nozzle. It’s also Vulcan’s first flight for Amazon, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the broadband megaconstellation formerly known as Project Kuiper.

Later Friday, Nov. 13, SpaceX opens a 75-minute window at 5:45 p.m. EST for Starship Flight 15 from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. It’s the 15th test flight of the company’s reusable megarocket and only its second trip to orbit, after Flight 14’s success in September. About six and a half minutes after liftoff, the Super Heavy booster should return to the launch tower and be caught by its chopstick arms. SpaceX has made that catch before with the rocket’s V1 and V2 boosters, but this will be a first for the new V3 booster. The upper stage, called Ship, will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites as it did in September.

You can watch the launch live on SpaceX’s website.

The next day, SpaceX will try to catch Ship, too. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea where the vehicle flips upright, fires its engines, and sets down on the water. This time, after about 14 orbits at roughly 171 miles (275 km) up — a flight of more than 22 hours — Ship must run that same landing maneuver over Starbase, settling into the tower’s arms instead.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for the catch is prepared. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile. If the catch works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full. On Saturday, Nov. 14, Rocket Lab is targeting 12:30 a.m. EST for The Mountain God Rises, the 100th launch of its Electron rocket, from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. Electron will deploy a QPS-SAR satellite for the Japanese company iQPS in Rocket Lab’s 11th dedicated launch for the operator. The iQPS constellation uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR), bouncing microwaves off the ground to map Earth’s surface even through rain, smoke, and total darkness.

On Monday, Nov. 2, Rocket Lab launched The Sea God Surveys from New Zealand at 11:41 a.m. EST, delivering another QPS-SAR radar satellite for iQPS. It was Electron’s 99th flight and Rocket Lab’s 10th mission for the Japanese operator. That evening at 7:15 p.m. EST, CAS Space’s Kinetica 2 lifted off from Jiuquan and placed 18 satellites for China’s SpaceSail broadband constellation in polar orbit. It was only the rocket’s second flight, following its debut in March.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, a Long March 2C launched from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China with three Yaogan 51 satellites. Yaogan is the label China gives its government Earth-observation spacecraft, which are widely believed to perform military reconnaissance.

Friday, Nov. 6, brought two launches about an hour apart. Galactic Energy’s Ceres 2 put four satellites in orbit from Jiuquan at 6:37 p.m. EST. Then, after several days of delays, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-432 mission from Vandenberg at 7:48 p.m. EST, landing the booster on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Saturday, Nov. 7, Russia’s Aerospace Forces launched a Soyuz-2.1b from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in northern Russia. The payload is believed to be a GLONASS satellite for Russia’s version of GPS. The week closed Sunday, Nov. 8, when a Long March 12 lifted off from the Wenchang commercial launch site on Hainan Island at 3:24 p.m. EST, carrying nine more satellites for Guowang, China’s state-run internet megaconstellation.

On Friday, Nov. 20, CASC is targeting 6:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 8A launch from Wenchang, likely carrying another batch of Guowang satellites, according to Next Spaceflight.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2:00 a.m. EST, a Long March 12 is slated to fly another Guowang group from Wenchang, according to Next Spaceflight.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6323. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 10: Seek Saturn’s two-toned moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 9: Chase Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS

Challenge yourself to pick up Saturn’s moon Iapetus, which tonight reaches greatest eastern elongation 9.4’ east of the ringed planet. The two-toned moon is tidally locked to its parent world, which means it rotates in time with its orbit. At eastern elongation, Iapetus’ darker hemisphere faces earthward, reducing the moon’s magnitude to nearly 12. This, combined with its distance from Saturn, makes it more of a challenge to find, but you can give it a try if you’ve got a larger scope.

Try around 9 P.M. local time when Saturn is highest, some 50° above the southern horizon. It’s the brightest point of light in this region of the sky, hanging just below Pisces and to the far upper left of Fomalhaut, the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus (much closer to the horizon). Even if you can’t locate Iapetus or don’t have a large scope, Saturn is magnificent through a telescope. Its disk spans 19” and its rings are roughly 43” across, showing off their southern side. You should definitely spot its largest and brightest moon, mid-8th-magnitude Titan, just over 2’ west of the planet. Depending on your scope and when you look, you may also spot at least three other moons: 10th-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, closer to the planet. Tethys lies to Saturn’s west, while Rhea and Dione are to the east.

Sunrise: 6:39 A.M.Sunset: 4:48 P.M.Moonrise: 8:15 A.M.Moonset: 5:19 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (4%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Venus reaches a stationary point among the stars of Virgo at 10 A.M. EST on November 11. This brings its retrograde (westward) motion to an end; after today, Venus will begin moving eastward or prograde through the sky, swinging north of Spica.

You can easily catch the bright planet in the eastern sky before dawn. Venus’ brightness has increased over just the past few days, and it now blazes at magnitude –4.7. An hour before sunrise, you’ll easily spot it alongside Spica, standing just to the star’s upper right. Both are 10° high and rising as dawn approaches. Check out Venus through a telescope: its disk shows off a crescent phase just 10% lit, but stretches an impressive 53” in the sky.

Also just becoming visible at this time is Mercury, barely 1.5° above the horizon and glowing at magnitude 1.2. See if you can locate it about 13° east (to the lower left) of Venus, although you’ll need a particularly flat horizon free of trees, buildings, and lights. Mercury, too, rises as twilight brightens, which may make the planet harder to see in the growing light. Try scanning for it with binoculars, although make sure to put them away well before sunrise from your location

#6322. The 5 Best Water Storage Containers for Emergency Preparedness

Whether you’re waiting out a prolonged natural disaster or need to take it with you during an evacuation, these are the options we recommend.

During natural disasters, blackouts, or water advisories issued by your local government, access to fresh, potable water is essential. Along with other emergency supplies like food and a generator, water storage containers are essential for maintaining your health and wellness during an emergency situation.

The best water storage containers range from compact solutions suitable for urban dwellers to robust systems ideal for off-grid homesteads. Regardless of your needs, we've found a water storage container built to handle them. We focused on key considerations such as durability, capacity, portability, and ease of maintenance. So, if you're looking to prepare yourself before the next emergency, check out our picks below.

When choosing water storage containers for emergency preparedness, we looked at durability, capacity, portability, and how easy each container is to fill, store, and dispense from. Because no single container fits every situation, we included options for different needs: rigid jugs you can grab during an evacuation, portable options you can easily transport, and stackable or large-volume tanks for sheltering in place.

We prioritized food-grade, BPA-free materials, tight-sealing caps, and spigots or spouts that make pouring easy. A previous writer for this article used the Scepter BPA-Free Water Container on camping trips and road trips and included it in home emergency planning. For containers we haven't tested ourselves, we compared key specs like capacity, materials, and shape, and read thousands of owner reviews for recurring problems, such as leaky caps or spigots that wear out.

The Scepter Water Container stands out for its reliability and convenience, making it ideal for outdoor enthusiasts and emergency preparedness. With its lightweight, portable design, this 5-gallon tank is made from food-grade, BPA-free material, helping keep water free of unwanted taste, odor, or chemicals.

The large cap assembly, with a smaller pour-cap opening and vent, enables precise pouring, while a locking tab and plastic tether keep the cap securely fastened to the container.

The tall, narrow construction offers ample capacity without sacrificing portability. Whether off-roading or preparing for unforeseen circumstances, the Scepter BPA-Free Water Container is a dependable and practical choice.

The Reliance Aqua-Tainer is an affordable and reliable water storage solution for outdoor adventures and emergency preparedness. Despite its low price, it is surprisingly durable thanks to its thick walls.

Equipped with a hidden spigot, the Aqua-Tainer offers easy water dispensing while maintaining a sleek, compact design. Its ergonomic, contoured handle makes it easy to carry—ideal if you might need to evacuate at some point.

With a 7-gallon capacity, this FDA-approved, BPA-free container provides ample water storage for extended trips, camping, or emergency preparedness.

The Igloo 6 Gallon Water Container is a simple, affordable way to start your emergency water supply. Its heavy-duty plastic body is tough enough for camping trips, tailgates, and years of storage in a closet or garage. The container weighs just 2.2 pounds empty, and its two molded handles distribute the roughly 50 pounds of a full load, making it manageable to carry to the car during an evacuation. It's tall and narrow, so it takes up little floor space, and a few of them fit easily in a pantry or under a workbench.

The low price comes with trade-offs. You pour from a spout instead of using a spigot, so dispensing is slower and less precise. User reviews also say the push-in vent plug doesn't always seal tightly, so store it upright to avoid leaks. Still, for anyone who wants dependable water storage without spending a lot, the Igloo is hard to beat.

The Saratoga Farms kit gives you a complete emergency water supply in one box. It includes six 5-gallon containers made of food-grade, BPA-free HDPE, two screw-on, no-drip spigots, a cap wrench, and a bottle of water preserver. The preserver treats up to 110 gallons and keeps water safe for up to five years.

The containers have flat tops and bottoms that interlock, and you can stack three high without wobbling, so 30 gallons fits in a corner of a garage or pantry. Built-in handles make each container easy to carry, and a twist vent keeps water flowing smoothly when you pour.

Some owners say the lids are hard to seal, so it’s important that you tighten each lid with the included wrench before you put the containers away.

This WaterPrepared drum is a reliable 55-gallon container, well-suited for waiting out disasters. Weighing just 16 pounds (empty), this tank offers convenience at the cost of some portability. Still, its fairly compact footprint makes it perfect for attachment to ATVs or camping trailers.

Crafted from specially blended UV-proof plastic and HDPE, this tank helps prevent bacterial buildup, improving the safety of your water supply even during extended storage. Accessing emergency water is easy thanks to the included spigots, which are compatible with standard garden hoses, while the front-and-center “utility valves” add flexibility. And if you have limited storage space but want more than one tank, these stack.

Water storage containers are particularly useful as part of your emergency supplies during a natural disaster. Depending on the natural disaster and how long you'll be without access to other water sources, different storage containers may best fit your needs.

Some water storage containers are suitable for more than one type of emergency, but common natural disasters and the recommended types of containers for each are:

For sheltering in place, you may prefer a larger water storage container like a barrel or cistern. These aren’t easy to move, so for evacuation, choose smaller, portable containers with handles or wheels. Lastly, consider whether the containers can serve other purposes besides water storage, such as storing food or supplies, to maximize their utility in emergencies.

When deciding on container size, assess whether you’re preparing to shelter in place or evacuate. For sheltering in place, you may prefer a larger water storage container like a barrel or cistern. These aren’t easy to move, so for evacuation, choose smaller, portable containers with handles or wheels. Lastly, consider whether the containers can serve other purposes besides water storage, such as storing food or supplies, to maximize their utility in emergencies.

High-density polyethylene (HDPE), a popular food-grade material, is highly durable, corrosion-resistant, and non-leaching. HDPE containers are also lightweight, making them easy to transport, and they can withstand a wide range of temperatures without degrading.Stainless steel is another excellent material for water storage containers. It’s durable, non-corrosive, and does not react with water, helping maintain the quality of the liquid inside. Stainless-steel containers are also resistant to bacterial growth, making them suitable for storing water for extended periods.

Glass containers are also considered very good for water storage because they don't leach chemicals into the water and are easy to clean. However, glass is more fragile, and glass containers tend to be heavier than plastic or metal options, which may limit portability in some situations. Only consider glass if you don't expect to ever bring your container from place to place.

Water storage containers come in various sizes and capacities to accommodate different needs and scenarios. Small containers, typically 1-5 gallons, suit short-term emergencies or portable use. They’re convenient for storing water in vehicles or bug-out bags, or for one person to use during outdoor activities. Small containers and portable water filters are also ideal for short-term water-supply disruptions.

Medium-size containers, ranging from 5 to 20 gallons, balance portability and capacity. They are suitable for supplying water for small families or individuals for a few days to a week during emergencies. And they’re often stackable, making them space-efficient for storage.

Large containers can hold 30 gallons or more and are your best bet for long-term emergency water storage at home. Large containers may take the form of barrels, tanks, or cisterns and require more storage space. Many individuals also use these in areas without running water for non-drinking needs such as quick showers, washing dishes, or cleaning.

Bulk storage solutions are also available for communities or organizations preparing for large-scale emergencies. Water tanks or reservoirs with capacities ranging from hundreds to thousands of gallons are typical for these situations. They are suitable for storing water for communal use and may require specialized infrastructure for installation and maintenance. Because of that investment and because we’re focusing this article on water storage for individuals and families, we don’t include any here.

Potable water is essential during emergencies, so you may need to filter or purify water stored in the containers. Safety precautions and regular maintenance can prevent contamination and help keep the water safe for consumption during emergencies.

To keep your water potable, there are several safety precautions you can take, including:

If you’re concerned about water quality, consider treating stored water with chlorine or other purification methods to inhibit bacterial growth and maintain safety. Water filtration systems can also help remove harmful contaminants before drinking.

Regular maintenance helps prevent contamination and ensures the containers' longevity. Proper water storage container maintenance tasks include:

Yes, water storage containers can impact the taste of water. Different materials, such as plastic, metal, glass, or ceramics, can leach subtle flavors or odors into the water over time, especially if you don’t clean the container properly.

For example, plastic containers may release chemicals like BPA into the water, while metal containers can impart a metallic taste. Additionally, stagnant water in poorly maintained containers can develop a stale or off-putting taste. Choosing a high-quality, food-grade container and cleaning it regularly can minimize negative effects on the taste of stored water.

The best materials for water storage containers are typically food-grade and inert, so they don’t impart taste or odor to the water. Glass containers are excellent for small quantities because they’re non-porous, non-reactive, and won't leach chemicals into the water. Stainless steel is another popular choice because it’s durable, non-corrosive, and won’t impart a metallic taste.

Food-grade plastic containers (HDPE or PET) are also suitable, but make sure they are BPA-free to avoid potential health concerns. Ceramic containers, especially those with a food-safe glaze, also work for water storage.

That depends on its quality, storage conditions, and the container type. Generally, commercially bottled water has a recommended shelf life of around 1-2 years if you store it in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight and chemicals.

Tap or purified water can last much longer—potentially indefinitely—if stored in clean, airtight containers made of food-grade materials such as glass or BPA-free plastic. Regularly rotate stored water and periodically check for signs of contamination or changes in taste or odor. Additionally, treating water with a preservative like chlorine dioxide can extend its shelf life.

#6321. Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Sanders: Those tiny sensors are listening to the nearby neurons that control the muscles required for speech.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

Sanders: This volunteer has used the device to talk to her grandkids on the phone. But this is just the very beginning for this research project. There’s so much more to test.Casey is still working on his system, too — particularly, streamlining the process. When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6320. Nov. 10, 1861: The birth of Robert Innes

Born Nov. 10, 1861, in Scotland, Robert Thorburn Ayton Innes would reshape our understanding of our cosmic neighborhood when he discovered our nearest stellar neighbor, Proxima Centauri, in 1912. Innes suspected that Alpha Centauri, a binary system made up of Alpha Centauri A (Rigil Kentaurus) and Alpha Centauri B (Toliman) and then thought to be the nearest stars to Earth (besides the Sun) – had a third member.

The director of the Union Observatory in Johannesburg, South Africa, Innes began a systematic survey for the missing companion star, comparing five years’ worth of photographic plates using a blink-microscope. He noted that a small, faint, red star seemed to move in concert with Alpha Centauri; further research revealed it was in fact closer to Earth than its companions. Innes announced the find in 1915, and later named the body Proxima Centauri – proxima meaning “nearest” in Latin.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Antonacci, N., Labombarda, M., Ricci, C., Buscemi, S., Casadei, R., & Minni, F. (2013). A bizarre foreign body in the appendix: A case report. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery, 5(6), 195–198. https://doi.org/10.4240/wjgs.v5.i6.195
