#6318. The Sky Today on Wednesday, November 11: Venus comes to a halt

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 10: Seek Saturn’s two-toned moon

Venus reaches a stationary point among the stars of Virgo at 10 A.M. EST. This brings its retrograde (westward) motion to an end; after today, Venus will begin moving eastward or prograde through the sky, swinging north of Spica.

You can easily catch the bright planet in the eastern sky before dawn. Venus’ brightness has increased over just the past few days, and it now blazes at magnitude –4.7. An hour before sunrise, you’ll easily spot it alongside Spica, standing just to the star’s upper right. Both are 10° high and rising as dawn approaches. Check out Venus through a telescope: its disk shows off a crescent phase just 10% lit, but stretches an impressive 53” in the sky.

Also just becoming visible at this time is Mercury, barely 1.5° above the horizon and glowing at magnitude 1.2. See if you can locate it about 13° east (to the lower left) of Venus, although you’ll need a particularly flat horizon free of trees, buildings, and lights. Mercury, too, rises as twilight brightens, which may make the planet harder to see in the growing light. Try scanning for it with binoculars, although make sure to put them away well before sunrise from your location, which may differ from the time given below.

Sunrise: 6:41 A.M.Sunset: 4:47 P.M.Moonrise: 9:15 A.M.Moonset: 6:05 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (8%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

#6317. We Found the 6 Best Beginner Telescopes for First-Time Stargazers and Young Astronomers

These beginner-friendly scopes balance price, portability, and easy setup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve recently looked up at the night sky in awe of the stars, you might be inspired to get a closer look. Stargazing is a hobby many dream of taking up but don’t know where to start. Although exploring the cosmos sounds like a daunting concept, it’s made a lot easier with a good beginner-friendly telescope.

With so many types of telescopes out there, each with unique specs, features, and accessories, it’s not hard to get tripped up in the jargon and maybe purchase something that’s not right for a first-timer—which is why we've found great telescopes for every type of novice stargazer. Whether you're trying to adopt this hobby on a budget or you're looking for a student scope, we've got you covered.

To find the best beginner telescope, we researched models across different apertures, focal lengths, and magnifications, as well as models with user-friendly features like smart technology, remote controls, and cell phone holders. With all this in mind, we considered a variety of telescopes across different price points and styles, including compound and refractor telescopes, and selected five that we think are best suited for those starting out on their stargazing journey.

The Gskyer Refracting Telescope is an entry-level instrument that has everything a beginner astronomer might need. Featuring a 70mm aperture and a 400mm focal length, it offers clear, bright views of celestial objects and comes with two replaceable eyepieces.

The telescope is equipped with an adjustable mount that enables smooth movement along vertical and horizontal axes for easy targeting. It also comes with a handy carrying bag for portability and compact storage, while a phone adapter allows users to capture images through the eyepiece.

Additionally, the included remote control provides you with the ability to operate the scope hands-free. Some users reported that the tripod could be more stable, but otherwise, this is a perfect telescope option to start stargazing with.

The paired app of this telescope let’s your phone act as a guide as to where the best star gazing is. Mount your phone on top of the telescope and the arrow appear to literally point you in the right direction for the bets and brightest in the sky.

The kit includes two different lenses and a tripod. At just under 9 pounds, the setup is easy to around camp sites and state parks.

The Ecoopro telescope features a 70mm aperture and a 360mm focal length, which is great for taking in closer celestial objects, like the moon, and observing stars on wide viewing areas. (Some even reported using it for daytime birding.)

The telescope features an adjustable tripod and two replaceable eyepieces that magnify to 51x and 128x, respectively. Its design is very lightweight for easy portability, and it requires no tools to set up.

Keep in mind that the tripod for this telescope is on the shorter side, so bring a camp chair with you for your stargazing or you might end the night with a sore back.

This compound option from Horox combines the benefit of mirrors and lenses to gather and focus light. With its 70mm aperture and an 850mm focal length, it offers high resolution and contrast in both terrestrial and celestial observation.

It comes with a tripod and a phone adapter for easy astrophotography, and its optics support a range of magnifications that provide good views for both beginners and more experienced enthusiasts in astronomy and photography.

Like the Gskyer telescope above that we named Best Overall, be aware that some users have reported this scope's tripod to be somewhat flimsy and unreliable.

The ZWO Seestar S50 Smart Digital Telescope is an all-in-one, portable system designed for both beginners and experienced astronomers. It features a 50mm aperture and a focal length of 250mm, providing a compact optical system.

The telescope has a smart autofocus mechanism, utilizing software for precise object tracking and alignment. It integrates with mobile devices via Wi-Fi for users to control the telescope remotely through the Seestar app. This model also features a built-in camera for astrophotography, supporting both real-time and long exposure imaging.

Because of this telescope's smart capabilities, it does require Wi-Fi, so if you were planning on stargazing on your next remote camping trip, this is not the best option for you.

For the junior astronomer in your life, this telescope has everything to get started with stargazing. With a 50mm objective lens and 400mm focal length, it provides magnifications ranging from 20x to 66x, with two interchangeable eyepieces.

The included adjustable tripod ensures stable viewing, while the lightweight design makes it very easy to carry out to the deck or backyard.

Since this is designed for students, it lacks any extra features that might overcomplicate using it, such as a phone adapter or remote control.

The three main types of telescopes—refractor, reflector, and compound—each have their pros and cons. According to NASA, refractors use lenses and are generally easy to maintain, and are great for lunar and planetary viewing as well as stargazing. Reflectors, which use mirrors, offer more aperture (more on that below) for the price, but you require realignment of the telescope's reflective components on occasion in order to get the best focus. Refractors also tend to have a longer focal length.

Compound, or catadioptric, telescopes combine lenses and mirrors for a compact option, suitable for both planetary and deep-sky observing. For beginners, simplicity is key. A small, grab-and-go telescope might be better than a bulky model that’s difficult to transport or set up. Most of the models we looked at are refractors.

Aperture—the diameter of the telescope’s main lens or mirror—determines how much light the scope can gather and, by extension, how much detail of stars and planets you’ll see. Bigger isn’t always better, though. A large aperture typically means a telescope is heavier and more expensive.

Focal length affects how much visual magnification a telescope offers, but more isn't always better, and too much magnification can reduce image quality. For general observation and capturing wide fields of view, telescopes with shorter focal lengths—typically between 400mm and 700mm—are ideal. If you're aiming to, for example, examine planets in really close detail, a longer focal length of 1,000mm or more is usually better (but this is probably overkill for beginners).

Many beginner telescopes come with a basic tripod or mount. In terms of other features, look for included accessories like eyepieces, which control magnification, and finderscopes, which help locate objects in the night sky. Some assembly is usually required, but most entry-level scopes are relatively straightforward. Keep optics clean with a soft brush or air blower—never wipe lenses with your fingers or rough cloths.

Ideal viewing conditions include dark, clear skies and low humidity. Avoid observing right after sunset when the atmosphere is still warming or from areas with excessive light pollution. Use star charts or mobile apps to help locate constellations, planets, and deep-sky objects. With a bit of preparation and patience, you’ll soon be exploring the cosmos with confidence.

#6316. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6315. Nov. 11, 1875: The birth of V.M. Slipher

Vesto Melvin Slipher was born on a farm in Mulberry, Indiana, on Nov. 11, 1875. He graduated from high school, taught briefly at a country school, and then enrolled at Indiana University in Bloomington. In 1901, one of Slipher’s professors, Wilbur Cogshall, persuaded the founder of the fledgling Lowell Observatory to bring the young astronomer on staff. Percival Lowell was reluctant; as far as he was concerned, the association would be temporary. In the end, however, Slipher would stay at the observatory for 53 years. In 1915, he became assistant director, and when Lowell died the following year, Slipher became acting director and then director by 1926. He served as the observatory’s chief until retiring in 1954 at age 79.

In the fall of 1912, Slipher recorded a plate of the “Andromeda Nebula” that he felt was sufficiently good to obtain its radial velocity. No radial velocities of nebulae were known at that time. He recorded better plates in November and December 1912, and measured the plates over the first half of January, finding that the nebula was moving three times faster than any previously known object in the universe. On Feb. 3, 1913, he wrote to Lowell that the Andromeda Nebula was approaching Earth at the unheard-of velocity of 186 miles per second (300 kilometers per second), still an accurate value. “It looks as if you had made a great discovery,” wrote Lowell. “Try some other spiral nebulae for confirmation.”

By the 1914 American Astronomical Society meeting, Slipher was able to announce results for 15 spirals. Nearly all were receding at high velocities. Three years later, Dutch astronomer Willem de Sitter theorized that the universe is expanding. It was Slipher’s observations of the so-called spiral nebulae that established this fact. And then in 1923 came Hubble’s discovery of the nature of galaxies. By 1929, Hubble derived his crucial velocity-distance relationship for galaxies, using, as Hubble wrote Slipher, “your velocities and my distances.” Slipher and Hubble had together uncovered the expanding universe, the nature of galaxies, and a way to measure extragalactic distances.

David J. Eicher is editor emeritus of Astronomy magazine.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

#6313. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6311. The 8 Best Carpet Cleaners to Lift Set-In Stains and Eliminate Odors

You could always rent a unit, but you'll save some cash in the long run using one of these reliable models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Vacuums are great for everyday cleaning, but if you need something to go the extra mile, a carpet cleaner gets deep into fibers to lift dirt, pet hair, and tough stains through a mix of scrubbing power, suction, and cleaning solution. This freshens up the look of your carpet beyond what a regular vacuum is capable of, and extends its life by removing debris that damages the fibers if left untreated.

While it’s possible to rent heavy-duty carpet cleaning machines from home improvement stores, in the long run it’s more convenient and economical to purchase your own and use it as needed. We typically recommend them for spot treatment of spills and stains, as well as for a deep clean of your carpets once every couple of months depending on foot traffic. Most carpet cleaners are corded uprights (though there are a few canister-style models), and they typically include attachments for dealing with specific messes, like mud or pet stains.

Our favorite models come from trusted brands like Bissell and Hoover—and many cost roughly the same as regular vacuums. These are the best carpet cleaners we recommend, along with advice on how to pick the right model for your home and needs.

This list was compiled based on our extensive research and general familiarity with household cleaning gadgets. We focused first and foremost on brand reliability—prioritizing names like Bissell and Hoover that are known for producing high-quality models that hold up over time and get the job done. Furthermore, we also looked for brands that offer solid warranties and customer service lines in the case of any faulty products.

From there, we wanted to provide a range of options, so all price points and room and home sizes were reflected in our choices. To do this, we pored over verified customer reviews and product specs to create a list that meets our standards.

We believe each carpet cleaner on this list fills a specific role or category better than other, similar models. So, regardless of whether you're looking for a quick spot treatment machine to store in a cupboard or an industrial-strength option for a public venue, we've got you covered.

Beyond this, we recently tested out the Tineco Carpet ONE Cruiser in person. Our evaluation method involved basic cleaning and setup that you might use it for on a regular basis, as well as specific testing of individual special features. We also paid close attention to the actual ease of setup, cleanup, and storing the device as part of our overall assessment.

For our latest update, we evaluated newer carpet cleaner models with upgraded features to give home users more versatility. We also carefully reviewed the latest customer feedback to ensure our recommendations reflect the best machines currently on the market. Additionally, we drew on our own experience using a range of carpet cleaners in our busy (and often messy) homes.

This carpet cleaner stands out for more than its powerful cleaning ability. The steam and water cleaning combination in tandem with the two scrubbing rollers breaks down set-in dirt and stains easily and efficiently.

Best of all, even with this deep level of cleaning, your carpet dries in about 30 minutes if you use the quick-drying mode. Most other models at this price point don't have this feature, which is helpful for households with kids or pets that must be corralled away from wet carpets.

Other highlights of this full-size model include an attachable hose and two different cleaning heads for removing set-in stains and lifting pet hair from furniture, respectively.

Bissell provides two sample cleaning solutions as well: one for general deep cleaning and one that’s formulated for removing pet urine.

Full Bissell Revolution HydroSteam Carpet Cleaner Review

This portable and affordable carpet cleaner fits comfortably on a shelf or in a cupboard. It's mainly designed for spot cleaning, yet offers plenty of power, with a three-stage cleaning process that involves spraying cleaning fluid, scrubbing the affected area with a stain tool, and suctioning up the stain and remaining fluid.

Beyond the basics, the carpet cleaner comes with a self-cleaning attachment for circulating clean water through the hose and tanks to prevent gunk or mildew buildup over time.

While portability is the main draw, it has its disadvantages. The clean water tank only holds 16 ounces and the small head makes it tedious for cleaning larger areas.

Full Bissell Little Green Mini Portable Carpet and Upholstery Cleaner Review

If you want a carpet cleaner with a user-friendly cleaning and drying system, this Hoover model is the right choice. The carpet cleaner has a sensor for quick washing and drying that's operated by simply pushing the unit forward for washing and pulling it backward for drying.

This lets you clean a portion of your carpet and dry it in quick succession. Another feature we appreciate is the dry boost button that generates hot air for even more effective drying.

While the cleaning and drying mechanism is the standout feature, we also like the automatic solution dispenser. Simply snap in the solution container and the machine mixes the cleaning liquid with water for the correct ratio every time.

During our in-person testing of the Tineco carpet cleaner, two things became abundantly clear: the carpet in our office is horrifyingly dirty, and the power drying feature is a complete game changer.

We used the Tineco cleaning formula without any kind of spot treatment beforehand, deliberately rolling it back and forth in straight lines. The results were a tank full of the murkiest water, accumulated fibers, and dirt I have ever seen with my own two eyes, but we also experienced distinctly cleaner carpets.

I particularly liked the power-pushing design that lets you push and pull the device across the carpet while barely lifting a finger. This didn't play a huge role given the relatively small size of the carpet I cleaned, but it would certainly play a much larger factor in rooms where I would be pushing it back and forth for an extended period of time.

Beyond this, the drying feature completely changed how easy the whole process is. Instead of cleaning and then spending a massive chunk of time simply waiting for the carpet to dry, I was able to go over the carpet again using the PowerDry feature and it was literally dry to the touch seconds afterward. The only drawback is that the dirty water tank isn't the largest (0.45 gallons), so it did require us to empty it pretty frequently.

Many carpet cleaners are quite heavy, weighing upward of 18 pounds. The Hoover PowerDash is one of the lightest full-size models available, weighing just over 12.5 pounds. It’s also much smaller than other full-size options, so it's a smart choice for homes low on storage space.

The simple design has a 0.5-gallon water tank and a separate compartment for dirty water, and its antimicrobial brush roll helps lift pet hair out of rugs while protecting against odors. This carpet cleaner uses hot air to help rugs dry faster and comes with a nozzle clean-out tool to make maintenance a breeze.

While its weight is certainly a plus, it does shed it by removing extra features like an attachable hand tool for upholstery cleaning and spot stains.

If pet hair, muddy paw prints, or mystery stains are a regular presence in your household, Bissell ProHeat 2X Revolution Pet Pro Plus is one of the most capable upright cleaners we’ve used. It uses dual DirtLifter brushes to agitate carpet fibers and pull out embedded dirt, while maintaining water temperature during cleaning for more efficient stain removal.

We especially love the CleanShot pretreatment feature, which lets you target stubborn spots before running the main cleaner over them. Express Clean Mode is another excellent feature for households with pets or kids, since it helps carpets dry in about 30 minutes and you don’t have to wait long before getting back to your normal routine. The only slight nuisance that our tester noticed was that this pick is slightly louder than other upright cleaners they’ve used in the past.

For homeowners who want near-professional results, Bissell’s Big Green is one of the most powerful machines available for residential use. The large water tanks allow extended cleaning sessions without constant refilling, which we found especially useful for people tackling large carpeted areas.

It also has a dynamic extra-large brush with eight rows of bristles to remove even the most stubborn dirt embedded in carpet fibers. A nine-foot hose and six-inch tough stain tool allowed us to clean hard-to-reach areas, while an adjustable handle makes cleaning wall-to-wall carpet more comfortable. However, the trade-off is weight. This is a heavy machine that requires more storage space and effort to move.

Full Bissell Big Green Professional Carpet Cleaner Review

Our tester is a big fan of Shark, especially since many of its products are lightweight and fit in small spaces. Shark’s CarpetXpert is no exception, as it’s a nice middle ground between portable spot cleaners and bulky full-size machines. We like that it’s compact while still offering strong suction and integrated scrubbing brushes. This combination makes it effective at lifting stubborn dirt without feeling overly cumbersome to maneuver around furniture.

The built-in spot-cleaning tools are another bonus if you’re prone to stains on stairs or upholstery. Best of all, this machine fuses two formulas that simultaneously target both stains and odors so your carpet will not only look clean, but smell fresh as well. This feature makes it a smart choice for homes with pets or kids while staying compact. Just bear in mind that its smaller tanks will require you to refill it a little more frequently.

Full Shark CarpetXpert Upright Carpet Cleaner Review

Over the lifespan of this article, we’ve made several changes to the carpet cleaners that we’ve featured. Many were considered and ultimately left off this guide or removed over time. Here are a few notable options that, while not quite making it on our current list, are still worth considering.

Bissell Little Green Multi-Purpose Carpet Cleaner: While we have the Bissell Little Green Mini on our list, the classic Little Green didn’t make the cut this time around. Both are better suited to small stains and upholstery, and we found the general cleaning power differences between the two not as compelling when evaluating them as overall carpet cleaners. So in this case, we leaned toward the less expensive choice.

Costway Multipurpose Steam Cleaner: The Costway steam cleaner is a great choice for folks looking to avoid long drying times and the use of excessive cleaning solutions and concentrates. The powerful steam is great for brightening carpets and upholstery and breaking down dirt stains. While versatile, we ended up leaving it off due to the lack of scrubbing power.

Rug Doctor Mighty Pro X3 Carpet Cleaner: This commercial-grade carpet cleaner’s 2.5-gallon tank is great for powering through heavy stains and covering tons of ground. The powerful suction capabilities also cut down on drying time by pulling up more moisture per pass than a regular carpet cleaner. The handheld spot cleaner is also great for upholstery. While we still like the Rug Doctor, we prefer the slightly smaller and more affordable Bissell commercial carpet cleaner for heavy-duty work.

Commercial-grade carpet cleaners feature the largest water tanks and the most powerful scrubbing or steaming features to dislodge dirt and remove stains. This allows them to cover much larger areas of carpet at a time before they require a refill with water or cleaning solution.

Similarly, because they are commercial grade, most of them last for years and rarely need a repair. The trade-off, of course, is that they aren’t easy to store and cost more than smaller models do. For the most part, they've got more power and capacity than you'll actually need.

For most households, we recommend a full-size carpet cleaner. They take up about as much space as a standard upright vacuum and come with a gallon-size tank that allows them to run for approximately 15 to 20 minutes. This is typically enough to cover small rooms in one tank and larger rooms with a single refill.

If you have small rugs or sections of carpeting, a portable carpet cleaner is the way to go. They’re generally no bigger than a handheld vacuum and feature an attached hose and a handful of cleaning tools. These are best for spot cleaning and small stains on furniture items. Many full-size models come with attached hoses for spot treatment as well.

Most carpet cleaners work by shooting a mix of water and cleaning solution at the carpet and then vacuuming it back up once it removes the set-in dirt and grime. This baseline design is typically effective for pulling up moderate dirt and light stains, but it may not be enough for larger issues.

Many of the carpet cleaners we recommend offer more than just water and suction. Several full-size models have built-in roller brushes that scrub the carpet to dislodge dirt in tandem with the cleaning spray and suction functions.

Some models, like the Bissell Revolution HydroSteam, clean using heated water or steam to more effectively break down dirt and set-in grime, while others use hot air to dry carpets after a wash, which is particularly helpful in homes with kids and pets where you won't have the time to let the carpet dry naturally.

Some full-size models, such as the Hoover PowerDash Pet Compact Carpet Cleaner, often come with special hoses and heads for upholstery cleaning or spot treatment on stains. Others come with tools designed for digging into carpets and lifting away pet hair and dander. These have scrubbing brushes on the end that pull up dander and hair more easily than models with traditional suction designs.

Most carpet cleaners on this list will provide sample cleaning solutions from their brand, which you can try out for yourself before committing to any one individual option. For the most part, the specialized options built for specific stains likely won't make a huge difference in day-to-day cleaning in comparison to generic ones. Concentrated formulas are well suited for lifting up serious dirt and stains similar to your laundry detergent, but may not be necessary for light refreshes in low foot traffic areas.

In fact, many people use vinegar solutions or substitute with a mix of laundry detergent, fabric softener, and water. While we don't necessarily recommend that, these homemade options should work fine in a pinch and will still be effective in cleaning your carpet.

Most households will find that an upright cleaner will provide the best balance of power and convenience, since these machines deep clean entire rooms efficiently.

“Upright is great if you’re cleaning whole rooms with wall to wall carpet,” says Ryan Knoll, owner of Tidy Casa, a professional cleaning company that services more than 600 homes a month. He also owned a carpet cleaning company for many years, learning firsthand (and often the hard way) what works and what doesn’t when it comes to upright versus portable carpet cleaners.

However, Knoll says portable carpet cleaners have rightfully earned their spot as well. “Portable carpet cleaners are great for spot cleaning and getting into smaller spaces,” he explains. “Think, pet accidents, upholstery, or cars.”

Some carpet cleaners include attachments designed for upholstery, car interiors, and stairs. These tools are great for cleansing fabric surfaces around the house, but most experts advise against using carpet cleaners on hardwood or tile floors since excess moisture can damage those materials.

“These carpet cleaners do one thing really well: they push moisture through the carpet and pull it back out,” Knoll says. “This is what catches all the muck and gets that deep clean. With that said, wood floors don't like moisture, so this is a no-fly zone for wood. Tile is the same.” Instead, Knoll recommends using a steam mop for tile or finished cement surfaces.

Cleaning professionals generally recommend deep-cleaning carpets once or twice a year. “For most homes, every 6 to 12 months will keep things super fresh,” Knoll says. “This works great for homes with 2 to 4 people, maybe a pet or two. For busier homes with lots of kids and pets, stepping it up to 3 to 4 months helps.”

#6310. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6307. ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus

ZWO has added a new entry point to its smart telescope lineup. The Seestar S30 Plus went on sale Nov. 10 for $499 — $474 for a limited time — undercutting the S30 Pro by $200 and making it the cheapest Seestar available.

“Many people are interested in astrophotography but hesitate when they see the equipment and setup traditionally involved,” ZWO founder Sam Wen said in a press release. “With S30 Plus, we wanted to give beginners more room to explore and create without taking away the simplicity that makes Seestar easy to start with.”

Since the original S50 debuted in April 2023, the Seestar line has continued to grow, most recently with this year’s 4K S30 Pro and S50 Pro. The S30 Plus heads in the opposite direction from the Pro models — and with the original S30 reportedly discontinued, it now holds down the entry-level slot.

Effectively, the new Plus model is an S30 Pro with a few features stripped out to meet a lower price. Like the Pro, it carries two cameras: a telephoto for galaxies, nebulae, and other deep-sky targets; and a wide-angle for broad sweeps of the night sky. The telephoto camera keeps the Pro’s 1.2-inch (30 millimeters) aperture and four-element apochromatic lens, including an element of extra-low-dispersion (ED) glass.

The biggest change is to the sensors. Both of the Plus’ cameras shoot 1440×2560 images (3.7 megapixels, or roughly 2K), versus the S30 Pro’s 8.3-megapixel 4K output — still a step up from the original S30’s 2.1 megapixels. But the difference in sensor size doesn’t mean less detail — only a difference in field of view. The Plus has the same pixel size as the Pro, so zooming in on your photos reveals the same level of detail.d

RELATED: Review: ZWO Seestar S50 smart telescope

On the telephoto side, the Plus swaps the Pro’s larger Sony sensor for a 1/1.8-inch SmartSens SC485SL chip. Both have the same 2.9-micrometer pixels behind the same 160 mm lens, so the Pro’s bigger chip just spans more sky: about 4.6°, compared with the Plus’ 3°. That’s still enough to comfortably frame targets like the Pleiades star cluster and the Orion and Rosette nebulae, along with the Moon’s full disk — or the Sun’s, with the included solar filter in place.

The wide-angle camera uses the same 1/2-inch Sony IMX586 sensor as the Pro, behind a lens with identical specs (6 mm, f/1.75). But where the Pro takes in a 63° view, the Plus crops it down to the same 2K format as its telephoto sensor, covering a smaller 43.5° field — still wide enough for the Milky Way, whole constellations, star trails, and time-lapses.

The Plus does give up a few of the S30 Pro’s handier features. The Pro can run both cameras at once, stacking a nebula through the telephoto while the wide-angle captures the Milky Way and landscape around it; the Plus only shoots with one at a time. Its wide-angle camera also can’t stitch Milky Way panoramas, though a telephoto mosaic mode for larger deep-sky targets remains. And onboard storage is halved to 64 GB.

In the box, buyers get the scope, a tabletop tripod, a carrying case, a USB-C cable, and a magnetic solar filter. The 3.6-pound (1.65 kilograms) unit runs up to 6 hours on a charge and has UV/IR-cut and duo-band light-pollution filters built in.

Like every Seestar, the S30 Plus is driven entirely from a phone through the Seestar app. Users simply pair the device to their phone, let it calibrate, and then pick a target — or let the app suggest one. The S30 Plus automatically slews to the target, centers it, and begins tracking and live stacking, with the image building in detail on screen as frames accumulate.

The app can also identify and label constellations in the wide-angle view, and it can queue up automated imaging plans to run through the night. Finished shots can be tweaked and shared straight from the phone. For those who’d rather process elsewhere, the scope saves stills as JPEG and FITS files and video as MP4 and AVI.

The Seestar S30 Plus is available now for $499 through Seestar’s and ZWO’s online stores, Amazon in the U.S. and Europe, and authorized dealers worldwide. It’s now the cheapest way into the Seestar ecosystem — and owners who outgrow it can easily step up to a Pro model.

More details are available at ZWO’s product page.

#6306. These 7,400-Year-Old Cave Drawings Were Hiding in Plain Sight for Decades. They’re Finally Getting Their Due.

Buried under centuries of graffiti, a trove of Paleolithic art only appears when light hits it just so.

Known for its ancient artifacts, the Catalonian village of Espluga de Francolí has been one of the most recognized troves of Paleolithic cave finds in Spain. Even the “Espluga” in its name translates to “cave.” The village is surrounded by mountains with limestone caves or covas whose human history reaches back thousands of years, and while Cova de la Font Major has been a tourist attraction since 1957, something that almost should have been obvious went unseen.

Cova de la Font Major had already been investigated by archaeologists by the time it was converted into a museum in 1993. By then, it was thought that the cave had been thoroughly scoured for artifacts and other evidence that it was inhabited, and that its irregular walls had been unsuitable for cave art because of their uneven coloration and texture. Part of what became known as its Adventure Route is the Gatoneres de cal Palletes, a series of smaller galleries branching off from the main gallery. Visitors filed past for decades, never noticing the engravings concealed in the dark. Cut into the pale limestone were animals and abstract symbols, each one made by human hands.

Part of the reason that these drawings had never been observed is that they have to be illuminated from certain angles in order to be visible. An archaeological team led by Josep Maria Vergès and Míriam Salas-Altès of the Catalan Institute of Human Paleocecology and Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) identified 280 motifs scratched into the soft rock, which now make up the highest known concentration of Paleolithic figures found on a cave wall in Catalonia. It’s also the third largest cave art assemblage on the eastern Iberian Peninsula. It was unexpectedly discovered during a 2019 excavation campaign, although it was obscured by modern graffiti left behind by tourists and others who’ve visited the site since explorers first crept in through the well of a townhouse courtyard in 1853. It also seems that the art incorporated stone variations.

“While the intentional integration of these natural features remains interpretative and cannot be definitively demonstrated, their proposed use is supported by precise anatomical alignment with some features and the recurrent use of similar elements across the corpus,” Vergès and Salas-Altès said in a study recently published in Antiquity.

Some of the animal figures, including horses, deer, goats, and aurochs, appear to trot along the seams between different types of rock. They share the walls with abstract motifs, which make up most of the cave art. Researchers also documented parallel lines, some of them cut across the animals, as well as convergent lines and tangles of loops. The meanings of these symbols can only be guessed at, and so can their age. Direct dating of material from Cova de la Font Major is difficult, though the team thinks uranium dating may work on calcite deposits that formed over at least one figure. Even then, a date for one drawing won’t necessarily reveal the age of the others. For now, the closest anchor comes from radiocarbon dating, which places the cave’s earliest Neolithic occupations between 7,050 and 7,400 years ago.

The cave was also used for late Neolithic burials on the cusp of the Bronze Age. Right before it was opened to the public in 1957, archaeologists unearthed a human femur that was radiocarbon dated to 5,600–5,700 years old. Also found near the entrance was a hoard of later Bronze Age artifacts that included pins decorated with sun imagery, an axe, a dagger, and fragments of a blade that could have been a dagger or sword. Deeper in the cave, charcoal dated to 26,000 years ago may be the oldest sign of human presence, aided by similar charcoal discovered near the prehistoric shrine known as Sala del Llac and in other spots inside the cave. Much later, in the Iron Age, people used another part of the cave for rituals. They left behind ceramic vessels that may have been offerings to deities, along with metal artifacts and food remnants.

“[This discovery is] a substantial advance in the understanding of Paleolithic rock art in the eastern Iberian Peninsula,” the researchers said. “Gaps in the Paleolithic record may reflect limitations in research strategies, visibility conditions or preservation factors, rather than the actual absence of rock art practices.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6305. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

L. Davin et al. Modeling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia. PLOS One. 2026. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388
