#6304. The 23 Best Gaming Gifts, According to Our Editor With 15 Years in the Industry

Whether they play on PlayStation, Switch 2, or PC, these are the items that are sure to bring joy.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

With rising memory and GPU costs, the gamer in your life may still be wishing for a new laptop, gaming rig, or console this holiday season—or even something small like a keyboard or a high-end controller. And let’s not forget: At $70 for the biggest new releases, the games themselves are not small purchases.

All of which is to say, there’s even more reason to give your loved ones something gaming-related. More often than not, the best gear is a bit of a splurge, but there’s a lot of cool stuff out there that’s worth the spend.

I’ve been writing about games and gaming gear for 15 years, and I test new and exciting gear all year. Here are some of the best, coolest, and most useful bits of kit out there that are sure to light up their faces. (And their desks… And their couches.)

With no new consoles announced, all of the core consoles will make for great gifts, but the Switch 2 is the newest kid on the block, and thus the one that will likely stay active the longest. The Switch 2 was a significant tech improvement over the original Switch when it launched last year, and Nintendo has launched a substantial number of exciting exclusives over the past year, many of which are truly all-ages experiences: kid-friendly, so families can play worry-free, but with the innovative gameplay and polish that will hold an adult’s attention.

Lately, I’ve been playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, the latest entry in the long-running strategy RPG franchise. That’s on the niche side for a Nintendo game, but there’s a wide array of fun, distinctive games, like Pokopia, the Pokemon habitat-builder; Donkey Kong Bananza, a platformer you can literally break apart piece by piece; and Mario Kart World, which brings some huge changes to the long-running classic racer.

And, while the Switch 2 will not be able to play GTA VI (at least not at launch), it will get its mega-blockbuster this November: a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a game that most critics and fans of a certain age put up among the best games of all time.

Earlier this year, HP folded its two gaming PC brands—Omen and Victus—into HyperX, the PC gaming peripherals brand it purchased back in 2021. That means HyperX makes PCs now! I’ve always been a huge fan of the brand, which was best known for headsets but also made good keyboards and mice, among other things, so I was excited to see what the first HyperX PCs could do.

The HyperX Omen 15 is a capable mid-range gaming laptop equipped with either a Ryzen 7 or Intel Core i7 CPU, an Nvidia 5060 GPU, 16 GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. The display is a 2.5K (2560 x 1600p) IPS panel with a 180Hz max refresh rate, which is more than enough to handle what a 5060 will throw at it. At a time when gaming PC prices are shockingly high (note the conspicuous lack of a desktop or GPUs on this list) I think this is a solid machine from a trustworthy brand, which is really all you can ask for at a time like this.

All gaming PCs are expensive this year, but the handheld gaming PC market has gotten especially out of control. If you want to be nice to someone and splurge nearly $2,000, the new model I’ve seen this year is MSI’s Claw EX AI+. It’s the first handheld furnished with Intel’s Arc G3 Extreme processor, a chip made specifically for handhelds instead of laptops. That has made it both more performant and, crucially, power-efficient than most of the handhelds I’ve seen and tried. And, unlike a Steam Deck, it is Windows-based out of the box, which makes it easier to use Steam, Xbox Game Pass, and all the other storefronts without any tinkering.

If you’re willing to spend top dollar to buy the most bonkers version of a gaming peripheral, SteelSeries is usually a good brand to look at. After designing and redesigning its impeccable multiplatform headset, the Arctis Nova Pro, the brand has turned its attention back to the controller, and released a new, equally impressive Xbox-style gamepad, the Aeon Pro.

SteelSeries took a lot of the features from the Arctis Nova headset and ported them over to the Aeon Pro. There’s a charging dock with multiple inputs so you can hot-swap between Xbox and PC on the fly. It also comes with a pair of replaceable batteries (the same ones in the Nova Pro/Elite), so you can always switch batteries and keep playing. Even if you forget to use the dock, you will never run out of battery with this controller.

You also get all the standard features you’d expect on a premium controller—swappable Hall effect analog sticks, four customizable rear paddles, adjustable trigger travel—it features sublimely clicky mechanical buttons and balanced weight in your hand. At $260, this is the very definition of a giftable controller: It’s more money than anyone would want to spend on a controller themselves, but a daily player will absolutely appreciate the luxury of owning one.

Low-profile gaming keyboards, which feature less “travel” or a smaller distance from unpressed to fully bottomed out, are an acquired taste. Mechanical keyboards, with longer travel, tend to be more comfortable, but many players are comfortable with low-profile keys because they feel more like a laptop keyboard and/or because the keys are optimal for “hair trigger” settings that cater to twitch reflexes. When a quick action is all that stands between you and certain death, a low-profile keyboard might be the difference between a dodge and your demise.

Razer does well with just about everything, but I find myself recommending the brand’s keyboards about as often as anything, and its newest low-profile option really worked for me this year. With adjustable actuation and other features that allow you to really optimize for the fastest possible response, it’s a high-performance keyboard for players who want to go all in on multiplayer performance.

In the same vein as the Aeon Pro, SteelSeries has reinvented its mouse line with a four-pack of new mice: The Rival Pro, Rival Pro Mini, Sensei Pro, and Sensei Pro Mini. That sounds like a lot of mice, but really it comes down to two shapes: The more ergonomic Sensei and the more streamlined Rival, both of which come in a standard or lighter “mini” size. (Mini mice are better for small hands, of course, but also preferred by “claw” players who hold their hand above their mice for quick-clicking.) While they are different, I’d say both Sensei and Rival have a decidedly competitive build, which is why I’d specifically recommend Rival Pro.

Like the Aeon Pro controller, Steelseries has ported over its swappable battery system (though the mice have smaller puck-sized batteries), but the big innovation is a new, faster wireless connection, which they call “Ultra 8K wideband.” 8K polling—the number of times the mouse sends signals back to your PC per second, sort of like a “refresh rate” for mice–is now a common claim among high-end gaming mice, but not every mouse delivers it consistently. Steelseries claims that Ultra 8K Wideband, which relies on line of sight between the mouse and a small base station (that also charges the backup battery), ensures a steady 8K connection. And, like all esports mice, it’s incredibly light, about 53 grams.

It ain’t cheap, but if your gamer plays a lot of competitive online multiplayer games, like Call of Duty, Fortnite, Valorant, or Marvel Rivals, this is the kind of mouse they’re looking for to get a competitive edge (and show off to their friends).

I’ve been known to recommend some incredibly expensive gaming headsets in the past, so this year my most gift-worthy option is a little more reasonable, if not cheap. The newest riff on Logitech’s flagship gaming headset, the Pro X3, offers a great balance of audio quality, mic clarity, comfort, and style. I’ve long been a fan of the advanced EQ and post-processing work that Logitech manages to pull off via G Hub, its companion app, though it still sounds clear and sweet on PS5, where you don’t have access to those fine controls. It’s also the most stylish new headset I tested this year. The black aluminum and faux-leather-coated padding look great on a stream, or even a video call at work.

I haven’t played Grand Theft Auto VI yet, but I don’t need to touch it to know that it’s at the top of every gamer’s wish list this holiday season. It’s been more than a decade since Rockstar Games released the last Grand Theft Auto game, but in that time, the series’ popularity has only grown. With the game launching November 19, the hype has reached a fever pitch as release day approaches. Houston Rockets center Steven Adams joked that NBA productivity will drop on launch day. There are a couple of stories out there with advice on how to ask for time off to play.

If you haven’t watched the Netflix special about the game, GTA VI follows a Bonnie and Clyde-esque criminal couple in Vice City, which is loosely based on Miami. Like past games, it seems to boast incredibly detailed and cinematic visuals, particularly for an open-world experience where you can go anywhere, do anything, and, per the name, steal anyone’s car.

Speaking of which, I feel like most people are aware of GTA and its adult themes because of various satires and news stories about the rest of the series, but just in case: This game has a lot of violence, and seemingly some sexual content as well. If you are shopping for a kid, treat access to this game the same way you would an R-rated movie.

Released in 1998 on the Nintendo 64, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is often touted as the pinnacle of the franchise, bested maybe only by the original Switch’s Breath of the Wild. After nearly 30 years, Nintendo has rebuilt this classic from the ground up. I’m normally not easily swayed by pure nostalgia, but it’s incredible to return to Ocarina of Time and realize how deeply ingrained it is in my mind. It’s been a very long time since I played the original, but I breezed through the first few hours as if it had been yesterday. And the things that have changed—new graphics, voice acting in cutscenes, and an orchestral score, to name a few—all bring the game to life in a new way, without detracting from my memory of playing it before.

Obviously, I’m approaching it as an old-head and a fan, but I do think the game still holds up quite well for new audiences as well. So much of the Zelda gameplay that younger fans know and love is built on a foundation created here, and that essential sense of adventure is still very much alive.

If the Ocarina of Time remake is not enough for your favorite Nintendo fan (or if they’ve already pre-ordered it), there is a lot of new Zelda merch coming out alongside the new game this fall. My personal fave is this backpack, which I checked out at a Nintendo event earlier this year. It’s surprisingly big, 18 by 22 by 4 inches (w x h x d), with a built-in laptop sleeve. Most importantly, it looks just like the shield, and the exterior is made from polyurethane with rubber details, rather than simply painted on, so they won’t rub off or fade.

Everyone’s heard of GTA VI. Everyone’s heard of Zelda. When you give a gamer either of these gifts, you’ve done right by them, but you’ve also picked the most obvious choices. They aren’t going to know you read this guide. That you put in the work to find a great game for them. One of the biggest surprise hits in a crowded fall game calendar, Blood of the Dawnwalker, on the other hand, shows that you’ve been paying attention to what critics and players have been talking about.

This action-RPG about medieval vampires comes from developer Rebel Wolves, which is led by senior staff from CD Projekt who worked on The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077. As Coen, a daywalking vampire, you have to save your human family from a vampire lord. Like The Witcher, this game has a compelling narrative with nuanced writing. There’s a lot to dig your teeth into, so your gamer will be telling you about it for a while.

We’ve been talking about OLED TVs for a long time, but manufacturers have only put OLED panels in PC monitors for a couple of years. OLED gaming monitors are here, but are generally pretty expensive. If you don’t shop for PC monitors often, you might be shocked when I tell you that this 27-inch, 1440p display is “relatively affordable at only… $570!?

But making the jump to an OLED display, like switching to an OLED TV, can be a game changer. Organic light-emitting diode (OLED) technology allows for dynamic brightness control to generate more accurate colors, sharper contrast, and maximize HDR output. Put another way, they make games “pop” in a way that your average LED display just won’t. Alienware has put out a few well-made and relatively obtainable options, including the AW2725DF.

I always rankle a bit at the concept of a “gaming TV”: All of the best TVs handle games well. But there are a couple of features that go from “nice to have” to mandatory when I go to recommend a new big screen with games in mind. In addition to the usual attention to color, brightness, and display technology, a higher refresh rate is a must, as is variable refresh rate support. And if there’s a good “game mode” in the settings, that’s a nice plus, too.

Giving someone a TV, any TV, is a hugely generous act, but in the spirit of “giving them what they wouldn’t buy themselves,” I’d recommend going all out and giving your gamer the Samsung S95H, the true best OLED of the year when you take price out of the question. It’s expensive, but makes games look absolutely incredible, with tremendous color accuracy, brightness, and the “perfect” blacks of an OLED screen.

All of the consoles (and desktop gaming PCs) give you a way to add more storage to your system so you can store more games at a time. Games take up more space than ever, so having the extra storage is convenient: It gets annoying when you have to delete a game every time you want to download something new. I’ll admit, it’s a utilitarian gift—basically the equivalent of buying someone a pair of warm socks—but one that will make any player’s life more convenient.

On PC and PS5, we’re talking about an M.2 SSD hard drive, which loads games at high speeds. Xbox has a proprietary expansion card system, which is easy to install. Finally, the Switch 2 relies on high-speed micro SD cards for extra storage. There are many brands for each option, but the differences in performance aren’t huge. The most important thing is compatibility: If it doesn’t specifically state that it works with your gamer’s console of choice, you need to check the specs and make sure. (Or pick any of the options below.)

Shop PS5 Storage Shop Xbox Storage Shop Switch Storage

IKEA launched a fun new line of Xbox-inspired gaming furniture and housewares earlier this year, and there are some great, utilitarian pieces if you’re looking to spruce up your setup. One thing that caught my eye, a potential stuffer, is this controller display box, which gives you a cool way to store your gamepads or use them as decoration. Especially if you’re picking up limited edition controllers, these give you a cool way to show them off rather than simply leaving them next to your TV.

While I haven’t tested any of these, I think a lot of the YXSTABY line looks pretty fun. There’s a neat gaming side table, which features built-in storage underneath, an easel-style TV stand, and a D-pad-shaped throw pillow. All of these are relatively affordable, too, so they’re great choices if the tech’s looking a bit too pricey.

Once upon a time—maybe a decade ago or so—the Blue Yeti was the USB microphone that launched a million podcasts. A long time has passed since then: Blue was acquired by Logitech, and the Yeti fell out of vogue. Well, Logitech has relaunched the iconic audio starter kit under its gaming banner, Logitech G, with new focus on streaming video games and, more specifically, helping streamers automate the technical side of things.

The Yeti 2 upholds the original model’s legacy as a stellar starter mic (for streaming, podcasts, or any deskside audio you need to capture), but the new and improved model has some fascinating features, including the ability to detect and adjust your EQ settings based on your proximity to the microphone, and an LED screen that lets you manually change audio settings without digging into menus on your PC (where you already have a lot going on). This is a great pickup for someone who’s thinking about getting into streaming, or is looking for an easy plug-and-play upgrade that doesn’t require too much finicking to figure out.

If you have someone in your life who can’t stop talking about GTA VI, chances are they’ve already preordered the game. To meet them where they are in their fandom, you have to jump to the next step and get them something that allows them to show off the depth of their fandom.

There’s a ton of unofficial GTA merch out there, but realheads accept no substitutes, and PS5 players will be stoked to get a new Vice City-themed DualSense with the “VI” on the touchpad. (Also, depending on how long they’ve had their console, it may be time for a controller refresh, anyway. Analog stick drift is a problem we all learn to live with, but sometimes it’s just better to start fresh.)

Not every gaming gift needs to be electronic. Sometimes it can be a toy where you build a scale model of electronics. The latest in a now long line of game console–based sets, Lego just released a scale model of the original PlayStation, in honor of “over 30 years of play,” according to Sony. Whether you have a gamer in your life who’s a die-hard PlayStation fan, a collector who’s been decorating their space with hand-assembled consoles, or just someone who loves to tinker, building a 1,911-piece PlayStation brick by brick seems like a fun, relaxing way to spend a weekend.

Press Reset is the only item on this list that wasn’t released in 2026, but I think it’s a very good time to read it if you or the gamer in your life hasn’t yet. This series of longform nonfiction stories from Bloomberg video game industry reporter Jason Schrier provide detailed histories of how some major games from the last 20 years were made. The connective tissue between the stories, which are woven together in surprisingly personal ways, have a common theme: The development houses that made the games shut down afterwards.

The video game business has been in a bit of a transitional period for the past few years: A wide realization that rising costs, both for developers and consumers, has led to projects getting cancelled, companies downsizing or closing, and more. For gamers, who often like to think they have much better understanding of what’s going on in the game world than they really do, these stories illustrate the many ways that making a video game can go wrong, whether you’re working with a small independent team or one of the biggest, most well-funded companies in the business. It’s a fascinating book, and a must read for anyone interested in how games are made.

If you’re a fighting game fan playing on Xbox or PC, HyperX has a really interesting new Hitbox-style “leverless” fight stick called the Clutch Tachi. It’s compact, with snappy mechanical switches under the buttons and customizable RGB lighting. It’s also tournament-ready with a competition “lock” switch and the ability to switch between up to four different control settings for different games.

The thing I find most intriguing, though, is the fact that HyperX has released 3D printer files for the buttons and top plate so you can design and print your own custom parts. Some hardcore players like to assemble or customize their fight sticks, but that kind of work generally requires a fair bit of research and technical confidence. Having a brand encourage and enable this kind of customization makes it a lot easier for folks to try tinkering, and I think that’s really cool.

Mike Epstein is a Senior Commerce Editor at Hearst Enthusiast Group, producing reviews for buying guides Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products. Prior to joining Hearst, he was a video game and technology critic for over 10 years, with bylines at IGN, Gamespot, Variety, Lifehacker, Kotaku, GamesRadar, Flavorwire and Digital Trends, among others. Now, he’s a jack of all trades, helping reviewers share everything they know about all kinds of technical gear, from snowblowers, to running shoes and bicycles, and every kind of gadget imaginable.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6302. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6301. Finland Is Throwing an Epic Dinner Party for 16 Singles—Here's How to Get Invited

The Nordic countries are well known for their rather gimmicky yet innovative travel campaigns luring travelers to the icy north. From doctors prescribing travel to Sweden as a medical treatment to Oslo's viral mock-documentary narrated by a jaded local called Halfdan. Preceding these by a decade, Danish tour operator Spies Travels famously promoted its ”Do It for Denmark!” campaign focused on Denmark’s low birth rates, offering “ovulation discounts” to couples who proved they conceived on their romantic trip.

Now, Finland has announced it's flying out sixteen international singles this February for a "blind group date with likeminded travelers and local Finnish singles.”

The country is touting the so-called Love At First Bite campaign as an epic blind dinner date, designed to help participants “discover Finnish food, meet new people, and perhaps even find love.” The singles will be divided and hosted in two group dates in capital city Helsinki and Tampere located in Europe’s largest lake district, Finland’s Lakeland region.

Joining the singles over candlelit tasting menus crafted by local celebrity chefs will be local single Finns. Get ready for lots of prolonged eye contact—the Nordic way of flirting—under low light as you bond over the likes of wild trout, reindeer, chanterelle mushrooms, and sea buckthorn. For those heading to Tampere, the destination is monikered the “world’s sauna capital,” so chances of sweating with your fellow single strangers is probably on the menu too.

I’ll admit, when the campaign was launched worldwide, my Finnish friends and I wrinkled our noses in confusion. Romantic and sexy aren’t the first words that come to mind when you think of Finland. And it's not the Nordic country you'd first go to for love if we're talking stereotypes. The Danes have their extroverted charm, the Swedes their chic worldliness, and the Norwegians typically have more money to spend on you. Popular Nordic comedians Helgi and Erlend riff on these regional stereotypes, depicting their Finnish character as stoic, quiet and mentally tough. The very Finnish ethos of “sisu” means grit and the tenacity to push through tough times. But maybe those are qualities you'd want in a lifelong partner as you navigate challenges together.

So the campaign got me thinking a little deeper. Named the happiest country in the world for the ninth consecutive year in a row, Finns are satisfied with their lifestyles firmly rooted in the outdoors, nature, and a slower pace of life. In this contentment is where you’ll find Finland’s hidden sexier side.

In a country of roughly five million, there are two million saunas. And few places are more intimate than sweating together naked in a sauna, dipping in chilly lakes during winter, then warming back up indoors in many more ways. There’s also something rather romantic about grilling wild-caught salmon for two over an open flame in the backcountry.

This isn’t the first time the country has dabbled in an unconventional approach to dating. The viral “Sinkkukori” phenomenon introduced pink shopping baskets as a way for singles to covertly signal their availability. Now Finland is taking a more overt approach to romance. As the well-known nineteenth-century English idiom reminds us, the quickest way to the heart is through the stomach, and Finland certainly wants to put this to the test.

To shoot your shot at finding love in Finland, apply by November 10, 2026 at 11:59 AM Finnish time. All you have to do is make a video answering the question: what would you serve on a dinner date, and why? Just like a proper prospect, Finland would like to know your preferences in advance so it can woo you in the most epic and intentional way. If that isn’t romantic, I don’t know what is.

This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

#6298. The Best Way to Eat Swiss Fondue? Floating on Lake Brienz

I could say that I was surprised to find myself and my family floating along in a red Zodiac on the deepest lake in Switzerland, eating cheese fondue and sipping white wine as the sun set. But really, it was all by design. When I designated myself as chief planner for an autumnal family trip to the Alpine nation with my adult children and their partners, I searched for an activity that would knock their socks off. I found it in Interlaken, with a floating fondue experience. Yes, you read that right.

I love Switzerland, and have visited the land where the hills are alive with the sound of cowbells more than 30 times in my life. And while I’ve done many amazing things in and around the Swiss Alps—skiing, hiking, trottinetting, whittling my own Swiss cow from a block of wood—I knew getting my Gen Z crew excited about family time involved finding something a little more unconventional.

We were going to be staying in the Bernese Oberland, a picture-postcard region with legendary sites like Grindelwald, the Jungfrau and Eiger mountains, and Interlaken. Everyone was up for hiking and taking cable cars to waterfalls; paragliding was sadly vetoed. But a unique culinary experience would surely work, I thought—the way to their hearts is through their stomachs.

Luckily, I had heard about a Cheese Fondue Float experience offered by a company called Outdoor Switzerland a few years ago. Back then, it was raclette—toasted cheese scraped onto boiled potatoes—that served as the dish du jour. But fondue, Switzerland’s national dish, is much more well-known, so the company savvily swapped raclette trays for caquelons (ceramic fondue pots). I found the experience listing on Get Your Guide, and reviews praised the change, highlighting the delicious cheese and wine and the gregarious fondue fun. I confirmed a private booking for the six of us a month before we left home, and kept my fingers crossed for good weather.

I needn’t have worried—my prayers were answered with glorious temperatures and bluebird skies on the day of the tour, a leisurely Sunday in September. A five-minute bus ride from downtown Interlaken brought us to the small village of Bonigen, the launch site located on scenic Lake Brienz. After shaking hands with our guide, a tall, friendly Dutchman named Hild, we donned life jackets, listened to the mandatory safety briefing, and stepped into the boat, alternating sides to keep the weight even. Once comfortably settled around the pretty red-and-white-checkered tablecloth, which was already topped with plates, cups, and two fondue pots, Hild slowly rowed us onto the lake.

An overhead shot of the pretty tablescape and gorgeous lake

Lake Brienz is the deepest lake in the country, and it’s surely one of the most scenic too. Moving out from the shore, we encountered spectacular views of towering mountains, their peaks mirrored in the impossibly blue water. I poured the prepared cheese fondue into the heated fondue pots, and the mixture began bubbling, filling the air with a sharp aroma as it warmed into readiness.

The fondue float experience includes white wine (one 500-ml bottle per person), as well as water and hot tea. We took turns pouring wine into our copper cups as my eldest son took command of the Bluetooth speaker, setting a lively mood with traditional Alpine tunes played on accordions and hackbretts (a kind of dulcimer), mixed with the occasional yodel ditty. At one point, our float’s music and laughter brought friendly waves from passengers on a passing cruise boat, along with toots from the ship’s horn. We whooped and waved in return.

Once the cheese was steaming hot, we dipped and swished bread cubes into the melted goodness, savoring the delicious alchemy of bread and cheese alongside celebratory toasts in honor of our family adventure. As the cheese disappeared, the fondue pot heated the remains into what the Swiss call “la réligieuse”—toasted cheese bits that are scraped from the bottom of the pot. We fought playfully over dibs on the last delicious morsels—trust me, they’re good to the last perfectly browned crumb.

Raising a glass to a unique family adventure

The entire experience lasted about an hour and a half, and during that time, the six of us managed to drink all six wine bottles on board. None of us are big drinkers, but the beauty of the surroundings inspired the good times to flow, and, well, so did the wine.

Photos and videos captured our cheesy adventure, but the memory of enjoying such a unique culinary and cultural experience with my favorite people in the world will be forever burned into my mind. You can have a fondue anywhere, but while floating in one of the most iconic locations in one of the most beautiful countries on earth? Even my discerning Gen Z travel companions agreed: “That’s extra.”

The Cheese Fondue Float experience on Lake Brienz in Interlaken is available to book on the Outdoor Switzerland website, as well as on GetYourGuide and Viator. It is offered between September and April, weather permitting. If booking in the colder months, bundle up with coats, beanies, and gloves, as you’ll be out on the water for up to an hour and a half. Private charters are available for groups up to eight people; kids eight years and up are welcome. More of a dessert person? Outdoor Switzerland also offers a Swiss Chocolate Fondue experience. Get cozy under blankets, sip hot tea, and dip marshmallows and fruit into creamy melted Swiss chocolate while a qualified guide rows you merrily along the beautiful Brienzersee.

#6297. The Wonder—and Weirdness—of Exploring a National Park in the Dark

I’ve spent the majority of my life doing outdoor activities: camping, hiking, biking, kayaking, you name it. It’s intrinsically part of who I am, something that defines my siblings and I so deeply it feels like it’s braided into our DNA.

Perhaps that’s because, when I was just two-and-a-half years old, my parents took my siblings and me on a two-month-long road trip from New York to Arizona, hitting dozens of state and national parks on the way. We still talk about that adventure, lovingly referred to as the Out West Trip. It was the first time I visited Utah’s national parks, known as the Mighty 5: Zion, Arches, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Bryce Canyon.

Once night falls in Utah's national parks, most travelers head back to their campfires or motor lodges—except for those willing to brave the dark and explore their nocturnal side.

A lot has changed since I first visited. Now, millions of visitors head to Southern Utah every year, flocking to these five well-known national parks in addition to the whopping 46 state parks across the whole of Utah. Even in the staggeringly hot and dry summer season, these protected areas teem with tourists from all over the world—Zion alone reported over 1.4 million visitors in June, July, and August of 2026, while Arches reported over 445,000 in the same season.

Once night falls in the Utah desert, though, the temperatures cool off, most tourists head back to their campsites and motor lodges, and the stars shine through that clear desert sky. All of the Mighty 5 are certified dark sky parks—Utah, in fact, boasts the highest concentration of certified International Dark Sky Places in the world. So maybe it's no surprise that, in recent years, these destinations have embraced night-centric recreation, showcasing a lesser-known version of themselves for those willing to brave the dark.

In Capitol Reef National Park, the The Temple of the Sun summit stands against a sky full of stars.

It's why, nearly 30 years after my first Utah park trip, I decided to return—this time, experiencing Southern Utah’s state and national parks once the sun set. I’m a night owl, but I also wanted to revive that sense of wonder I felt so long ago when I first visited. I knew the parks by day, but by night? They were brand new to me. And so, in late September, my friend Sarra and I plotted a week-long road trip linking four national parks and three state parks in Utah. Our goal was to take it easy during the daylight hours with a gentle hike or two, and store up our energy for a nocturnal expedition come sundown. We wanted to get to know Utah’s parks in a way that too few do.

It’s 9 p.m. when we walk into Capitol Reef National Park with hiking guides Samuel and Suzanne Francis, the married owners of Western Whiptails Adventures. The sun has set by a couple hours; my friend and I rely on flashlights, while our guides trust themselves in the dark. As we begin on the trail, I’m struck by the silence surrounding us, serene in a way I’ve experienced only in the redwoods, where the massive trees cradle you against human noise; by day, the stone of Utah’s parks almost reverberates with the many overlapping voices of the crowd. Now, there is no sound left to bounce.

The view of the Hickman Bridge in Capitol Reef National Park at midnight.

Our goal is to hike to Hickman Bridge, a natural sandstone arch—completely in the dark. It’s a 1.8-mile round-trip that begins with an initial climb on switchbacks, flattens out in the middle, and then resumes a narrower uphill path with a bit of a scramble required to reach the view. It’s a hike that should take about 1.5 hours in daylight. Sam says he and Suz have led hundreds of guided tours throughout the park and surrounding public lands, but nothing quite like this. “Capitol Reef’s landscape takes on an entirely different character at night,” he says.

I feel the ground under my sneakers shift from hard-packed dirt to softer sand as we set out, and the herbal scent of pinon and Utah juniper trees tickles my nose. We’re surrounded by dust and desert, but the area feels alive with the chirping of bugs and rustling of leaves.

Suz leads us to little-known petroglyphs, then points out a site where the Fremont people once stored corn. Sarra and I shine our flashlights and look on in admiration. It’s a respite in the adrenaline-pumping stretch of the hike—we have gained a couple hundred feet of elevation, and I am imagining the drop-offs that I’m quite sure lie beyond the tiny circle of my flashlight. My grip gets tighter and I begin to sweat through my layers, realizing that the dark can't quiet my fear of heights. Suz is up ahead, climbing like it’s second nature: “If you turn your flashlights off, your eyes will adjust,” she says, turning back. I laugh, knowing there's no way I can get myself to follow her advice.

The nearly full moon directly over the sandstone summit in Capitol Reef National Park

A hard-to-find petroglyph site in Capitol Reef National Park

“Many animals in Capitol Reef are nocturnal or crepuscular, especially during warmer months,” Sam says, listing off the species we share the night with as we plod on. “Bats, kangaroo rats, desert cottontails, foxes, desert bighorn sheep, mule deer, or even the rare ringtail.”

Once we reach flatter ground, I concede to turn off my light, blinking to let my eyes adjust. I realize the nearly full moon above is blindingly bright—and yet we can still make out hundreds of glittering stars sharing the sky. “The darkness really offers a unique connection to the landscape,” says Sam. I can't help but agree.

And then we finally catch sight of the stone bridge, bathed in moonlight and backlit by stars, appearing especially mammoth in the low light. We sit beneath it, the silence wrapped around us, the space above looking unimaginably infinite. “I’ve seen this bridge plenty of times during the day,” says Suz, agreeing with me, “but at night, it's even better.”

The starry sky shines over Dead Horse Point State Park, where after-dark activities include scorpion spotting and stargazing.

While Capitol Reef's night hike was nothing short of thrilling, another type of excitement awaits us at Dead Horse State Park. The park is known for its dramatic red-rock canyon vistas and hiking trails that cross them—and yet the evening programming is just as robust, with scorpion searching, stargazing, sunset walks, and astronomy talks all included in the $20 entrance fee. Unlike Capitol Reef, where we were possibly the only visitors on the grounds that night (despite it being open 24 hours), Dead Horse is known for its nocturnal programming (much of which begins around 8 p.m., and runs until the park closes at 10). According to Ally O'Rullian, public information officer at Utah State Parks, Dead Horse Point naturalist programs have “likely included dark sky viewings” since as early as the mid 1970s, and this new slate of activities was added to the regular calendar in 2015 as part of its application for International Dark Sky status. We are far from the only ones out tonight—it feels as though this is how the Dead Horse is meant to be appreciated.

A group of travelers gather around a state ranger as they prepare for a scorpion search

We've opted to go scorpion searching, which is exactly as wacky as it sounds. Scorpions are biofluorescent, meaning they emit a visible bluish glow under UV lights. And so we gather at the Visitor Center, where ranger Jimmy Burch is handing out special flashlights. This is one of the most popular activities at the park, Burch says, and perhaps unsurprisingly, the one with the greatest youth turnout. We do feel like kids, as our group of a dozen or so of all ages start down a gentle, meandering path, shining our torches on brush and rocks to see if we can find anything hiding among them. Shine a UV light directly on a bush with a scorpion in it, Burch says, and it would be nearly impossible to overlook the glowing body within. “If you hear hissing, step away,” he cautions, as we sweep the area. Burch assures us that no one has ever been stung on one of these walks.

We are nearing the end of “scorpion season” in late September, as the weather is getting too cold for the critters to wander freely. In winter, scorpions enter a low-activity state and hide in dark, quiet locations, like underground burrows, conserving their energy against the cold. I wonder if that means we won't see much—but then, after just a few minutes, a boy in my group begins to call out, “Scorpion, scorpion, scorpion!” Burch heads over, congratulatory as he crouches down a few inches away from the tiny, glowing arachnid. The rest of us follow, taking turns leaning closer to take in its luminous body, just a few inches long. It turns out that scorpions are perfectly happy to hang out under the UV light, surrounded by a large group of people taking photos. It doesn't move a single muscle as we pap it in awe.

Setting up kayaks at the edge of the Sand Hollow State Park reservoir, just as the moon begins to rise

Jaw-dropping colors appear in the sky over Sand Hollow State Park and its reservoir.

Ready for something a bit calmer, we make the early morning drive to our final destination: Hurricane, Utah—about 25 miles away from Zion National Park, and home to the lesser-known Sand Hollow. Initially, we had plans to do nocturnal canyoneering in Zion, but when the weather turned, it gave us permission to settle into a slower place.

For the past two years, Sand Hollow State Park—known for its large reservoir set against red-rock cliffs—has been offering a monthly full-moon paddle in the warmer months, to complement the hiking and biking trails that families enjoy year-round.

The paddle is only available from April through September (depending on the weather) and starts at moonrise—which is just after 7 p.m. for us, when our group meets ranger Carlie Mallow on the shore of the reservoir. Just on the other side of sunset, the sky still has tinges of light to it, and we can hear the gentle chatter of dozens of other people who are still swimming, fishing, and hanging out on the water's edge as we pull our kayaks into the water. The park is open until 10 p.m., and those accompanied by a ranger can stay even later. I feel as though I'm at an after-hours summer camp, as I notice the people on piers, jumping in the water, and sitting at picnic tables nearby.

Two kayaks at the edge of Sand Hollow State Park reservoir at the end of the moonlit paddle

The night is relatively warm, as we make the gentle paddle out. We take pauses to float and listen to history; Mallow points at an island in the middle of the water: "a family of raccoons lives there", she tells us.

We let our kayaks rest when we near the isle, collecting among the rippling water to watch the moon continue its rise. I hear the water brushing against my kayak, and realize my eyes are now more used to navigating these wild spaces in the absence of the sun.

Our group is substantial. Sometimes there will 30 kayaks or paddleboards on the water at a time, Mallow says. “The moonlit paddle is pretty popular,” Mallow tells us from her own kayak, as we circle the island. "We hope programs like these both spark adventure and curiosity in visitors, and encourage neighbors to fall in love with their backyard.” As we navigate the water, we come across night fishers and a swimmer (“people train for the Ironman here,” says Mallow). I wonder if the scuba divers who were on the shore when we pushed off were entering or exiting. Before this trip, my imagination couldn't have fathomed so many ways to experience these lands after sunset.

As parks get increasingly crowded, I have to wonder if nighttime adventures will become a part of my regular routine. There are always new ways to discover America’s national and state park system—and now, I know that darkness can make even the most familiar places feel like a whole new world. Once you get past the fear of it—the dark, the height, the critters—you are free to soak up the feeling of being so small against the endless night sky, amazed by all the life that continues even once the sun has gone down.
