#6241. The Best Ski Resorts in the US and Canada: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

For our 39th annual Reader’s Choice Awards, voters weighed in on their favorite ski resorts in North America—including the US and Canada. Big Sky’s decade-long transformation has paid off, landing the Montana resort in the top spot this year. But Colorado reigns as the top US ski destination, with 10 resorts making our top 30. Meanwhile, six East Coast resorts were recognized, including Mont-Tremblant in Quebec, Canada. And in the western US, new enhancements at Alyeska Resort helped get Alaska back on the list.

From Taos to Telluride and Stowe to SilverStar, these ski resorts were picked by our readers as the best in North America for their trails, lodges, lifts, and après-ski scenes. Whether you’re a powder hound or après ski devotee, these ski resorts ticked all your boxes.

View the 2025 Readers' Choice Awards winners for best ski resorts as a list with scores for the United States here and Canada here.

Aspen-Snowmass’s four mountains are each wildly unique, and Buttermilk might be the most playful. More like one giant terrain park, it’s home to seven different parks for everyone from beginners to pros. Its 22-foot Zaugg-cut Superpipe is the stage for star-studded sporting competitions including X Games Aspen and The Snow League. But Buttermilk is also the mountain for easygoing beginner terrain and awesomely intense trails for uphillers—those showoffs practicing the cardio-busting trend of trekking up a mountain on skis.

Where to stay: Just a free, five-minute shuttle ride away in downtown Aspen at your pick of great hotels, including the Little Nell, Limelight Aspen, St. Regis Aspen, and Hotel Jerome.

Stats: 8 lifts and 44 trails. One-day lift tickets average from $189; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective.

The longest continually operating ski resort in Colorado, Winter Park is a Rocky Mountain playground known for its varied terrain and consistent snowfall (roughly 350 inches a year). It’s also one of Colorado’s most accessible mountains. Located just 67 miles west of Denver, it’s an easy drive from the airport, or take the Amtrak Winter Park Express ski train and get dropped off just steps from the lifts. This season, the resort is more than doubling snowmaking on a key base trail, again improving upon its recent $40 million snowmaking system upgrade. Families continue to find tons of value. Back this season, kids can nab a free ski or snowboard rental with a three-day adult gear rental package and every kid 14 and younger who signs up for a Winter Park Ski and Ride School lesson gets a free lift ticket for the day. The Gondola is free to everyone after 4 p.m. every Thursday through Saturday from mid-December through the end of March. That means you can wrap up the day at Mountaintop Après at Sunspot Lodge whether you skied or not.

Where to stay: Zephyr Mountain Lodge has studios, 1, 2, and 3-bedroom condos with full kitchens. In town, Gravity Haus Winter Park offers co-working spaces as well as gear demos and rentals. A-Frame Club is an Instagram-sensation with its 31 A-Frame cabins and historic saloon.

Stats: 23 lifts, 171 designated trails and 1,212 acres of off-piste terrain. One-day lift tickets from $108; on the Ikon Pass.

Where to stay: The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Resort and Spa is fresh off a $20 million renovation. Other favorites include The Westin Riverfront Resort & Spa Avon, Vail Valley, The Osprey, a RockResort, and the Ritz-Carlton, Bachelor Gulch.

Stats: 24 lifts for 167 trails. One-day lift tickets from $116; on the Epic Pass.

Skiing in Alaska is a different experience than anywhere in the lower 48. Located just 40 miles southeast of Anchorage, Alyeska’s terrain is uniquely Alaskan, boasting everything from high alpine to the steep faces the 49th state is known for. Experts can push their limits, but with over 55 percent intermediate terrain, tree skiing, wide open groomed runs, and a lower mountain venue perfect for beginners, Alyeska caters to all ability levels. Aside from resort skiing, Alyeska serves as a backcountry basecamp offering guided ski touring, cat skiing, or heli skiing with top-notch outfits like SMG Alaska. And when it comes to après-ski, a trip to the mountaintop Bore Tide Bar for an off-menu Fizz cocktail is an Alyeska ritual.

Where to stay: The 299-room Alyeska Resort has eight dining venues, including stellar sushi spot Sakura and fine dining restaurant, Seven Glaciers, with its panoramic views. The eighth-floor Black Diamond Club feels like a hotel-within-a-hotel thanks to perks like a private lounge that serves complimentary breakfast and après bites. The resort’s 50,000-square-foot, indoor-outdoor Nordic spa is the perfect place to spend a down day.

Stats: 7 lifts for 76 runs, with an additional 1,400 vertical feet accessible via hike-to terrain when conditions allow. One-day lift tickets from $77; on the Ikon Pass.

Tamarack’s primarily east-facing slopes receive an average of 300 inches of snowfall annually. Readers love the diversity of terrain, which welcomes everyone from beginners and families to experts and powder chasers. The resort’s 2,000 mountain acres and 2,800 feet of vertical deliver everything from open bowls, steeps and signature cornice drops to high-speed corduroy groomers, natural tree-skiing glades and three terrain parks. At 6,700 feet, the new Mid-Mountain Lodge crowns the top of Tamarack Express with panoramic dining and event space, while a vibrant alpine-style village anchors the base with lodging, dining, and après. And Tamarack's Nordic trail system winds through open meadows and forested terrain for classic and skate skiing, snowshoeing, and fat biking.

Where to stay: Tamarack Resort has accommodations ranging from studios to four-bedroom penthouses plus amenities such as a pool, hot tubs and gear valet. The Lodge at Osprey Meadows is steps from the lifts and has studios and two- and three-bedroom condos.

Stats: 7 lifts for 59 runs. One-day lift tickets from $99; Ikon Pass Bonus Mountain

Founded by the late Robert Redford in 1969, Sundance Mountain Resort is a beloved escape tucked into Utah’s Wasatch Mountains at the base of the 12,000-foot Mount Timpanogos in Provo Canyon. Steep bowls give experienced skiers a thrill, while a third of the runs are green and beginner-friendly. Just an hour from Salt Lake City (hello, easy airport access!), the 5,000 acres of protected wilderness that surround the resort will help you find solitude. This season’s debut of Electric Horseman, a high-speed quad, marks the first phase of Sundance’s back mountain expansion, adding 60-plus acres of terrain and bringing the resort to 605 skiable acres. At the heart of the terrain expansion is Storyteller, a new signature ridgeline run carved from the terrain formerly known as the Far East Ridgeline. An additional 100 acres of terrain are planned for the 2027-2028 winter season. Off the slopes, guests can explore the resort’s renowned Art Studio & Gallery (think silversmithing and pottery classes), or unwind at the Spa and The Springs.

Where to stay: The Inn at Sundance Mountain Resort, which opened in January 2026, introduced ski-in/ski-out hotel accommodations to the resort for the first time, with 63 thoughtfully designed rooms in the heart of the village.

Stats: 10 lifts for 72 trails. One-day pass is $169.

Spanning six peaks and over 3,000 acres in the Yampa Valley, Steamboat is revered for its tree skiing, trademarked Champagne Powder snow, and family-friendly amenities. But many folks keep coming back for its deep Western roots and a down-home vibe that extends from the mountain to the town. A multiyear, multimillion-dollar redevelopment has reimagined Steamboat. The base area now features Wild Blue, a high speed ten-person gondola that takes skiers and riders from the base to the top of Sunshine Peak in 13 minutes, plus Skeeter's ice rink, and the Range Food & Drink Hall. Beginners can hone their skills mid-mountain at Greenhorn Ranch with natural feature-based instruction, while experts can test their mettle on 655 acres of challenging terrain in Mahogany Ridge and Fish Creek Canyon. One of the most accessible resorts in the Rockies, Steamboat is served by 18 major U.S. cities including Portland, Austin, and Houston.

Where to stay: The Steamboat Grand is a favorite for its massive heated pool and hot tubs. Ski-in/ski-out Sheraton Steamboat Resort Villas is conveniently located next to Christie Peak Express. Gravity Haus is an affordable, slopeside boutique stay. The Amble opened this summer and has 42 residences and resort amenities.

Stats: 23 lifts for 184g trails. One-day lift tickets from $131; on the Ikon Pass.

Of the four mountains that make up Aspen Snowmass, the ultimate rite of passage is here at Aspen Highlands’ massive Highland Bowl. Here’s how to do it: Hike some 45 minutes to the top of the bowl, soak in rewarding 360-degree views that include the twin-peaked Maroon Bells and own the drop into almost 2,500 feet of steep bowl skiing. Reward yourself at mid-mountain with the Merry-Go-Round’s signature Boomerang Burger, topped with onion rings, pastrami bacon and grilled cheese buns.

Where to stay: The Little Nell for five-star service and a great spa or its more casual sister property, Limelight Aspen. That Gant for apartment-style residences with full kitchens.

Stats: 5 lifts for 144 trails. One-day lift tickets from $189; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

With nearly 5,000 acres of diverse terrain, Heavenly offers the best of both California and Nevada skiing and riding including wide-open groomers, glades, and 1,600-foot mogul runs. Sparkling Lake Tahoe views, an average of 300 days of sunshine a year, and high-energy events and après make Heavenly a dream getaway for your party crew that is always looking for the next adventure. The unique Skyline Trail is a must-do run, taking in majestic mountain landscapes, flat valleys, and lake panoramas while crossing from California to Nevada. Plus, the Heavenly Village is located in the heart of South Lake Tahoe, surrounded by snow-based activities and restaurants, and fun events throughout the winter season. If the views of Lake Tahoe inspire you on the slopes, a trip to the shore is just minutes away.

Where to stay: Basecamp Tahoe South is just a four-minute walk to the gondola and offers a variety of rooms from bunks to luxe tents. Zalanta Resort at the Village is steps away from Heavenly Village and residence-style rooms include gourmet kitchens and private balconies. Lakefront Edgewood Tahoe Resort has a partnership with Ski Butlers to have gear delivered directly to your room.

Stats: 27 lifts for 111 trails. One-day lift ticket from $115; on the Epic Pass.

A winter haven for East Coasters, this Poconos resort’s snow-making capacity could cover the George Washington Bridge with one foot of snow in 24 hours. The mountain’s 900-foot vertical drop is great training before venturing to bigger mountains in the West. More than half of the mountain, however, is covered in beginner-friendly greens. Families love the amenities, including one of the country’s largest snow-tubing park, an indoor water park, and a plethora of dining options including ski-in/ski-out Trail’s End Pub & Grille, known for its creative burgers and craft beer, and Alpine Outpost, a new grab-and-go spot along the Coolmoor teaching trail.

Where to stay: Camelback Lodge, the only ski-in/ski out resort in the Poconos, recently refurbished 453 guest rooms that come in 16 different configurations including bunk rooms and a suite that can sleep up to 14 guests.

Stats: 14 lifts for 45 trails. One-day lift tickets from $78; on the Ikon Pass.

Hard-core skiers who live for hike-to terrain and super steeps have always been fans of Taos Ski Valley. But a revitalized base area with an ice-skating rink, improvements to beginner and intermediate terrain, and $3 million in glading and expanding snowmaking capacity have made this New Mexico mountain destination way more family friendly. Taos Ski Valley leans into sustainability, equity, and inclusivity as the first ski resort in the world to have been B-Corp certified, and one of a few to be Certified CarbonNeutral®. The challenging terrain of Kachina Peak and the moguls of Al’s Run are the big draw for experts. This season ups the resort’s luxury appeal with the introduction of Taos by Belvedere, a fully hosted, all-inclusive mountain experience that features slopeside penthouse accommodations, a private chef, privately guided skiing, restorative wellness therapies, and insider access to local experiences. For dining, the Bavarian is an institution known for its brats and German beers (they also host a sleigh ride dinner during the winter), and newcomer Corner Office gives the state its first natural wine bar. Down days are far from dull thanks to surrounding cultural attractions including the Taos Pueblo UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Where to stay: Located adjacent to Lift 1, The Blake offers a variety of accommodation options that include hotel rooms, suites, penthouses, and condos; decor blends rustic European architecture with one of North America’s finest collections of Southwestern art, including original works by Georgia O’Keeffe.

Stats: 13 lifts for 110 trails. One-day lift tickets from $75; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

The largest of the SkiBig3 resorts in UNESCO-designated Banff National Park earns its keep with 4,200 acres spanning four different mountain faces and a solid mix of beginner, intermediate, and expert runs from every chair. Here’s what else makes it a dream for all walks of skiers: steeps backed by an awe-inspiring wilderness, bowls dusted in famously dry powder, four terrain parks for beginners to experts, and long cruisers—one of which winds on for five miles. The ‘West Bowl’ is a freeride playground with some 480 wilderness acres to explore. And the recent addition of the Juniper Express Quad provides an ideal learning zone for beginner and intermediate skiers and riders looking to advance their skills. This season, Lake Louise is enhancing its recently opened Richardson’s Ridge terrain with new groomed runs, glades, and improved snowmaking, alongside a major Top of the World chair upgrade designed to increase capacity and reliability.

Where to stay: Located lakeside in Banff National Park, Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise looks like a fairytale castle and its new Basin Glacier Waters Thermal Wellness Spa will have you wishing for a down day to spend soaking in its healing waters. A member of Relais & Châteaux, Post Hotel & Spa has a saltwater pool and is known for its extensive wine cellar and talented culinary team.

Stats: 13 lifts for 169 runs and back bowls. One-day SkiBig3 lift tickets from $172; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

Nestled on the northern edge of British Columbia’s North Okanagan wine region, SilverStar is one of Canada’s best-kept secrets, with 3,065 skiable acres that receive 275-plus inches of annual snowfall. Guests can skip the rental car and take one of the regular shuttles from Kelowna International Airport, just 55 minutes away. The resort has exceptionally groomed terrain for all abilities and families appreciate that kids age 5 and under receive free lift tickets all season. Alpine skiing is just one of many winter activities on offer. You’ll also find 65 miles of groomed cross-country ski trails, 9 miles of fat-tire bike trails, 4 snow tubing lanes, and a natural skating pond. The dining experiences, such as the Ravenwood snowshoe raclette dinner and the Paradise Camp snow cat dinner tour, are not-to-be-missed. And La Stella, a new Italian spot with wood-fired pizzas debuts this season.

Where to stay: SilverStar’s mid-mountain location means most accommodations are ski-in/ski-out. Snowbird Lodge, Silver Creek Lodge, and Lord Aberdeen have prime locations in the heart of the village, steps from the Summit Express Gondola. Firelight Lodge offers convenient access to the Nordic trail heads.

Stats: 10 lifts for 132 runs. One-day lift ticket from $119; on the Ikon Pass.

Originally known as Little Gap Ski Area when it opened in 1977, the resort changed its name in 1989 to better reflect the grandeur of our mountain. With a vertical drop of 1,082 feet, Blue Mountain boasts the highest elevation in Pennsylvania. Whether you’re a beginner or expert, you’ll find the perfect challenge on the mountain’s 171 acres. You can conquer 15 green, 6 blue, 16 black diamond, and 3 double black diamond trails across the region’s most varied terrain. Home to the East Coast’s largest snowmaking system, the mountain delivers some of the most consistent conditions all season long in the mid-Atlantic region. For lunch with gorgeous views, pop into Slopeside Pub & Grill for wood-fired pizzas and hearty sammys like chicken cheesesteaks. For a quick, grab-and-go bite, swing by the new spud truck, serving up loaded baked potatoes.

Where to stay: Blue Mountain-area Airbnb rentals are the way to go here.

Stats: 15 lifts for 40 trails; One-day lift ticket from $48; on the Ikon Pass.

When it comes to earning credit card rewards, sometimes two cards really are better than one.

Maybe you have a card that earns bonus points on dining and groceries but falls short on other everyday purchases. Or perhaps you love your card's travel perks but wish it offered better earning rates outside of travel.

That's where pairing cards can come in handy. By choosing two cards with complementary benefits and earning categories, you can get more out of your spending without relying on a single card for everything.

Here are three American Express card combinations worth considering, depending on your spending habits and travel goals.

Frequent travelers who want a combination of premium travel benefits and strong everyday earning rates may get the most value from pairing the with the .

The Platinum is, at its core, a travel and lifestyle card that offers access to an extensive network of airport lounges worldwide through the Global Lounge Collection, along with a range of statement credits and other travel benefits.

The Gold fills an important gap in the Platinum's earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $50,000 and $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, respectively*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

By using the Platinum for eligible flights and the Gold for dining and groceries, you can earn elevated rewards across several major spending categories while enjoying premium travel benefits. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can also combine your rewards into one balance to use toward travel through Amex's transfer partners (after linking your accounts online).

The trade-off of this card combination is cost. The Platinum has an $895 annual fee, while the Gold has a $325 annual fee, bringing the combined annual cost to $1,220. For that reason, I'd only recommend this pairing to travelers who can take advantage of the Platinum's benefits and who regularly spend in the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: How these two cards got me over $4,500 in value in one year

If you spend a lot on dining and groceries but want to earn more than 1 point per dollar spent on other eligible purchases, the and could make a great pair.

The Gold earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year*) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year*). It also earns 3 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through amextravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

Then, use the Blue Business Plus for eligible business purchases that would earn only 1 point per dollar on the Gold. It earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*) compared with the Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up a single rewards balance to use toward travel through Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Gold has a $325 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee, so you won't pay extra to add a flat-rate earning card to the mix.

Just keep in mind that the Blue Business Plus is a business card, so you'll need to qualify to apply. This combination could be especially useful for freelancers and small-business owners with eligible business expenses that don't fall into the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: The 4 Amex cards I’d use to earn Membership Rewards points faster

If your business spends a lot on things like advertising, software or gas, the and could make a great pair.

The Business Gold earns 4 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in combined purchases per calendar year*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

What I like about the Business Gold is that you don't have to choose your bonus categories in advance. Amex automatically determines your top two eligible categories each billing cycle, which is helpful if your business expenses change from month to month.

For purchases outside those categories, the Blue Business Plus earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*). That's double the Business Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

For example, you might use the Business Gold for advertising and software expenses, then switch to the Blue Business Plus for other eligible business purchases. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up one balance to use with Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Business Gold has a $375 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee. This combination makes the most sense if you spend enough in the Business Gold's bonus categories to justify the annual fee while using the Blue Business Plus to earn more on other purchases.

Related: 7 reasons why the Amex Blue Business Plus Card should be in everyone’s wallet

Before adding another Amex card to your wallet, take a look at where you're spending the most money and what you want to get out of your rewards. The goal is to find a card that fills a gap in your current lineup, rather than one that offers more of the same.

And remember, earning more points isn't worth it if you're spending more than you normally would or carrying a balance and paying interest.

Related: Best credit card strategies for couples

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to choosing the best credit card combination. The key is finding cards that complement each other rather than simply offer more of the same benefits.

Whether you're looking for premium travel perks, stronger everyday earning rates or a way to maximize rewards on business expenses, pairing the right Amex cards can help you earn more Membership Rewards points.

Just make sure the additional rewards and benefits are worth the combined annual fees and that you're choosing cards that make sense for your spending habits.

Related: The best business and personal credit card combinations

#6239. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

Given the dire state of the BA offer with still flaky IT, dirty badly maintained cabins and dysfunctional (if at all) customer services a great option for those in the UK.

#6238. United Airlines Executive Says Iconic Dulles Mobile Lounges Will Retire, But “Won’t Be Forgotten.” What Comes Next?

United Airlines wants Washington Dulles to move beyond its mobile lounges. But when I asked Andrew Nocella whether he actually likes them, his response suggested that retirement may not mean disappearance. Could one become a bar or café? Could a limited transportation role survive? His answer left room for some speculation.

During a press gaggle at Washington Dulles yesterday, I asked United Airlines Executive Vice President and Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella a simple question: does he like the people movers? (it was in the context of their future place at an evolving IAD).

“I love it,” he responded, before explaining:

“The people movers, of course, is part of my history. I can remember, back in the day, coming out to the aircraft through the people mover, so it’s part of my history. But I do understand the need to evolve and change and innovate. And the people movers need to be innovated out. There are better ways to do it. But it will be an important part of the history of Dulles Airport and I can assure you that People Moves, while they will be retired, they won’t be forgotten.”

These vehicles are technically known as mobile lounges, though people movers is a fitting description too and I’ve called them “moon buggies” for years. Whatever you call them, I found that last assurance intriguing, even if we should be careful not to read too much into it.

Nocella did not announce a preservation project or describe a future use. But promising they will not be forgotten invites the question: how might Dulles preserve something so closely associated with the airport while finally moving beyond the need to use it?

My favorite possibility is turning one into a bar or café.

Imagine a retired mobile lounge parked in a suitable location, with its distinctive shape preserved and the interior converted into somewhere to have a drink while watching aircraft. Keep some of the original seating,  add photographs explaining its history, and suddenly an airport frustration becomes an attraction.

I would happily stop for a cappuccino. I suspect plenty of aviation enthusiasts would make a point of visiting too.

There would obviously be practical questions about access, utilities, and where to put it…maybe the wheels would have to be removed. A vehicle designed to transport passengers is not automatically suitable for operating a restaurant. But as a concept, it strikes me as a fun way to preserve a piece of Dulles without requiring anyone to ride it to immigration.

Nostalgia becomes much easier to appreciate when you can choose whether to participate!

Think how cool it would be to take one of these and put it inside the new Polaris Lounge in Concourse E that will be coming in the years ahead.

Another possibility is that the mobile lounges disappear from most journeys but continue in a narrower role.

I wonder, for example, whether there might be a useful way to run passengers between the D and E gates during the airport’s lengthy transition. Could a mobile lounge provide a convenient connection while the rest of the concourse development catches up? It woudl certainly save a lot of walking.

That is a question, not something Nocella proposed and I do realize that keeping an aging fleet operating for a limited purpose could undermine the savings and simplicity that retirement is supposed to deliver.

Still, “retired” can mean different things. Retired from routine passenger service would not necessarily preclude an occasional special ride or some other carefully limited use.

Of course, “won’t be forgotten” may mean something much less elaborate.

A preserved vehicle, a display in the terminal, or a design reference inside a future lounge could honor the mobile lounges without retaining their transportation function.

I would prefer preserving at least one actual vehicle rather than relying exclusively on photographs. These machines are unusual enough that future travelers should have an opportunity to see what generations of Dulles passengers experienced. I still love them and will always love them.

Nocella’s answer was affectionate, but clear about the need for change. He did not offer a retirement date or reveal what remembering the mobile lounges will look like.

But I do hope that assurance becomes something tangible. A mobile lounge café or bar would get my vote, preferably inside the new Polaris Lounge. A useful transitional shuttle or occasional heritage ride could be interesting too and much easier to maintain than a vintage aircraft.

For years, passengers have boarded these vehicles because they had to. It would be wonderful if Dulles eventually gave us a reason to step inside one because we wanted to.

What would you do with a retired Dulles mobile lounge?

#6236. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

Who’s ready for first class on United Airlines’s smallest regional jet?

The first Mitsubishi CRJ-450, a premium variant of the CRJ-200, is “on track” to begin carrying passengers by the end of the year. That's according to Andrew Nocella, United's chief commercial officer, who discussed the arrival of the CRJ-450 on the sidelines of the  brand-new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Monday.

The plane will debut at the airline’s Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD) hub, he added.

First look: United unveils gorgeous new Washington Dulles concourse, massive lounge

“It’ll be very exciting and it’s really critical that we connect big cities to little cities, and that’s what the CRJ-450 allows us to do,” said Nocella.

Nocella did not say where the CRJ-450 could fly from ORD but it is widely expected to serve some of the smallest cities in United's network, for example Akron-Canton, Ohio, or Fort Wayne, Indiana.

United unveiled the CRJ-450 in March in an effort to expand its premium offerings to smaller markets. Instead of the usual 50 economy seats on the CRJ-200, the 450 has seven first-class, 16 extra-legroom economy and 18 economy seats — for a total of 41 — a luggage closet for carry ons and high-speed Starlink inflight WiFi.

United's new CRJ-450: Could this be the fanciest regional jet in America?

The CRJ-450 is essentially a premium overhaul to the standard CRJ-200 that has been a workhorse of regional flying for much of this centutry. Passengers have routinely disliked the CRJ-200 for being small and cramped, an experience United hopes to improve with the less-dense CRJ-450 variant.

The plane is similar to the CRJ-550, a 50-seat premium variant of the CRJ-700 that typcially seats around 70 passengers. United debuted the CRJ-550 in 2019.

The CRJ-450 is the smallest plane in United’s premium airplane menu. Larger offerings include the Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” for premium domestic routes, the A321XLR for long-haul routes and up to the Boeing 787-9s with the “elevated” interior that features the new Polaris Studio in business class.

“We have realized that the demand for premium was much higher than we ever knew,” United CEO Scott Kirby, said in March. “It’s like we’re finally creating supply to meet the demand for premium.”

United regional affiliate SkyWest Airlines will operate the first 40 CRJ-450s under the United Express brand. The first two CRJ-200s are undergoing the necessary modifications and certification at one of the Utah-based regional carrier’s maintenance facilities, SkyWest President Wade Steel said at the end of October.

“The first airplanes just take longer naturally just because you’re working through the first-time issues,” he explained. Subsequent CRJ-200 conversions will take 2 to 3 weeks.

Steel, and SkyWest CEO Chip Childs, emphasized that the first CRJ-450s would enter service with United by the end of the year despite at the time having only about eight weeks left in 2026.

Both executives were bullish on the opportunity for the CRJ-450. Steel estimated demand for around 100 aircraft in the coming years as major airlines seek to increase premium offerings across their fleets.

“Putting first class seats on a CRJ-200 in a very good LOPA [Layout of Passenger Accommodation] with an outstanding interior is a very valuable aircraft,” said Steel

Delta Air Lines, for example, joined United in offering the CRJ-550 on regional routes in 2024. SkyWest flies the CRJ-550 for Delta.

American Airlines is the only major U.S. carrier not offering the CRJ-550. However, the airline can fly more larger regional jets, particularly the Embraer E175, than either Delta or United under a more lenient contract with its pilots.

#6234. Frontier Airlines Starts Selling First Class From $129. I Am Seriously Considering Booking It.

Frontier Airlines is now selling its new first class seats, with wider seating and no middle seats in the first two rows. Extra-legroom seating, USB-C power, and Starlink internet are also part of the cabin transformation. I welcome the investment, though a better seat will only get Frontier so far if the rest of the experience does not improve alongside it.

Installation is underway, with completion expected March 5, 2027. Reservations are open for travel beginning that day.

Promotional pricing requires purchasing the flight and bundle together by November 16, 2026, at 11:59 pm ET, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. Availability is limited.

USB-C power is planned for the first eight rows. Both power and Starlink installations begin in 2027 and progress aircraft by aircraft throughout the year. Booking the new seat does not mean every other advertised improvement will be available on your flight.

For me, reliable internet and the ability to keep a laptop charged substantially determine how useful a flight is. A comfortable seat is welcome, but on a daytime trip I also must get work done…it is an essential part of the package.

I have to say, I’m quite excited about these developments.

As much as I loved warmed mixed nuts, a hot meal, and sparkling water saved with lime and ice in a glass…the Frontier network is respectable and a comfortable seat with Wi-Fi and power are more important. If Frontier can charge half or what American or United are asking on the same route, I’m totally up for flying Frontier more.

The bigger question is whether Frontier can persuade passengers to pay more and then give them a reason to come back.

A first class seat loses much of its appeal if a cancellation leaves you with poor alternatives or resolving an ordinary problem becomes an ordeal…two areas where traditional network carriers still have a huge advantage. Selling a premium product raises expectations even when the price is relatively low.

I do not expect Frontier to become a full-service airline simply because it installs eight larger seats. But I would expect the airline to understand that passengers purchasing those seats are buying some relief from the compromises associated with budget travel, again myself included.

That makes this an opportunity. If Frontier can offer a comfortable seat at a sensible total price and deliver dependable transportation and maybe a little bit more service than the “Big Front Seat” on Spirit Airlines, I think there is a market for it.

Frontier Airlines is moving forward with first class, and I welcome more choice at the front of the aircraft. The new seats could make the airline more attractive to passengers who value comfort but remain sensitive to price, like me. Even the extra legroom seats are something I would consider, with Starlink being an even bigger game-changer.

While I would happily try it, the real test will be whether Frontier delivers an experience that makes me want to book it again. A larger seat with Starlink can get someone through the door…but Frontier must deliver that.

#6233. Always-Sunny San Diego Keeps Getting Better—Here's How to Explore

San Diego's calendar of sunny days, endless string of beaches on which to enjoy them, and family-friendly attractions have long drawn visitors year-round to the city and surrounding county. Lately new, design-centric hotels and a growing slate of destination restaurants are joining the enduring pleasures to create an era of vibrancy for all travelers to enjoy.

A surfer emerges from the waters of La Jolla Cove

With walkable streets, vintage shops, and craft breweries, North Park and Hillcrest districts are also rich in restaurants and nightlife. In North Park, sample French bistro fare at the Smoking Goat or Iberian seafood at Mabel's Gone Fishing, then end at listening bar Part Time Lover. Hillcrest, the epicenter of the LGBTQ+ scene, is home to the Brass Rail, the city's first gay bar, and Urban Mo's Bar and Grill, a beloved hub.

Soaring sea cliffs and palm-lined boulevards are only part of La Jolla's appeal—visit arts and culture institutions like La Jolla Playhouse and the Museum of Contemporary Art, and try classic restaurants such as George's at the Cove or The Marine Room for lunch with a view.

Historic neighborhood Barrio Logan is the heart of the city's Mexican American culture. Grab a mocha at Por Vida and queue for tacos and tamales at Las Cuatro Milpas, a stalwart since 1933.

The vintage elegance of peninsula Coronado, long a vacation spot for the well-heeled, endures thanks to buzzy openings attracting visitors across the bridge for a stroll on palm-lined Orange Avenue.

Up the coast in North County, Encinitas is the quintessential Southern California beach town, a quirky little mecca for yoga, wellness, and, of course, surfing at beaches like Swami's and Moonlight.

Next door, find everything in Carlsbad from outlet shopping and golf to fine dining—don't miss chef Eric Bost's Michelin-starred bistro, Jeune et Jolie. He runs two other restaurants in the area: Lilo, with a coastal tasting menu, and lively Campfire, designed to look like a glamping site.

San Diego's biggest hotel news is coming out of Coronado. Few stays channel classic Americana quite like the Hotel del Coronado, which, over its 138-year history, has hosted everyone from Marilyn Monroe to Franklin D. Roosevelt. It underwent a massive revamp in 2025, but that's not the only change afoot here: Across the street the sleek Bower Coronado also began welcoming guests in summer 2025; it was joined by the maximalist, seashell-inspired Baby Grand this spring. Last May, Hilton's new Outset Collection unveiled The Margot Hotel, with 135 sprawling suites, in the Gaslamp Quarter, right by Petco Park, home of the Padres. January will see the debut of the nearby 231-room Le Méridien San Diego Pinnacle, a gleaming tower close to the trendy restaurants and nightlife of Little Italy. Up in Carlsbad, an erstwhile Sheraton resort was reborn in March as the botanical-themed Hotel Solea, Autograph Collection, a stone's throw from Legoland.

LA Bryson’s Nocturnal Nostalgia (2021), on display in Liberty Arts District

Everybody knows a visit to the world-class San Diego Zoo and a ballgame at Petco Park are must-dos, but there's much else to consider. With 17 museums dedicated to everything from science and architecture to world music and Comic Con spread throughout a 1,200-acre expanse, Balboa Park has enough going on to keep you busy for a whole visit. Cast a wider net and you'll find creativity surging all over the city. Set in the Spanish Colonial Revival–style former Naval Training Center, the Liberty Station Arts District was recognized this year as one of California's state-designated cultural districts, thanks to its dense concentration of galleries and performing arts venues. Up the coast in Oceanside—a thriving creative enclave that's home to the Oceanside Museum of Art and a downtown arts district splashed with dozens of murals—surfer Ryder England opened Dear Tomorrow, a community art house with residencies, a shop, and events including botanical dyeing and figure drawing. In the San Diego Black Art and Culture District in Encanto, celebrated street artist Maxx Moses established Graffiti Gardens, a vibrant community hub with plenty of alfresco space to showcase his murals. You'll find lots of murals in historic Barrio Logan too: In the 1970s artists and activists painted vast murals at the base of the San Diego–Coronado Bay Bridge; today Chicano Park is a National Historic Landmark. Nearby, in a 45,000-square-foot former bakery, James Brown and Isabel Dutra opened Bread and Salt, a sprawling center for experimental art and craftsmanship. Every second Saturday join the Barrio Art Crawl, which pops into galleries, breweries, and record shops throughout the neighborhood. But the city's biggest draw remains its natural beauty. Some of the best hiking trails are along the cliffs of Torrey Pines Natural Reserve, like the three-quarter-mile Beach Trail, which winds through clusters of pine trees and wildflowers on the way down to the sand. If you're inspired by the surf culture and want to hit the waves yourself, ease in at La Jolla Shores or Tourmaline Surfing Park, but if you're more seasoned, you can try your luck at Windansea Beach or Sunset Cliffs.

Handmade ravioli with sage from Dora Ristorante

The proximity to Tijuana—drive 20 minutes from downtown and you're at the border—means you can sample the full pantheon of regional Mexican flavors here, including at Nómada, in Carlsbad, chef Alex Carballo's ode to Sinaloan fire-based cooking, or Carne y Hueso, a new North Park restaurant from sisters Chantelle and Crystal Godinez, who champion indigenous ingredients from Puebla, Jalisco, and Oaxaca in dishes like bone marrow sopes with hand-pressed masa and huitlacoche tetela with mole rojo. There's also a bounty of impossibly fresh seafood plucked from the coast, like at By the Sea, which opened in August near the beach in Coronado in a second-floor dining room styled to resemble a Mediterranean villa. It's directly opposite another newcomer to Orange Avenue, the splashy alfresco Greek restaurant Night Hawk at the Baby Grand, complete with large Greek statues and seating in grottoes. À L'ouest, chef Brad Wise's boisterous brasserie, was a hit the second it touched down in North Park in February; upstairs, the speakeasy Georgette's makes the wait for a table much more fun. And eating out in La Jolla has never been more interesting, thanks to a host of new destination restaurants: Chef Travis Swikard's Fleurette serves French-Californian fare such as “Oeufs & Eggs” with San Diego uni; across the street from the La Jolla Playhouse, Dora Ristorante, named for chef Accursio Lota's Sicilian grandmother, dishes up perfect pretheater bites of house-made gnocchi with pork sausage sugo and Pecorino; and Lucien earned chef Elijah Arizmendi San Diego's only new Michelin star this year. Also on deck: the ambitious 5,000-square-foot Roseacre development with multiple concepts under one roof, led by chef Erik Anderson, previously of the Michelin-starred Coi in San Francisco. Over in Liberty Station, meanwhile, a former navy outpost in Point Loma is being reimagined with restaurants, galleries, shops, and gardens. In 2027 the long-awaited Admiral will open its doors here, while the eventual 2028 completion of the entire project will transform five vacant World War II–era buildings into a new arts and dining hub.

“I grew up surfing Pacific Beach, right next to Tourmaline Surfing Park. I surfed there once or twice a day, seven days a week. In La Jolla there's a place called Marine Street Beach, which is great for bodysurfing; you get barreled on every ride. Up in North County, Swami's Beach is more crowded—you'll see a lot of pros there.” —Travis Swikard, chef, Fleurette and Callie

“We have a lot of arts here: Balboa Park and the museums, La Jolla Playhouse producing pieces that end up on Broadway. The Symphony has gotten a lot of love, and at the Rady Shell at Jacobs Park, you can see everything from pop concerts to the most classical Rachmaninoff.” —Roxana Velásquez, Maruja Baldwin executive director and CEO, San Diego Museum of Art

“I was born and raised in San Diego, and I'm not leaving. Picking my favorite Mexican food is tricky. My go-to order at Roberto's is rolled tacos with guacamole and cheese, because that's what I grew up on. Mexico Viejo is one of the most solid taco-stand type of places—I get the bean-and-cheese and the rice-and-guacamole burrito.” —Tony Hawk, professional skateboarder

#6232. Frontier Begins First Class Ticket Sales

Frontier on Tuesday opened reservations for its upcoming First Class, which is set to debut in March 2027.

The new seats have up to 37 inches of pitch, the carrier said, and will be arranged in a two-by-two configuration at the front of the cabin. Installations are already underway. Reservations are available now for travel beginning March 5.

Frontier first announced plans to add a First Class product in late 2024.

The airline will also add extra-legroom seating, with up to 34 inches of pitch, in rows three through eight. These seats will be available with Frontier’s Premium bundle, which includes a carry-on bag and priority boarding.

Frontier plans to roll out two additional perks through 2027 – in-seat USB-C power at every seat in the first eight rows, and Starlink wireless internet service. The carrier decided on Starlink in July; it will be the first airline in the U.S. to use a new system managed directly by Starlink, officials said at the time.

“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” Bobby Schroeter, chief marketing officer at Frontier, said in a news release. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power, and fast, reliable Starlink Wi-Fi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us.”

#6231. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6230. American Airlines Bringing Back First Class “Mini-Meals” On Shorter Flights

American Airlines reportedly plans to bring back “light bites” in first class on flights of 700–899 miles, beginning between New York and Chicago. I love this concept. A shorter flight does not require an elaborate meal, but something fresh would be a welcome improvement over another trip through the snack basket.

JonNYC reports that American will restore its light-bites concept on shorter domestic first class flights, starting with New York–Chicago service (0r flights from New York and Chicago).

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

We do not yet have a firm launch date, menus, or a detailed rollout schedule.  American’s published dining page still lists a snack basket on flights of 500–899 miles during meal times, with meal service on longer flights. The proposed change would give passengers at the upper end of that snack-basket range something more substantial.

A full meal is not necessary on every flight, but there is a lot of room between a hot entrée with multiple accompaniments and a bag of pretzels. A ramekin of warmed mixed nuts followed by a small fresh plate would be a very fitting compromise.

Think small dishes like a bowl of fruit in the morning or hummus with vegetables in the afternoon. The point is that a modest offering can still feel thoughtful and satisfy a bit of hunger…it also adds a premium touch that would nicely distinguish American from Delta and United (Alaska Airlines, to its credit, already serves meals on shorter flights).

A recent example: I flew from Boston to Chicago on AA, a flight of 867 miles and blocked at over 2.5 hours. No real food in first class, just a snack basket. A light meal would have been very appreciated and I was hungry.

There is something frustrating about boarding a first class flight around meal times and discovering that the route falls just short of the meal threshold…so-called “exception markets” used to exist, but have been cut on AA (oddly, except for Chicago – Denver).

My hope is that American focuses on quality, though I already give AA credit for better food than on Delta and United.

I am certainly quick to criticize American when the experience falls short, but I have also enjoyed some very good meals onboard. That is worth applauding, as is this change. A larger seat remains the primary reason many people buy domestic first class. Still, when airlines ask passengers to pay a premium, the experience should reflect some care beyond the dimensions of the seat, especially when AA will be charging a lot more than Frontier.

American Airlines reportedly plans to restore light bites in first class on flights of 700–899 miles, beginning on New York / Chicago routes. The timing and actual food remain to be seen, but I am enthusiastic about the direction. This is a sensible and competitive improvement, and I hope American gets it right and expands it.

#6229. The Beachy Bungalow in La Jolla That Let Me Cosplay as a California Surfer

As a travel editor, people are always shocked when I tell them I’ve only been to California once. Especially when I tell them that my one trip was to Napa—a blur of rolling hills and full-bodied Cabernets. There are so many sunny cities I’ve dreamed of visiting in the Golden State, but the world is big, and the flights from NYC are long. This fall, I finally got the push I needed to see more of America's most populous state: One of my dearest friends decided to get married in San Diego. My husband and I booked our plane tickets without blinking an eye, eager to see two fabulous people tie the knot and experience some excellent beaches, sunsets, and burritos along the way.

While deciding where to hunker down during our visit, I couldn’t get La Jolla out of my mind. A vibey little surf town about 14 miles north of downtown San Diego, it seemed like the perfect base—just a short drive from the wedding venue in Rancho Santa Fe, and boasting plenty of iconic restaurants (the Marine Room!) and attractions (the sea lions!). When I found Hamilton I, an adorable bungalow just three blocks from the beach, available for rent through Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy, it sealed the deal. I nabbed it for three nights.

Check Availability at Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy

Tucked into a long, quiet side street off of one of La Jolla’s main roads, I knew Hamilton I would do us just fine from the moment our Uber dropped us off. We had spent the first two days of our trip in downtown San Diego, getting our fill of the city; the energy in this neighborhood was just different. Imagine the shaka sign, but as a feeling. We walked past Hamilton II, the bungalow’s sister property, before reaching our home's front door, where a keypad granted us entrance. The first thing I noticed upon stepping inside was the sun-dappled living room, with its massive TV and walls bursting with beachy-cool art. The next was the basket of snacks in the kitchen left by the hosts—a huge green flag in my book.

Happy to have some space to spread out, my husband and I dropped our suitcases and toured the rest of the home, which has three small bedrooms (two kings, one queen), two bathrooms, a washer and dryer (huge news for us city folk), and a dining nook with a long oval table and eight rattan chairs. We chose to sleep in the largest of the three bedrooms, the only one with an en suite bathroom, and used the other two bedrooms as our closets. As I mentioned, the bedrooms aren’t huge and share walls at the back of the bungalow, so the property is probably best suited to close groups of friends or families with kids.

The biggest draw of the home is the backyard, accessible via a sliding door in the living room. You come to California for the sunshine, and the compact but well-designed outdoor space allows guests plenty of opportunities to soak up every last ray. Depending on the time of day, you can bounce between a smattering of adjustable lounge chairs, a small dipping pool, an outdoor dining table next to a barbecue, and a lounge area with a firepit. Despite backing onto a busy street, the backyard feels like a little oasis, thanks in part to the walls of greenery bordering the space.

Over the course of our three days at Hamilton I, my husband and I hit most of La Jolla’s most popular attractions, either by foot or via a quick Uber ride. We managed to dip our toes in the salty sea, kayak over to La Jolla Cove, wander through nearby Coronado, peruse the shops in La Jolla Village, eat a shocking amount of Mexican food, attend a magazine-worthy wedding, and so much more in so little time, returning to the bungalow to sleep peacefully each night. Every amenity we could have needed had already been thought of by the host, from extra blankets and fans to strong Wi-Fi and water pressure. We also had 24/7 access to a dedicated hospitality manager, who sent a couple of check-in texts throughout our stay to make sure everything was hunky-dory (it was).

Every morning, we’d make coffee in the kitchen or pick it up from a nearby café, passing longboarders and surfboard-toters along the way, then sit out in the backyard to wake ourselves up with the ultimate duo: caffeine and vitamin D. Having an entire home to call our own was such a treat, and cosplaying as a laid-back surfer couple, if only for a few days, was a welcome salve for our New York City–dwelling souls. I mean, who can be mad when you have the beach a few blocks away and laundry in-unit?

By the end of our stay, it was clear to us why our friends decided to get married in San Diego, and why it has become an increasingly popular travel destination as of late: Good vibes go a long way, and this part of California has them in spades. Also, the burritos are as good as people say. I’ll be back for more adventures in the Golden State—and I’ll be looking for a home away from home just like Hamilton I when that time comes.

#6227. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6226. United Airlines Finally Plans Boeing 757-300 Makeover With Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins

United Airlines plans to give its Boeing 757-300 fleet a long-overdue cabin update, adding larger overhead bins, entertainment screens at every seat, and power throughout the cabin. These aircraft have needed attention for years and were always included in the United Next refresh plan, though I am somewhat surprised to see United keep these workhorses in the fleet.

United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United’s “United Next” strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat Power Supply System (ISPS), new class dividers and cabin headers, and new UAL branding elements. Additionally, all seats and monuments will be refreshed throughout the cabin.

United:“United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United's "United Next" strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat…

As I mentioned above, the surprise is not that United is refreshing its entire narrwobody fleet, which it has promised for years now, but that it is actually moving forward with the 757-300s rather than phasing them out. However, I also understand that an A321neo or 737 MAX is not necessarily a direct replacement for this workhorse.

My understanding is that one reason this project took longer to get moving was the lack of a certified larger-bin option for this particular aircraft. United had to work through that certification hurdle rather than simply order an existing installation, which puts the delay in context.

United listed just 21 Boeing 757-300s in its year-end 2025 fleet disclosure, each with 234 seats. Undertaking a specialized modification for a fleet that small is a more substantial commitment than fitting the same equipment across hundreds of aircraft. For passengers, however, the size of the subfleet is beside the point. If your flight is operated by a 757-300, the overhead storage and cabin condition are part of your United experience.

More useful bin space should make boarding less stressful: currently there are far too many bags that must be gate checked because the smaller overhead bins force larger (but standard) carry-on bags to be placed on their sides.

I will also be happy to see entertainment screens included throughout the aircraft. When traveling with my children, individual screens are especially useful.

JonNYC also mentions power and it will be great to have USB-C, but the aircraft already have universal A/C power outlets in every cabin.

But what JonNYC does not mention and I consider most important is that these aircraft will get Starlink. Currently, most 757-300s still have an ancient Panasonic Wi-Fi system that often does not work. I specifically avoid the 757-300 for this reason and have been burned almost every time I have flown it with non-operable Wi-Fi. Some 757-300s have been upgraded with Viasat, but I am unwilling to fly on the 753s unless absolutely necessary. The new cabins will be welcomed, but Starlink is the most important upgrade.

I do not object to an aircraft simply because it is older: Delta has shown that a 30-year-old aircraft with mood lighting, fast Wi-Fi, and seatback screens can feel just as comfortable as a more modern aircraft. Refreshed seating and better amenities can change that experience substantially, even when the aircraft itself has been flying for decades.

This investment suggests United sees a continuing role for the 757-300 for many years in the future.

The Boeing 757-300 is finally in line for the kind of cabin attention it has long needed. Larger bins, seatback entertainment, and Starlink Wi-Fi will make a noticeable difference. I figured these aircraft would just be retired, but it appears they will fly the “Friendly Skies” for many years to come.

#6225. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.
