#6224. United Airlines CEO Talks Starlink In Veterans Day Message

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Veterans Day message to thank the 8,500 veterans who work at the airline. But before turning to their service, he spent a substantial part of the message discussing Starlink, winning customers from competitors, and his belief that United is the best airline in the world. The opening offers another glimpse into what Kirby sees as the opportunity ahead in 2027.

I typically share Kirby’s internal Veterans Day message each year (he also posted publicly on LinkedIN). His appreciation for military service and his affection for the United States are familiar themes. This year, though, he began with a thank-you for the summer operation and a look ahead at how better Wi-Fi might persuade passengers to switch airlines.

Happy Veterans Day everyone. Before I start on my Veterans Day message, I want to thank everyone for a really incredible summer. All the hard work you do. There was a lot of weather this summer, but the United team just did a great job so thank you. I also want to tell you how excited I am for 2027. In 2027 we’re going have a unique advantage in Starlink. And what that means is we’re gonna have a lot of customers who are loyal to other airlines today try us because of Starlink and I can already can hear this from customers. What’s going to happen is I hope they’re going to realize that United really is the best airline in the world when they come try United. We’re gonna be able to get those customers to come to United because of Starlink but to stay with United because everything else United is better. So thank you in advance for what you’re gonna do to win new brand loyal customers in 2027 for us at United.

But what I really wanted to do today is thank the 8,500 veterans that work here at United Airlines. I think all of you know that I am deeply patriotic. I love this country. I feel fortunate to have been born in this country and think it’s the greatest country in the history of the planet, but that wouldn’t be the case if it wasn’t for all the veterans who work at United but all the other veterans and the people that serve today. So to all the veterans not just at United, but around the world who have served to put their lives on the line to keep this country free and great, thank you for your service. Thank you for everything that you’ve done. And today when you’re out working and you see a veteran, and I’m sure you will because there’s so many United, give them a special thank you for their service. So to everyone at United, thank you for everything that you’ve done. And the veterans, a special thank you on Veteran’s Day and I look forward to seeing you in the friendly skies.

The commercial opening is an unusual preface to a Veterans Day tribute, though Kirby explicitly separates it from the message that follows. That makes sense considering he is addressing all employees and using the opportunity to discuss more than one subject. Still, his emphasis is revealing.

Kirby sees Starlink as a reason for passengers loyal to other airlines to give United a try, which is likely true. The more ambitious part is his expectation that the rest of the experience will persuade them to stay.

Reliable, fast internet can absolutely influence my booking decision. If I need to work during a flight, connectivity is more important than modest differences in the seat or meal and I’m hardly alone.

The second proposition is true, though certainly easier said than done. A passenger attracted by Starlink still has to navigate the airport, interact with the crew, and arrive at the destination. A great internet connection may get someone to book once. How United handles that journey, especially when something goes wrong, will help determine whether the passenger returns.

I remain unconvinced that there is one universally “best” airline. But Kirby is giving his employees a clear assignment: use the opportunity created by Starlink to earn repeat business. That is indeed a useful objective and to Untied’s credit, it improving operational performance and overall onboard product are giving front-line staff the means to deliver.

Turning to Veterans Day, Kirby’s message is direct. He credits those who have served with protecting the country he loves and asks employees to thank the veterans they encounter at work. I appreciate that practical request and will do the same today in my own interactions (I’m not flying, though).

Gratitude does not require agreement with every military deployment or government decision. We can (and should) scrutinize those decisions while appreciating the people asked to carry them out and the sacrifices their service entails.

Kirby’s Veterans Day message combines a familiar expression of patriotism with an enthusiastic commercial outlook for 2027. His expectation that Starlink will bring new passengers through the door does indeed create a golden opportunity for United. Whether United earns their loyalty will depend on what happens beyond the Wi-Fi connection.

But today’s central message deserves its own acknowledgment. To the veterans at United Airlines and elsewhere, thank you for your service.

#6223. When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds

You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind. On a first visit, you want time to take in the massive scale of the Inca city on its forested ridge above the Urubamba River, and then to walk among its stone walls. That picture, of course, depends on the weather. Here, where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, a single bank of cloud can hide Waynapicchu, the peak behind the ruins, and with it the panorama you came to see.

The drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours. The weeks just after the rains offer greener slopes—and often thinner crowds—to anyone prepared to pack for showers. The best time to visit Machu Picchu comes down to matching the conditions to the type of visit you want, as well as confirming that your route is available before you commit to booking trains and rooms. Below are the questions that first-time visitors ask most, with advice from travel advisors and experts.

For a first visit, May and September—before and after the June-to-August rush, respectively—will have generally favorable walking weather, before the rains creep back in October. The two months aren’t interchangeable, especially if you hope to walk to the Sun Gate or the Inca Bridge. The 2026 route calendar opened those seasonal paths in September but not in May, so check the 2027 dates as soon as they’re published.

April brings greener slopes to anyone who can live with a little more water. “It’s also shoulder season so there aren’t many tourists yet,” says Alice Farkas, who leads marketing and communications at Aracari, a company based in Lima that plans private trips across South America. Kiernan Cochran, product manager at Andean, which plans trips throughout Peru, also favors April into early May. Even so, Cochran’s team books those weeks for travelers with much the same lead time as high season, since popular routes fill early.

When it comes to visiting Machu Picchu, daily timing might matter even more than which time of year you visit.

November through March offers significant savings on airfare and accommodations, though strategic planning remains essential. Permits for popular routes like Huayna Picchu still require three-month advance booking during these months (compared to six months of required lead time during peak season).

Mosquera makes a case for embracing the rainy season: "It's actually my favorite time. The site becomes magical with fewer crowds given that overtourism is one of Machu Picchu's greatest threats. The rain isn't nearly as disruptive as people imagine, as it mainly falls in the evenings, not all day. February is particularly special because the Inca Trail closes for maintenance, making the site even quieter." (Note: If you plan to arrive by trek, options will be more limited during these moments.)

The wet season transforms the landscape dramatically. Stone terraces flush vibrant green, hidden waterfalls emerge, and morning mist creates atmospheric reveals of the citadel. The timing also aligns perfectly with Peru's coastal summer. "More travelers are discovering this split-season strategy," says Mosquera. "You can explore misty ruins early in the trip, then travel down to Lima's world-class restaurants or Máncora's beaches where summer's in full swing." Temperatures at Machu Picchu remain moderate year-round, with rain typically following predictable afternoon patterns rather than all-day downpours.

The dry months from June through August draw the main crush of tourists, when the most desirable entry hours can sell out along with hotels and trains. Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun, culminates in Cusco on June 24, and Peru’s Independence Day on July 28 brings another surge. In 2026, the daily cap was 4,500 visitors on ordinary dates and 5,600 on specified days, including June 19 through November 2, though that calendar doesn’t automatically carry over to 2027. Those places are also divided by route and hour, so your preferred route and entry time may be full even when the site has space overall.

Once each year’s tickets are released, Andean suggests booking sought-after routes about six months ahead in high season and at least three months ahead in low season.

Allow four or five nights in the region, as Cochran recommends, and begin in the Sacred Valley if your itinerary allows. Its Inca towns and terraces also mean the citadel isn’t your first encounter with the culture that built it. Cusco, where flights land for now, sits at roughly 11,150 feet. Heading straight down to the valley gives you a gentler start, and you can return to explore the city afterward. Cusco’s long-delayed replacement airport, Chinchero International, is under construction on the plateau above the Sacred Valley at about 12,340 feet, higher than the city itself. Its opening is targeted for late 2027, so most 2027 trips will still begin at the old one.

Ollantaytambo, at about 9,160 feet, is halfway between Cusco and Machu Picchu, and where travelers board the train to the latter. The town of ‘Ollanta’ has Inca-era streets and archaeological sites to explore, and is well worth a stop either going to or coming from Machu Picchu (the lovely El Albergue hotel sits just beside the train station).

From there, travelers catch the train to Aguas Calientes, also known as Machu Picchu Pueblo, which is the small town at the base of the ancient citadel. Spend the night prior to your Machu Picchu visit in Aguas Calientes for an early start up the mountain. Some allow just one day at Machu Picchu; others who want to appreciate the landmark from a few perspectives should budget two. You may, for instance, want to experience an upper terrace or a mountain climb alongside Classic Circuit 2, which is the standard walk through the Inca city (more on these routes below). If so, book that second route for another day. Either way, you can usually spend a full day at Machu Picchu and still catch a late afternoon/early evening train out, or bed down for another night in Aguas Calientes and depart the next morning.

Before buying anything sold simply as “Machu Picchu admission,” take a look at the official route maps, since the three circuits divide the site by elevation and access. For a single visit, Andean favors Classic Circuit 2. Its routes 2-A and 2-B each pair a viewpoint with a walk among the Inca buildings of the urban sector. Route 2-B takes its view from the lower terrace, a distinction worth knowing if you have a particular camera angle in mind.

For the upper-terrace panorama, choose Circuit 1’s route 1-B, which keeps you above the main streets, while route 1-A adds the climb up Machu Picchu Mountain which offers the classic view down onto the site. The Sun Gate and Inca Bridge carry seasonal tickets of their own. Circuit 3 covers the lower royal sector, including the Temple of the Sun. Its route 3-A adds the steep ascent of Waynapicchu (often spelled Huayna Picchu), which is the distinctive peak in the background of most Machu Picchu photos, and 3-B stays below. If Circuit 2 sells out, Andean suggests booking Circuits 1 and 3 separately to combine the panorama with a closer look at the ruins. Choose wisely before you arrive, since a ticket cannot be switched to another route at the gate.

Hikers face their own paperwork. Permits for the classic Inca Trail are limited and booked through authorized operators, and the shorter one-day trail from kilometer 104 of the rail line needs a permit and an operator, too. That day hike is Cochran’s own favorite—the final leg of the historic Inca route to the Sun Gate, without the multiday inn-to-inn or camping journey required. Ask what your hike covers before buying a separate admission.

Under the September 2026 rules, trail arrivals enter on a designated Circuit 3-B ticket, which matters if you also want Circuit 2 or the upper panorama. Heavy rain can also shut the kilometer 104 path outside the usual February maintenance period, which is something to keep in mind for any rainy season travel.

Your train booking does not include admission (treks are on a case-by-case basis; ask!), so buy entry through the Ministry of Culture’s Tu Boleto portal, where you choose your route first and your entry hour second. Enter each visitor’s details carefully, matching names and information to the same identification document they’ll present at the gate. The ticket fixes the holder’s name, date, time, and route; current rules allow no changes to the name or date after purchase.

The purchase process changed in September 2026, when the ministry began a 30-day trial of direct paid checkout in place of the earlier unpaid hold. Under the portal’s current purchase manual, you have 15 minutes from the start of an order to enter everyone’s details and pay. Have documents and payment ready, and follow the instructions on screen. Rail and admission are also released on separate timelines. PeruRail opened 2027 train sales on September 22, but Yuriko Aquino of PROMPERÚ, Peru’s tourism promotion agency, says the Ministry of Culture has yet to announce when 2027 admission will go on sale or what the daily visitor cap will be. If you buy rail first, read the fare’s change terms before you pay.

Within the overall cap, up to 1,000 tickets a day are held for in-person sale in Machu Picchu Pueblo, valid for entry the following day. If you’re counting on that uncertain fallback, budget a night in town. Whichever way you buy, a guide is recommended for a standard citadel visit, while Inca Trail hikers follow their operator’s separate requirements. Guides can be booked through your hotel or at the entrance to the site.

From Cusco, most travelers cross the Sacred Valley by road to Ollantaytambo and board the train there for the ride along the Urubamba to Machu Picchu Pueblo. From town, a separate shuttle bus climbs to the entrance in roughly half an hour. Check boarding points and total travel time before choosing a fare, since PeruRail’s January-to-April departures from Cusco involve a bus-and-train transfer.

For a first visit, Cochran favors a morning train from the Sacred Valley and an afternoon Circuit 2 entry, when her team generally finds the site less crowded; three or four hours is usually enough to take it in. Among the premium trains, she points to Belmond’s Hiram Bingham, PeruRail’s Vistadome Observatory, and IncaRail’s First Class.

Whichever train you choose, leave a cushion between arrival and admission. Peru’s tourism authority advises reaching the shuttle station about an hour before your gate slot, or setting out about two hours ahead if you plan to walk uphill. A train that pulls in just before your entry time leaves little margin for the bus queue and the gate check.

Down in Machu Picchu Pueblo are two fantastic Peruvian-owned options—Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel, with scattered adobe casitas among orchids, and Sumaq Machu Picchu Hotel, which faces the Urubamba River. Both are close to the shuttle stop. Sanctuary Lodge, a Belmond Hotel, is the only property up on the mountain at the gates of Machu Picchu, which spares you the morning shuttle ascent, though hotel guests still enter on the same timed admission as everyone else.

#6222. JSX Adds Two Nonstop Routes From New City

JSX announced Tuesday that it will begin flying to New England for the first time in February 2027.

The carrier will operate from Jet Aviation’s terminal at Hanscom Field in Bedford, Massachusetts, northwest of Boston. Flights to Teterboro Airport in New Jersey will begin Feb. 8, with four flights on weekdays, two on Saturdays, and three on Sundays.

JSX markets the route as New York City service and requires passengers to sign up for its free Club JSX membership to book.

Service to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport will follow on Feb. 11, with one flight each day on Mondays and Thursdays through Sundays. JSX will use 30-seat aircraft on both routes.

“We’re excited JSX has chosen Hanscom to operate these flights to the New York and Florida markets,” Hanscom Field Director Chris Willenborg said in a statement.

JSX outlined its plans for Hanscom Field at an advisory commission meeting in September. At the time, the carrier was targeting a January launch and had also proposed flights to Naples, Florida. Naples was absent from Tuesday’s announcement.

There are just weeks left in 2026, and if you haven't quite reached the United MileagePlus elite status level you're hoping to secure for 2027, the clock is ticking.

From earning bonus Premier qualifying points with the right credit card to taking a last-minute flight, here are five ways to close the status gap before Dec. 31.

United's elite status qualification year runs from Jan. 1 through Dec. 31. Status earned in 2026 is valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

To qualify, you must fly at least four flights operated by United or United Express and meet one of two thresholds: a combination of Premier Qualifying Flights and PQPs or a higher PQP-only requirement.

You can check your progress in United's Premier Status Tracker, including how your upcoming flights will count toward qualification.

Some United credit cards offer bonus PQPs toward status as part of their welcome offers, in addition to redeemable United miles.

For example, the (see rates and fees) is currently offering 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 redeemable United bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, an additional 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

The card has a $350 introductory annual fee.

It's still possible to get bonus PQPs in 2026 as part of a new cardmember bonus on select United credit cards, but you should act quickly.

The good news is you can earn PQPs through everyday spending on United credit cards. The bad news is that most United cards earn them at a relatively slow rate of 1 PQP for every $20 spent.

That means $1,000 in purchases on most United cards would earn you just 50 PQPs.

However, the (see rates and fees) earns PQPs faster than the other personal United cards, at a rate of 1 PQP for every $15 spent. So, that same $1,000 in purchases would earn you about 66 PQPs with that card.

Every little bit helps, especially if you're close to your next status level.

Related: Why I charged $50,000 on my United card to earn status

If you already have United flights booked before the end of 2026, you may be able to earn additional PQPs by upgrading your seats.

Purchasing Economy Plus seats, United's preferred seating or paid upgrades to first class can earn 1 PQP per dollar spent (excluding taxes and fees).

You can also earn 1 PQP for every 100 MileagePlus miles redeemed for eligible seat upgrades on United and United Express flights.

Just remember that PQPs from upgrades purchased separately from your original ticket may post separately after you fly, so keep an eye on your account.

Related: What it's like in United's new Elevated Polaris business class

One of the most obvious ways to close the gap toward United elite status is to book another flight (or two) before the end of the year as part of a modern-day mileage run. Unlike in the old days, how far you fly doesn't matter if you're on United for status. It only matters how much you spend.

Ideally, you're going somewhere fun to see a friend, see some attractions or have a great meal. But if you turn around and don't leave the airport before your next flight, you won't be the first — or last — status-seeker to do so. I've certainly done it when I needed a few more segments at the very end of the year.

If you're chasing PQFs, remember that you generally earn one for each eligible flight segment on United, United Express or partner airlines.

For United-operated flights, you'll generally earn 1 PQP per dollar spent on eligible base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges, excluding government taxes and fees. You can see the estimated PQPs and PQFs a flight will earn when selecting a fare during booking.

If you need a lot of United PQPs and want to take this to the next level, it is possible to earn PQPs at a faster rate with some United partners. You can learn all about that strategy here.

Finally, if you have an upcoming United flight, you may be able to purchase additional PQPs through United's Premier Accelerator program.

To check, open an existing reservation and look for the Award Accelerator option, which lets you purchase additional redeemable miles.

Depending on your reservation, you may also see a Premier Accelerator option that lets you purchase PQPs along with redeemable miles, as shown below.

This isn't usually a cheap way to earn status, but it can be useful if you're just short of your goal and don't want to take another flight.

United is making some big changes to elite status qualification beginning in 2027, including eliminating the PQF-plus-PQP qualification pathway and raising the PQP-only requirement for Premier 1K.

That means earning status could get harder for some United travelers next year.

If you expect to rely heavily on United credit card spending to earn PQPs toward status, as I do, there's another reason to consider getting a United card before the end of 2026.

If you have an eligible United card by Dec. 31, 2026, you'll get a 5% PQP boost in 2027. For example, if you earned Platinum status in 2026, you'll get a 900-PQP boost to start 2027.

And remember, the earns PQPs faster than United's other personal cards, so it might be the best choice if every PQP is going to count.

It also currently offers an increased welcome bonus of 90,000 miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, an additional 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

But no matter what United status level you are going for or how you plan to get there, just remember that all of your activities must be completed by Dec. 31, 2026, to count toward status this year.

#6219. I Gambled Our Business Class Flight Home On A 65-Minute Connection And Separate Tickets

In the interest of maximizing our time on the ground (it was a short trip after all) and avoiding an early morning and long drive to Zürich, I booked a separate ticket from Basel to Copenhagen on Norwegian with a rather tight 65-minute connection to catch our SAS flight to Chicago…

When I booked my tickets for this trip, there was no award space on SAS from Zurich to Copenhagen. I figured it would open (intra-Europe space reliably opens a day or two before travel) and it certainly did, but I wasn’t thrilled about getting up before dawn to drive to Zürich in order to make the flight.

The change fee on a SAS EuroBonus award ticket is about 75USD as well, which caused me to look for options out of Basel, which is 15 minutes away from my in-laws house instead of an hour. I knew easyJet operates service on this route, but I was pleased to see Norwegian Air is now operating and the fares were cheap…cheaper than the change fee on SAS.

It was 177EUR for all four tickets on Norwegian from BSL-CPH, which I found compelling, though it was not without risk. Connecting on separate tickets is always a risk and the connection here was only 1 hour, 5 minutes, which would include walking from the Schengen area to the non-Schengen area (where lines can be very long).

Nevertheless, we opted to take the risk, knowing that if the flight was delayed we would miss our connection and might be stuck in Copenhagen another day or forced to fly back to the U.S. in economy class.

There was another wrinkle. My kids and I are U.S. citizens, but my wife sill is not…she travels to the USA on a Green Card and I figured we would be unable to check her in because the Green Card would need to be verified. That turned out to be an issue…I could not compete her check-in, though I was able to for the kids and me.

Long story short: the gamble worked…but it was very close.

We took off early from Basel and the captain announced we would arrive 15 minutes early into Denmark.

But the weather was poor and we ended up circling and pulled up to the gate late…we know we had less than an hour to go to the transfer counter, collect my wife’s boarding pass, pass through passport control, and board our flight.

We landed at the furthest possible gate and had a long walk ahead of us.

My biggest concern was that even though I had initiated check-in on the SAS app, we might be too late to check-in for Heidi. Thankfully, although we did not reach the transfer desk until 40 minutes before departure, an agent was able to complete check-in and issue the boarding pass.

We saw immigration lines were very long for non-Schengen citizens, but short for us so we ducked into the SAS Lounge for Kanelbullar (Swedish cinnamon rolls) and then headed to the gate. I know, I really do push it.

We reached the gate 26 minutes before departure…the gamble worked. Barely.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

I love reading your posts, but you are NUTS doing this!

Hahaha nice gamble! If you have a backup plan and or flexibility for one more day in Copenhagen it’s worth the risk I reckon.

If you’d stayed in Copenhagen it would have been a treat for the kids and you wouldn’t have regretted it either so all good.

I’m surprised by how inadequate the immigration processing staff and gates are at CPH, even for EU citizens.

I’m confused by the line “We saw immigration lines were very long for non-Schengen citizens, but short for us …” You had indicated that you and the kids are US citizens which presumably meant you needed to use the non-Schengen lines. Were you allowed to use the Schengen lines?

They are dual citizens (but my wife is no a dual citizen).

#6218. These Music City Airbnbs Exude All of Nashville’s Southern Charm

In the two decades I’ve lived in Nashville, I’ve seen a lot of changes. When I first moved, my friends and family would ask why I lived here; now, they’re asking when they can come visit. And as the Music City grows, so does the number of gorgeous places to stay. Travelers can choose from vacation rentals in any neighborhood for any group size, whether that be large bachelorette parties looking to hang out near the honky-tonks, or solo music lovers who want to catch a show at the Grand Ole Opry. Houses with vast yards are good options for folks with kids, dogs, and songwriter friends who want to pull out the guitar, and some even boast private pools that let you keep the summer heat at bay. Nashville, of course, is known for its street of honky-tonks, and securing a modern condo downtown with a bird’s-eye view of all the action offers a one-of-a-kind experience that you won’t soon forget. No matter what type of stay you’re after, there’s an excellent Nashville vacation rental worth holing up in. Read on for some of my favorite vacation rentals in the city I call home.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, editor stays, ratings, amenities, location, decor, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Cozy fireplace, roomy layout, spacious yard, large dining table

Comfortable and quiet, this family-ready home in South Nashville will make you feel like a true local. With four bedrooms—three kings and a room with bunk beds for kids—all dressed in modern, neutral tones; two baths; and a dog-friendly policy, the whole family will enjoy a stay here. There’s even a dedicated workspace if you have to check in with the office while on the road. It’s an oasis slightly away from all the noise and activity that downtown brings, but just a short drive from any late-night action you desire.

Location: South NashvilleThings to do nearby: Geodis Park (the MLS stadium); the Nashville Fairgrounds; Adventure Science Center; Zanies’ comedy club; bars, restaurants, and shopping in Wedgewood-Houston

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Shou Sugi Ban traditional Japanese design, peaceful location, firepit

Just 16 miles away from downtown Nashville, this bed-and-breakfast tree house on 22 wooded acres can feel worlds away from Lower Broadway and the neon honky-tonk nightlife. But in half an hour, you could be back in the center of the action, should you want to be. It’s the perfect spot for those who like to balance their big-city trips with a bit of solitude and relaxation after a long day. At home, expect great views, a delicious breakfast, and the chance to truly disconnect—there’s no Wi-Fi or TV.

Location: Ashland CityThings to do nearby: Hiking trails on property, Beaman Park, Cumberland River kayaking

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Photogenic pink backdrop, free parking, wood-fired pizza oven, outdoor projector, guitar, local landlords

East Nashville’s self-named “Nashville Pinky” is bedecked in a paler pink than some other properties in the city, but it doesn’t scale back when it comes to making Music City fun. Spend the day at home watching movies on the outdoor projector and eating pizza from the wood-fired oven. There’s also a guitar if you want to pick your way through some songs, and vinyl records from the nearby record shop, The Groove. When you’re ready to head out, the neighborhood is full of bars, boutiques, and restaurants, and you’re a quick bus ride, bike ride, or Uber from Lower Broadway.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Five Points bars and restaurants, Shoppes on Fatherland, the Basement East music venue, Shelby Park

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private parking, stock tank tub, electric fireplace, cozy loft space

Finding a pet-friendly Airbnb isn't as easy as it seems, as many homes come with extensive rules regarding what Fido can and can't do, and high nightly fees in addition to the booking price. This two-bedroom guesthouse sits in a middle ground: There's a $75 fee per small or medium dog, who will have to hang out in a crate if you leave them home alone. There's a small backyard for your pup to explore (with a firepit for humans), and the neighborhood has wide sidewalks for safe, on-leash adventures. The tchotchke-filled home itself is best for families, since the primary bedroom lacks a true door, and the secondary bedroom has twin beds. Inside, there's also a kitchenette with an oven, mini-fridge, and coffee maker, and an indoor fireplace to curl up in front of.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Salt Ranch pool club, Cleveland Park shopping, bars and restaurants, Drkmttr music venue

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Relaxing atmosphere, private connected apartment for more space, big deck, private parking

The unofficial bachelorette capital of the world, Nashville is a hot spot for group trips—especially for women. And while the rowdier set may be found on Broadway driving past the honky-tonks in “party barges,” there's a more, well, sophisticated way to celebrate upcoming nuptials. To start, book this 1930s East Nashville cottage that's away from the crowds and has an explicit “no parties” rule. With two bedrooms in the main house plus a third in the connected apartment, and two queen-size sofa beds, there's plenty of room to spread out. Outside, the home has a backyard, two-level deck, grill, and firepit. Plus, you're only 10 minutes from downtown if you want to get in on the honky-tonk action.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Cumberland River kayaking; Shelby Park; Five Points restaurants, bars, and shopping; The Basement East music venue

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Chocolate-themed decor, location in a multi-use complex with a coffee shop and a chocolatier, blackout shades

You’ll definitely have sweet dreams when you stay in this chocolatier-owned apartment next door to her high-end chocolate shop. The rooms at Cocoa Casa are bright, colorful, and decorated with chocolate-themed decor, without being over-the-top or hokey. You can head next door to sample the goods from Poppy and Peep Chocolate (or take them home as souvenirs). The South Nashville location is within walking distance of coffee shops and more, but offers a little less hustle-and-bustle than the downtown scene.

Location: South NashvilleThings to do nearby: International food along Nolensville Pike; Wedgewood-Houston’s restaurants, bars, and luxury shops; Geodis Park (the MLS stadium); the Nashville Fairgrounds

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound porch, seasonal in-ground pool, piano, view of Shelby Park, bunk beds

This beautifully designed East Nashville farmhouse may come with a large price tag for a two-bedroom, two-bath home, but its location and heated pool (open April to October) are well worth it. Facing Shelby Park—and close to the greenway, which is packed with walking and jogging trails—the home is just 10 minutes from downtown Nashville. There's a wraparound porch to enjoy your morning coffee, plus hammocks and bikes to take in the fresh air. Inside, the bright white design gives the home a fresh, clean look. (If you have a big group, there are a few air mattresses available, and the hosts allow up to eight guests.)

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Kayaking; golfing; Shelby Park; Shelby Bottoms Nature Center; Five Points bars, restaurants, and shopping

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Location on a working organic farm, views of Tennessee hills, gourmet kitchen, farm animals

If you're a Nashville regular, it may be time to look outside of the city for your next vacation. About 30 minutes south of Nashville International Airport, this rental on Bloomsbury Farm is just far enough away to feel like a retreat, but not too far that you can't head into the city every day. It's also perfectly located for a visit to Franklin (a 20-minute drive), one of my favorite day trips from the city, and Arrington Vineyards for wine tasting. Set on over 400 acres of working farmland, the loft is kitted out with a full kitchen, living area, bathroom with a walk-in shower, and king-size bedroom, all overlooking the Tennessee hills. Bonus: The farm has turkeys, horses, and chickens—so if you're lucky, your host will pass on a few fresh eggs for your morning breakfast.

Location: SmyrnaThings to do nearby: Bloomsbury Farm tour, wooded paths, Smyrna Depot District, boat rentals at Fate Sanders Marina

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows; private balcony; access to laundry, pool, and gym in building; central location

A sleek, modern pied-à-terre, this apartment offers floor-to-ceiling windows with city views, complemented by leather and metal furnishings and a few scene-stealing art pieces, like the LED angel wings. It all adds up to a great photo op for the whole crew on a memorable Nashville vacation. Make use of the year-round heated pool and fitness center, and then walk a few blocks to Lower Broadway for the honky-tonk action. The home can sleep up to six across a king bedroom, queen bedroom, and pull-out sofa bed in the living room.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, Lower Broadway honky-tonks, Bridgestone Arena, Nashville Symphony Schermerhorn Symphony Center

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, laundry room, welcoming decor, large backyard, budget-friendly prices

The real perks of this serene East Nashville cottage are outside: The backyard offers space for kids to wear themselves out running around while you sit on the back patio, taking a breather. Inside, the two-bedroom home has a washer/dryer, room-darkening shades, and a bathtub. It's only about a 10-minute drive to downtown Nashville and 15 minutes from the Grand Ole Opry. And best of all, you can score it for under $200 a night.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: TopGolf; Salt Ranch pool club; Cleveland Park shopping, bars, and restaurants; Drkmttr music venue; Nissan Stadium

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Access to laundry, early luggage drop-off, elevator access, high ceilings

This industrial loft is among a variety of rentals in one of downtown Nashville's century-old buildings—and is run by local company Anchor Rentals, which also manages The Russell, a boutique hotel in a renovated East Nashville church. What that means for business travelers headed here is that they won't have to worry about the hosts canceling or not being in the area. This particular apartment, with its high ceilings, multiple workspaces, and well-equipped kitchen (which includes a microwave, coffee machine, and toaster oven for quick breakfasts), is a great spot for weekday visitors.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Ryman Auditorium, Lower Broadway, Frist Art Museum, Dolly Museum Nashville

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pack-and-play, toys for kids, minimalist design, groovy bar cart, French press coffee

Perfectly located 15 minutes away from both Vanderbilt and Belmont University on foot, this apartment in Music Row is an easy home base for parents visiting collegians or touring with high schoolers. With two bedrooms and one bathroom, it has enough space to comfortably fit four people. (If you're traveling with toddlers or infants, the home also offers a pack-and-play and children's books and toys.) There's also a full kitchen complete with a gorgeous Smeg fridge.

Location: Music RowThings to do nearby: Studio B; Vanderbilt University; Belmont University; restaurants, bars and shops in Hillsboro Village and Edgehill Village; Belcourt Theatre

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Nashville?

East Nashville and Wedgewood-Houston are two busy and buzzy neighborhoods with great dining scenes, music venues, and fun shopping. They’re also a quick Uber or bike ride to downtown, making it easy to experience it all. If you’re looking for something a bit quieter, check out the leafy Sylvan Park neighborhood. For something fit for families, head to Donelson, with easy access to parks and the Opryland attractions.

When is the best season to visit Nashville?

There’s no bad time to visit Nashville, but spring and fall offer more temperate weather, when it is easier to hike, bike, and paddle, or just stroll down Broadway without the steaminess of a southern summer collecting under your hat. Most people want to be in Music City during the warmer months to take advantage of outdoor concerts and street festivals, but if you come in winter, you’ll get to cheer on the NHL’s Nashville Predators and see the holiday magic of the five million lights at Gaylord Opryland.

In my opinion, a trip to Nashville should be about five days long, which offers you enough time to expand your vacation beyond Broadway and the honky-tonks. You’ll have enough time for a day or two in town—you can boot-scoot under the neon lights of Lower Broadway—and still have a few days for exploring the surrounding parks, greenways, museums, shops, and music venues away from the crowds.

#6217. Singapore Airlines Unveils the ‘Largest Double Bed in the Sky’ As Part of a $1.6 Billion Redesign

Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying first class. But Singapore Airlines—consistently voted as one of the best airlines in the world by CNT readers—is taking things to a whole new level, unveiling what it claims will be “the largest double bed in commercial aviation” as part of a major revamp of its long-haul cabins.

The airline announced the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines's new first class cabin

And the luxury doesn't stop there. The new suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces, and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows, and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies.

The new business class seats also come with adjoining seats, offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion.

But what about those of us traveling farther back? Premium economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage, and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The new economy class will feature more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines's new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive first class cabins for the first time.

There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the new double beds, but one thing is certain: cuddling up at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

#6216. A350-1000ULR Sets New Distance Record

Airbus’ A350-1000ULR has been officially recognized for breaking the Guinness World Record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial aircraft.

The record-breaking flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France, took place in July and was widely reported on, but was only recently confirmed by Guinness using data validated by the International Aeronautical Federation and flightradar24.

The nonstop journey covered 12,503 nautical miles and lasted 24 hours and 24 minutes. The -1000ULR flew over Sydney and the Pacific on a north-easterly routing toward Los Angeles, crossed North America and the Atlantic, and passed over London on its way to Toulouse. According to Airbus, the 13 people on board witnessed two sunsets and two sunrises.

The crew included three Airbus flight test pilots, two pilots from Qantas, and five Airbus flight test engineers. Also on board were two Airbus design engineers and a representative from the IAF.

Airbus is developing the -1000ULR for Qantas’ Project Sunrise, a yearslong effort to connect the east coast of Australia with far-flung destinations such as New York and London. The manufacturer expects to deliver the first of the type in April 2027. Qantas is aiming to operate the first Project Sunrise flight, from Sydney to London, later that year.

The Australian flag carrier has ordered 12 -1000ULRs.

“In responding to the challenge laid down by Qantas, our teams came together to extend the range of the A350-1000 in an efficient and economically viable way to undertake the world’s longest ever commercial flights,” Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus, said in a news release. “Flying 12,503 nautical miles non-stop, we have fully proven the aircraft’s capability to fulfill its mission. And the world record was the icing on the cake.”

#6214. Brit Jailed In Singapore After Hidden Camera Found In Airplane Lavatory

A man is facing quite some legal challenges after installing a hidden camera in an airplane lavatory, and then trying to control it remotely. Of course this is not only incredibly creepy and illegal, but if you’re going to do something like this, it probably shouldn’t be on a Singapore-bound flight, given the country’s strict laws.

The Straits Times has the story of how a 52-year-old British man has been jailed in Singapore, following an incident that happened on an October 7 flight from Osaka Kansai (KIX) to Singapore Changi (SIN). The man was traveling on a Boeing 787 belonging to Scoot, Singapore Airlines’ low cost subsidiary.

A short time after takeoff, the man reportedly installed a camera in the airplane lavatory, which had the function to be controlled remotely through an app on his phone. A short while later, a flight attendant, who was using the lavatory, found the hidden camera. She removed the device, and of course alerted the crew.

The passenger reportedly tried to remove the camera from the lavatory later, only to find that it was no longer there. The crew managed to figure out who it belonged to (it’s not entirely clear how), though in the meantime, he had already deleted the app on his phone, and all related pictures, to avoid detection.

He was detained upon arrival in Singapore, and his camera and phone were seized. The man was jailed, and his trial will take place in the coming weeks.

He faces charges of voyeurism and obstructing the course of justice. For voyeurism, one can be jailed for up to two years, fined, caned, or a combination of these punishments. For obstructing the course of justice, one can be jailed for up to seven years, fined, or both.

I’m not here to kink shame. People can conceptually be into whatever they want, as far as I’m concerned. The issue is when they non-consensually involve others in whatever that fantasy may be, especially when it violates the law (obviously). A few thoughts come to mind:

While not exactly the same thing, keep in mind that phones sold in South Korea have to make a sound when pictures or videos are taken, even if a phone is set to silent. That’s intended to combat illicit and covert photography of people, against their will. So obviously being creepy in this way is something that’s way more common than it should be…

A British national is facing some serious punishment in Singapore, after he installed hidden cameras in a lavatory of a Scoot Boeing 787. A flight attendant noticed these while using the lavatory, and removed the camera. He later came back to try to retrieve it, and was caught.

The man is now facing charges of voyeurism and obstructing the course of justice, and could be looking at years in jail.

What do you make of this Scoot hidden camera incident?

#6213. Lufthansa Takes Delivery of Its First A350-1000

Lufthansa this week took delivery of its first Airbus A350-1000, a type it says will offer a better customer experience while reducing operating costs.

The aircraft was formally handed over to the carrier on Tuesday in the presence of Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr and Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus. Nicknamed “Deutschland,” the jet is Lufthansa’s 700th Airbus airplane, and the seventh in a special commemorative fleet bearing 100th anniversary liveries.

The white and dark blue designs feature an oversized crane, a symbol first used by predecessor Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa Group has ordered a total of 15 A350-1000s. The first 10 will operate for the Lufthansa core brand, and will be based at its Munich hub.

“Deutschland” will fly to Munich on Wednesday, officials said, and operate its inaugural flight, to Tokyo-Haneda, on Dec. 3. The aircraft will also be Lufthansa’s first long-haul airplane equipped with Starlink satellite internet service.

“The fact that, as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus aircraft exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa, and in the year of our 100th anniversary, makes this a very special moment for us,” Spohr said in a statement. “Our partnership is a prime example of what Europe can achieve when it works together.”

Lufthansa’s -1000s will seat 300 passengers in four cabins – First, Business, Premium Economy, and Economy.

#6212. 14 Best Steakhouses in New York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

No single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak.

Read our complete New York City guide here, which includes:

Seagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan

I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel important. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H.

The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a new friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate.

4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded.

And so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the New York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H.

This summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one.

Head 10 blocks south of New York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F.

Gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H.

The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the New-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren

1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan

From the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—big leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa.

Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell

355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn

Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel

513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan

Buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S.

Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's New York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H.

56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan

The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is currently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, said to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs

Dinner and a show in New York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6210. Highest To Lowest: How To Get From JFK To Manhattan For Just $3

In the film Highest 2 Lowest (2025), starring Denzel Washington, legendary filmmaker Spike Lee portrays two distinct sides of New York City, depending on your altitude and bank account. Nowhere is that contrast more apparent than in the choices travelers face when commuting between Manhattan and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Whether you are a visiting traveler or an NYC resident, navigating to and from the city’s primary international hub is a perpetual balancing act between cost, comfort, and time. Previously, I detailed what is literally and figuratively the “highest” mode of airport transit: Blade’s helicopter transfers (starting at $195 and easily topping $300, though rides can cost you nothing out of pocket using Bilt Cash). Each Bilt Cash award expires 12 months after you earn it, on the last day of that month.

In this Reader Story, I’m taking you down, subterranean, to the lowest option available: the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) $3 bus-to-subway hack.

Duke Ellington was onto something: “Take the ‘A’ Train.” However, he didn’t specify which A train branch, nor did he mention that a quick bus transfer might be involved!

Even some locals may ask: “Wait, isn’t the AirTrain $8.75, plus a $3 subway fare?” That’s true if you exit the AirTrain at Jamaica or Howard Beach. However, there is a lesser-known and dramatically cheaper workaround: just $3 total from JFK to nearly anywhere in NYC with the MTA, provided you don’t mind adding a few extra minutes to your journey.

For the reverse trip, take any Lefferts Blvd-bound A train, ensuring the destination sign explicitly says “Lefferts Blvd” rather than Far Rockaway or Rockaway Park. Importantly, Far Rockaway A trains often display “JFK Airport” on their digital side displays because most travelers use the more expensive $8.75 Howard Beach transfer route, so do not board those if you want the $3-only route. Once on the correct train, get off at Liberty Ave / Lefferts Blvd, exit to the street, locate the bus stop, catch a JFK-bound Q10 or Q80 bus to the Lefferts AirTrain station, and take the free AirTrain directly to your terminal.

If you type “JFK Airport” into Google Maps or Apple Maps, the app will almost never display the $3-only hack. Navigation algorithms prioritize minimizing the number of transit transfers over saving money, automatically suppressing the bus transfer in favor of the standard $8.75 AirTrain connection at Jamaica or Howard Beach.

Even typing “Lefferts Blvd AirTrain Station” into navigation apps often causes confusion because the AirTrain station and the Ozone Park A-train terminal are located roughly 1.5 miles apart.

To force your map app to show the correct route, search for the street-level bus-to-subway transfer point at “Lefferts Blvd & Liberty Ave.” From JFK, this will display the Q10 Rush or Q80 bus taking you to the A train turnstiles; from Manhattan, it will guide you on the Lefferts-bound A train directly to your bus connection.

Other than extreme weather events, strikes, and major crises, all three legs of this route—the AirTrain, the Q10/Q80 bus, and the A Train—operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, though timing varies. During daytime and peak hours (6:00 AM – 10:00 PM), AirTrain cars run every 7–10 minutes, Q10 and Q80 buses depart roughly every 8–15 minutes, and A trains run frequently as express services through Brooklyn and Manhattan.

However, late-night transit frequency changes significantly in NYC, so keep that in mind for overnight or early-morning flights: AirTrain headways drop to 15–20 minute intervals, late-night Q10/Q80 bus departures stretch to every 20–30 minutes, and the A train may shift to local-only service (check MTA Service Status for possible re-routings).

Thanks to the flat-fare structure of the New York City Subway (as opposed to distance-based transit networks found in cities like London, Tokyo, or Washington, D.C.), that single $3 fare (and free transfer) unlocks access to nearly the entire city once you pass through the turnstiles at the Ozone Park–Lefferts Boulevard station.

Because there are no exit turnstiles or zone caps inside the subway network, you can ride from Queens through Brooklyn, up Manhattan, and deep into the Bronx, all on that same initial $3 tap—as long as you stay within the fare-paid zone. And, if you exit the subway system in Lower Manhattan, you can walk over to Whitehall Terminal and board the free Staten Island Ferry to reach the fifth and final borough. While attempting to tap onto a Staten Island bus or the Staten Island Railway (SIR) on the other side would consume a second $3 fare (and likely break the 2-hour transfer clock), at least JFK to Manhattan for $3 remains one of the greatest transit bargains in the world.

All told—AirTrain, bus, and subway—you can get between JFK and Manhattan in about 75 to 90 minutes. Depending on brutal rush-hour highway traffic, you might even tie or beat a $100+ rideshare. That said, I would recommend this route exclusively for those traveling light (backpacks and carry-ons), willing to spend the extra time, and comfortable navigating city transit. But for the right traveler, it is a relatively safe, clean, reliable, and wildly affordable hack.

To put the $3 bus-to-subway hack into perspective, it helps to see how it stacks up against the other primary options for traveling between Manhattan and JFK:

Of course, there are other, less conventional ways of getting to and from JFK:

Whether taking a $300+ helicopter ride or a $3 bus-to-subway hack, commuting between JFK and Manhattan truly captures the two contrasting sides of New York City that Spike Lee brings to life in Highest 2 Lowest.

For light packers on a budget, the Lefferts Boulevard Q10 transfer stands as the undefeated champion of pure value. Duke Ellington was right all along—if you want to get to Sugar Hill or anywhere else in the city without breaking the bank, simply take the “A” train!

With so many options available, what’s your preferred way of getting to or from JFK, and which are your preferred payment methods to maximize value?

#6209. Aeromexico Adds New U.S. Routes, Flights

Aeromexico is again expanding its footprint in the U.S. with assistance from longtime partner Delta.

The carrier announced Monday that it will connect Mexico City with Nashville, Tennessee, New Orleans, and San Juan, Puerto Rico. None of the three cities currently has nonstop service to the Mexican capital.

All three connections will operate four times weekly. Service to Nashville will launch first, on June 13, 2027, followed by New Orleans on June 17 and San Juan on June 24.

Flights to Nashville and New Orleans will use Embraer E190 aircraft with 99 seats. For the route to San Juan, the airline will operate Boeing 737 MAX 8s with 166 seats.

Aeromexico will also launch a second daily service between Mexico City and Austin, Texas, on June 3.

“The addition of Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan to our network will allow us to provide more connectivity options, bringing our customers closer to destinations known for their unique identity and remarkable attractions,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeromexico, said in a news release. “Together with Delta, we continue to open markets and create more opportunities that strengthen tourism and ties between Mexico and the United States.”

Last month, the partners announced new routes from Mexico City to Orange County, California, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Portland, Oregon.

Alaska Airlines is rolling out a new invite-only status level called Atmos Global Concierge. Like the other major U.S. airlines that have such a tier, Alaska is not publicly disclosing what it takes to earn an invitation — though you can be sure it will require a lot of spending.

News of Alaska's new invite-only tier began spreading across aviation blogs Tuesday, and the company confirmed the move to TPG.

"Atmos Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program," said Alaska in a statement, " ...  that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most."

For now, this is a beta program rollout, so it's likely to change over time.

In addition to published top tiers, like American Airlines' AAdvantage Executive Platinum, Delta's Diamond Medallion and United Airlines' Premier 1K, all three major U.S. carriers offer an even higher level of status generally saved for the elites who spend the most with the airline (and some travel providers and C-level executives and celebrities).

American Airlines has ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has 360, and United Airlines has Global Services. And now Alaska has Atmos Global Concierge.

None of these airlines publicly disclose the exact qualification requirements for their invitation-only programs, which makes pontificating about what it takes to qualify something of an unofficial pastime for loyalty die-hards.

Among the theories: Invites are tied not only to flight spending, but also to credit card spending and even to your home airport. For example, an American Airlines frequent flyer based at the carrier's Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) hub might have a harder time securing an invitation than a similarly high-spending traveler based in a more competitive market.

Alaska isn't revealing the full list of benefits that come with its new status, but it did share some details with TPG.

"Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences," Alaska said.

That means help with travel disruptions, such as a next-flight guarantee and dedicated, specialized assistance.

Reports suggest other benefits include the ability to gift Gold status, a free Clear+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. Those invited are also reportedly being given Atmos Titanium status, even if they haven't already qualified organically this year.

If Alaska follows the lead of its larger competitors, additional perks could include VIP airport transfers, higher upgrade priority and expanded lounge access. However, Alaska has not confirmed those benefits.

As for what it might take to get invited to this special club, it will likely require spending tens of thousands of dollars on tickets. Some reports suggest the invitations appear to be targeted at potential customers for Alaska's new international routes with lie-flat business class. On the flip side, some Titanium-level Alaska flyers haven't been invited even after earning as many as 250,000 Alaska Atmos status points and buying international business-class tickets.

"Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows," Alaska told TPG.

While this won't mean much for most of us, it's still exciting to see a new layer of potential perks for some of Alaska's most loyal flyers. Alaska has been one of the most innovative U.S. airlines when it comes to loyalty, so it's an interesting development to see the carrier recognize its highest-value customers with an invite-only tier that matches what the other big global U.S. airlines have done.

Alaska is also now the only major U.S. airline that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles (though you can choose to earn status by spending). A new top-tier status level is another way the airline is differentiating itself.

The American Express® Gold Card is one of Amex’s most compelling cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and it currently has a best-ever welcome offer that’s as high as 100,000 bonus points, making it a great time to apply. In this post, I’d like to go over all the details of the current Amex Gold Card bonus, including who is eligible, and why you might want to apply.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

The Amex Gold Card currently has a lucrative bonus, marketed as being as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards bonus points after spending $8,000 within the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Gold Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 100,000 points are worth $1,700, making it among the best welcome offers out there. Of course that assumes you’re eligible for this offer, which not everyone will be.

As a point of comparison, previously the Amex Gold Card bonus offered as high as 60,000 points, so this is a lot better. As a matter of fact, the current Amex Gold Card offer is potentially the best publicly available one that we’ve seen.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to roughly 20 airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Blue, All Nippon Airways Mileage Club, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give a couple of quick examples:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, you may not be eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had American Express Platinum Card® (learn more).

This is a reason to pick up the Amex Gold Card before you pick up the Amex Platinum Card. That’s because you’re potentially eligible for the Amex Platinum Card welcome offer if you have or have had the Amex Gold Card, while the inverse may not be true.

On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a couple of additional things to note:

The Amex Gold Card also offers Hertz Five Star status just for having the card (enrollment required), which can get you valuable perks.
